fields.document: {"version":3,"name":"Abbaye de Créteil","description":"A utopian community of writers and artists founded in October 1906 in the Paris suburb of Créteil, where the members lived together and ran their own printing press. Duhamel, Vildrac, Arcos, Gleizes and Mercereau belonged to it, and it lasted about fourteen months. Its importance is out of proportion to its length: the group is where Unanimism and part of early Cubist theory were argued out.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-abbaye-de-creteil","wd-q2275355"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-abbaye-de-creteil","wd-q2275355"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-abbaye-de-creteil","title":"Abbaye de Créteil — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbaye_de_Cr%C3%A9teil"},{"id":"wd-q2275355","title":"Abbaye de Créteil (Q2275355) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2275355"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Abecedariuses","description":"Poems whose lines or stanzas begin with the letters of the alphabet in order. Several psalms are built this way in Hebrew, and the device carried into medieval Latin hymns and into vernacular verse. The alphabet supplies both the length and the order, so the poet composes against a fixed frame.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named formal constraint with a body of work from scripture onward; LCGFT files it under Acrostics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-abecedariuses","wp-abecedarius"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"acrostics-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Abecedariuses under Acrostics; the alphabet is read down the initial letters in the same way.","sourceIds":["lcgft-abecedariuses","wp-abecedarius"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-abecedariuses","title":"Abecedariuses — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026211"},{"id":"wp-abecedarius","title":"Abecedarius — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abecedarius"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Abstract art","description":"Painting and sculpture composed from shape, colour and line without depicting a subject from the world. The picture is built on relations between its own marks, so the reading of it starts inside the frame. Wikipedia files non-figurative, non-objective and non-representational art alongside the term as near synonyms.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A direction with a large body of painting and sculpture in several national traditions and a century of argument about its boundary.","sourceIds":["wp-abstract-art","wd-q128115"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-abstract-art","title":"Abstract art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_art"},{"id":"wd-q128115","title":"abstract art (Q128115) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q128115"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Abstract Expressionism","description":"The American painting that emerged after the Second World War and dominated the 1950s, in two broad manners: the gestural attack of Pollock, de Kooning and Kline, and the large simple fields of Rothko, Newman and Still. It was the first American movement to take the international lead from Paris. Scale, surface and the artist's presence in the mark are its recurring terms.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-abstract-expressionism","wd-q177725","aat-300022099"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"expressionism","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as a subclass of Expressionism.","sourceIds":["wd-q177725"]},{"cellId":"abstract-art","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as a subclass of abstract art.","sourceIds":["wd-q177725"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-abstract-expressionism","title":"Abstract expressionism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_expressionism"},{"id":"wd-q177725","title":"abstract expressionism (Q177725) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q177725"},{"id":"aat-300022099","title":"Abstract Expressionism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300022099","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300022099"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Abstraction-Création","description":"A loose Paris association founded in 1931 to hold abstraction together against the pull of Breton's Surrealism, with several hundred members at its height. It published an annual, ran exhibitions and gathered geometric and non-geometric abstraction alike. It lasted until about 1936 and was a network more than a style.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-abstraction-creation","wd-q333316"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"abstract-art","explanation":"Its Wikidata item gives its movement as abstract art.","sourceIds":["wd-q333316"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-abstraction-creation","title":"Abstraction-Création — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstraction-Création"},{"id":"wd-q333316","title":"Abstraction-Création (Q333316) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q333316"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Abstract Photography","description":"Photography that does not read as a picture of a recognisable object, made by isolating a fragment, exploiting process, working without a camera or intervening in the material. Its line runs from Coburn's vortographs and Man Ray's rayographs to contemporary camera-less work. The medium's assumed link to the visible world is exactly what the practice tests.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-abstract-photography","wd-q333327"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-abstract-photography","title":"Abstract photography — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_photography"},{"id":"wd-q333327","title":"abstract photography (Q333327) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q333327"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Academic art","description":"Painting and sculpture made under the influence of the European art academies, with a settled hierarchy of subject, a taught sequence from drawing to painting, and history painting at the top. Its French nineteenth-century form, taught at the École des Beaux-Arts and judged at the Salon, is the version most argued with. It was displaced by the movements that defined themselves against it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-academic-art","wd-q189458","aat-300056465"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-academic-art","title":"Academic art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art"},{"id":"wd-q189458","title":"academic art (Q189458) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q189458"},{"id":"aat-300056465","title":"Academic art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300056465","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300056465"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Acmeism","description":"A Russian poetic school formed around 1912 by Nikolay Gumilev and Sergei Gorodetsky, with Akhmatova and Mandelstam its greatest poets. It wanted compact form, clear statement and the solid weight of things, in reaction against Symbolism's vagueness. Mandelstam called it a yearning for world culture, and the group's Guild of Poets met to criticise each other's work line by line.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-acmeist-poetry","wd-q420245"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-acmeist-poetry","title":"Acmeist poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acmeist_poetry"},{"id":"wd-q420245","title":"Acmeist poetry (Q420245) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q420245"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Acrostics (Poetry)","description":"Poems in which the initial letters of the lines, read downward, spell a word or a message. The device is ancient, found in Hebrew scripture and in Greek and Latin verse, and it has been used for dedications, signatures and concealment. The hidden text is a second poem the reader has to notice.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named formal device with a body of work across many centuries and languages; LCGFT files Abecedariuses under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-acrostics-poetry","wp-acrostic"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"visual-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Visual poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-acrostics-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-acrostics-poetry","title":"Acrostics (Poetry) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026214"},{"id":"wp-acrostic","title":"Acrostic — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrostic"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Action and adventure comics","description":"Comics built on danger, pursuit and physical action. The Library of Congress files space operas in comics under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A comics genre with a large serial canon; the Library of Congress files it under Comics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-action-and-adventure-comics"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"The Library of Congress record gives Comics (Graphic works) as its broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-action-and-adventure-comics"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-action-and-adventure-comics","title":"Action and adventure comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026216"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Action and adventure fiction","description":"Fiction driven by danger and physical action, where the pace of the plot matters as much as character or setting. The Library of Congress files space operas and subterranean fiction under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A genre with a large popular canon; the Library of Congress files it under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-action-and-adventure-fiction","wp-adventure-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"The Library of Congress record gives Fiction as its broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-action-and-adventure-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Returns from B6, which declined it as \"a plot-mode umbrella from readers' advisory\". Space operas and subterranean fiction are live cells whose records give this heading as their broader term. Strike this cell to keep the earlier ruling."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-action-and-adventure-fiction","title":"Action and adventure fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026217"},{"id":"wp-adventure-fiction","title":"Adventure fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Action Painting","description":"A manner of Abstract Expressionist painting in which paint is dripped, thrown or dragged onto the canvas and the physical act of painting is left legible in the result. Harold Rosenberg named it in 1952, describing the canvas as an arena to act in. It is also called gestural abstraction.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-action-painting","wd-q217213","aat-300112061"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"abstract-expressionism","explanation":"Its Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus record gives Abstract Expressionist as its broader concept: action painting names the gestural wing of that movement.","sourceIds":["aat-300112061"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-action-painting","title":"Action painting — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_painting"},{"id":"wd-q217213","title":"action painting (Q217213) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q217213"},{"id":"aat-300112061","title":"Action Painting — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300112061","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300112061"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Advice column","description":"A reader's question and a named columnist's answer, printed together. The Athenian Mercury ran the first in 1690 and the form has been continuous since. An answer is written to one person and read by everyone, so it has to be particular and quotable at once. Columnist personas are durable enough that they often outlive the writers behind them.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A newspaper and magazine form running continuously since 1690.","sourceIds":["wp-advice-column"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[{"cellId":"editorials","label":"shares a page","explanation":"Both are recurring signed newspaper columns written to a fixed length against a deadline.","sourceIds":["wp-advice-column"]}],"questions":["No parent yet. The natural one is a Columns cell, and the Library of Congress has no such heading."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-advice-column","title":"Advice column — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_column"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Aestheticism","description":"A late nineteenth-century movement holding that art exists for its own beauty. Whistler, Rossetti, Wilde and Beardsley are its figures, and it extends into interiors, wallpaper, book design and dress. Art for art's sake is its slogan and the position it had to defend.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-aestheticism","wd-q256922","aat-300018124"]},{"map":"writing","explanation":"The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-aestheticism","wd-q256922","aat-300018124"]},{"map":"design","explanation":"The movement worked in design as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-aestheticism","wd-q256922","aat-300018124"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-aestheticism","title":"Aestheticism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aestheticism"},{"id":"wd-q256922","title":"Aestheticism (Q256922) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q256922"},{"id":"aat-300018124","title":"Aestheticism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300018124","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300018124"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Afrofuturism","description":"A cultural aesthetic and philosophy that reads the African diaspora through science, technology and speculation, across music, writing, film and visual art. Mark Dery named it in 1993, gathering Sun Ra, George Clinton, Samuel Delany and Octavia Butler as one project. The writing cells for fiction, poetry and comics all descend from this direction.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-afrofuturism","wd-q3362516"]},{"map":"writing","explanation":"The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-afrofuturism","wd-q3362516"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as a subclass of science fiction.","sourceIds":["wd-q3362516"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Afrofuturist fiction, poetry and comics were written in earlier batches. Making this cell their shared parent is a D38 insertion and is left for a later batch."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-afrofuturism","title":"Afrofuturism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrofuturism"},{"id":"wd-q3362516","title":"Afrofuturism (Q3362516) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3362516"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Afrofuturist comics","description":"Comics written from Black diasporic experience in which technology serves Black freedom and the future is already occupied. Black Panther from 1966 is the earliest widely read instance, and later creators have worked the material deliberately as Afrofuturism. Drawn worlds let the aesthetic be stated directly.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Afrofuturist argument worked out in comics. The cell Afrofuturist fiction works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-afrofuturist-comics","wp-afrofuturism"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction-comics","explanation":"LCGFT files Afrofuturist comics under Science fiction comics; the technology and the future are its premises.","sourceIds":["lcgft-afrofuturist-comics","wp-afrofuturism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Afrofuturist fiction, Afrofuturist poetry and Afrofuturist comics. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-afrofuturist-comics","title":"Afrofuturist comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2020026011"},{"id":"wp-afrofuturism","title":"Afrofuturism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrofuturism"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Afrofuturist fiction","description":"Science fiction written from Black diasporic experience, in which technology is a resource for Black freedom and the future is a place Black people already occupy. Mark Dery named the tendency in 1993, reading Samuel Delany and Octavia Butler alongside the sonic worlds of Sun Ra and George Clinton as one project. The Library of Congress separates fiction rooted in African ground under the heading Africanfuturist fiction.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named movement with a coined name and a critical literature, which LCGFT files under Science fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-afrofuturist-fiction","wp-afrofuturism"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Afrofuturist fiction under Science fiction; it works with the same premises about technology and social change.","sourceIds":["lcgft-afrofuturist-fiction","wp-afrofuturism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-afrofuturist-fiction","title":"Afrofuturist fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2020026016"},{"id":"wp-afrofuturism","title":"Afrofuturism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrofuturism"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Afrofuturist poetry","description":"Poetry written from Black diasporic experience that puts Black people in the future and treats technology as a means of freedom. It shares its sources with the fiction, and the sonic and performance traditions around Sun Ra and dub give the verse a different set of resources. Tracie Morris, Douglas Kearney and others work in it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Afrofuturist argument worked out in verse. The cell Afrofuturist fiction works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-afrofuturist-poetry","wp-afrofuturism"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Science fiction poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-afrofuturist-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Afrofuturist fiction and Afrofuturist poetry. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-afrofuturist-poetry","title":"Afrofuturist poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2024026071"},{"id":"wp-afrofuturism","title":"Afrofuturism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrofuturism"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Alcaics","description":"A four-line stanza of Greek lyric attributed to Alcaeus of Mytilene around 600 BC: two eleven-syllable lines, a nine-syllable line and a ten-syllable line. Horace made it the workhorse of his Odes, and it was imitated in Latin for centuries and in modern languages by Klopstock, Hölderlin and Tennyson.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alcaics","wp-alcaic-stanza"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alcaics"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-alcaics","title":"Alcaics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2020026065"},{"id":"wp-alcaic-stanza","title":"Alcaic stanza — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcaic_stanza"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Alexandrines","description":"Verse lines of twelve syllables with a break in the middle, the standard line of French poetry from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth. The name comes from a twelfth-century Roman d'Alexandre, and the equivalent lines in German, Dutch, Polish and English each work slightly differently. In English the alexandrine is an iambic hexameter, used chiefly to close a stanza.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named metrical form that organised the verse of a whole national tradition; LCGFT files it under Iambic poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alexandrines","wp-alexandrine"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"iambic-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Alexandrines under Iambic poetry; the English alexandrine is an iambic hexameter.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alexandrines","wp-alexandrine"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-alexandrines","title":"Alexandrines — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026094"},{"id":"wp-alexandrine","title":"Alexandrine — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandrine"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Allegories","description":"Works whose people, places and events stand for something else, so that the story reads twice: once as narrative and once as the moral, political or doctrinal argument it carries. The Library of Congress files autos sacramentales, bestiaries and morality plays under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form worked in prose, verse and on the stage, with a canon that reaches The Pilgrim's Progress.","sourceIds":["lcgft-allegories","wp-allegory"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["The Library of Congress files Allegories under Instructional and educational works, a cataloguing container that is not a cell, so this cell has no parent. If a better parent exists, name it."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-allegories","title":"Allegories — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026218"},{"id":"wp-allegory","title":"Allegory — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegory"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Alternative histories (Comics)","description":"Comics whose premise is that a historical event went the other way. The changed world can be shown, so one panel establishes the divergence and the story proceeds. Watchmen is the widely read case.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The counterfactual premise worked out in comics. The live cell Alternative histories (Fiction) works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alternative-histories-comics","wp-alternate-history"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Comics; the direction is worked out through the form's own panel grammar.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alternative-histories-comics","wp-alternate-history"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Alternative histories (Fiction), Alternative histories (Drama) and Alternative histories (Comics). The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-alternative-histories-comics","title":"Alternative histories (Comics) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026154"},{"id":"wp-alternate-history","title":"Alternate history — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternate_history"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Alternative histories (Drama)","description":"Plays whose premise is that a historical event went the other way, and which follow what that would have meant. The stage form takes the argument close in, usually to a room and a small number of people who have to live in the changed world. LCGFT keeps plays presenting nonfictional alternative outcomes separate, as Counterfactual histories.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The counterfactual premise worked out in dramatic form. The live cell Alternative histories (Fiction) works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alternative-histories-drama","wp-alternate-history"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alternative-histories-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Alternative histories (Fiction) and Alternative histories (Drama). The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-alternative-histories-drama","title":"Alternative histories (Drama) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026155"},{"id":"wp-alternate-history","title":"Alternate history — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternate_history"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Alternative histories (Fiction)","description":"Fiction in which one historical event turns out differently and the story follows the consequences. A point of divergence from the record is the standing device; since the 1950s the genre has borrowed time travel and parallel timelines from science fiction. The Sidewise Awards have recognised it since 1996.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A speculative genre defined by a structural device, the point of divergence.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alternative-histories-fiction","wp-alternate-history"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-alternative-histories-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Is a premise a technique? Proposed because the point of divergence is a structural device with its own body of work and awards."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-alternative-histories-fiction","title":"Alternative histories (Fiction) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026220"},{"id":"wp-alternate-history","title":"Alternate history — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternate_history"},{"id":"wp-sidewise-awards","title":"Sidewise Awards for Alternate History — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidewise_Awards_for_Alternate_History"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Alternative literature","description":"Alt-lit, a writing movement of the late 2000s and 2010s that grew out of internet culture and self-publishing. Its manner is flat, deadpan and confessional, mixing autofiction with the register of chat and social media, and it circulated through small presses and personal accounts. The scene largely dispersed after abuse allegations against several of its central figures.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Atticism","description":"A rhetorical and linguistic movement from the first century BC that held up the Attic prose of fifth- and fourth-century Athens as the standard, against the living Koine of its own day. It produced lexica of approved words and shaped Greek literary prose for centuries afterwards. The programme is deliberate archaism, and it made written Greek diverge permanently from spoken Greek.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-atticism","wd-q746783"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-atticism","title":"Atticism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atticism"},{"id":"wd-q746783","title":"Atticism (Q746783) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q746783"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Aubades","description":"Poems of lovers parting at dawn, in which the coming light is the enemy. The troubadour alba is the medieval form, and the situation recurs in Donne, in Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet and in Larkin, who turned it towards the fear of death. The fixed situation makes it a genre.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named lyric genre with a fixed dramatic situation, a medieval origin and a continuous canon; LCGFT files it under Lyric poetry and Love poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-aubades","wp-aubade"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"lyric-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Aubades under Lyric poetry; the poem is a single voice at a single moment.","sourceIds":["lcgft-aubades","wp-aubade"]},{"cellId":"love-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Love poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-aubades"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-aubades","title":"Aubades — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026004"},{"id":"wp-aubade","title":"Aubade — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubade"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Autobiographical comics","description":"Comics in which the maker draws their own life, and therefore draws themselves. The practice came out of the underground comix movement with Justin Green and Robert Crumb and became a major strand through Spiegelman, Bechdel and Satrapi. Choosing how to draw yourself is a decision prose autobiography never has to make.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The autobiographical practice worked out in comics, where self-portrayal becomes a formal decision; LCGFT files it under Autobiographies and Biographical comics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-comics","wp-list-of-autobiographical-comics"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"autobiographies","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Autobiographies as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-comics"]},{"cellId":"biographical-comics","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Biographical comics as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-comics"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["The independent reference is Wikipedia's list article, which defines the form in its opening. A page on the practice would be better if one exists.","Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Autobiographical fiction and Autobiographical comics. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-autobiographical-comics","title":"Autobiographical comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026229"},{"id":"wp-list-of-autobiographical-comics","title":"List of autobiographical comics — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_autobiographical_comics"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Autobiographical fiction","description":"Fiction built from the author's own life, with invented characters and invented events mixed into remembered ones, and no claim that the reader can tell which is which. Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man and Proust's In Search of Lost Time are the standing English and French cases, and the contemporary practice is often called autofiction. The Library of Congress files works that present themselves as autobiographies with fictional narrators separately, as Fictional autobiographies.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A technique for making a work, defined by how life material and invention are combined; its LCGFT parent Biographical fiction was declined in pass 1 as subject-defined.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-fiction","wp-autobiographical-novel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"biographical-fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Biographical fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-autobiographical-fiction","title":"Autobiographical fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026231"},{"id":"wp-autobiographical-novel","title":"Autobiographical novel — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobiographical_novel"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Autobiographical poetry","description":"Poems in which the poet's own life is the material. The Library of Congress files confessional poetry under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Verse written from the poet's own life; the Library of Congress files it under both Autobiographies and Biographical poetry, and files confessional poetry under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"autobiographies","explanation":"The Library of Congress record gives Autobiographies as one of its two broader terms.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-poetry"]},{"cellId":"biographical-poetry","explanation":"The Library of Congress record gives Biographical poetry as its other broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographical-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-autobiographical-poetry","title":"Autobiographical poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026232"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Autobiographies","description":"A person's account of their own whole life, written by them. Augustine's Confessions around 400 is treated as one of the first in the West, and the line runs through Rousseau to the present. The word itself dates from 1797, long after the practice. The claim on the reader is that this happened and the writer was there, so memory and its unreliability are both in the register.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The practice runs back to late antiquity, and the word for it dates from 1797.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographies","wp-autobiography"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"biographies","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Biographies as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autobiographies"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Biographies is the intermediate Library of Congress heading and has no cell here. Add it if a reader would expect the step."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-autobiographies","title":"Autobiographies — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026047"},{"id":"wp-autobiography","title":"Autobiography — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobiography"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Autofiction","description":"Fiction written from the author's own life and published as fiction, usually with the author's name on the narrator. Serge Doubrovsky named it in 1977, for his novel Fils. It reads flat, close and digressive, and the interest lies in the gap between what happened and what the book says happened. The reader is meant to notice that the question of truth is unsettled and to read on anyway.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form named in literary criticism in 1977 and written since by many hands.","sourceIds":["wp-autofiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"autobiographical-fiction","explanation":"It is fictionalised autobiography, which the autobiographical fiction heading covers, and this cell is the narrower manner inside it.","sourceIds":["wp-autofiction"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"fictional-autobiographies","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Both put a life story in a novel's first person. The fictional autobiography invents the narrator, and autofiction gives the narrator the author's own name.","sourceIds":["wp-autofiction"]}],"questions":["Wikipedia's account is thin and Doubrovsky's 1977 naming is the whole of it. A scholarly reference on autofiction would strengthen this cell.","The live Fictional autobiographies cell already names autofiction inside its scope. If this cell stands, that sentence should come out of the parent."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-autofiction","title":"Autofiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autofiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Autos sacramentales","description":"One-act allegorical religious plays performed in Spain and Spanish America on the feast of Corpus Christi, on carts in the street, from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries. The characters are personified abstractions and the argument is always the Eucharist. Calderón wrote about eighty of them and is the form's central author; Charles III banned them in 1765.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic tradition with a defined period, a central author, a fixed allegorical method and a documented performance practice; LCGFT files it under Religious drama and Allegories.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autos-sacramentales","wp-autos-sacramentales"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"allegories","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Allegories as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autos-sacramentales"]},{"cellId":"religious-drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Religious drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-autos-sacramentales"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-autos-sacramentales","title":"Autos sacramentales — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026233"},{"id":"wp-autos-sacramentales","title":"Autos sacramentales — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autos_sacramentales"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Avadana stories","description":"Buddhist narratives that tie a virtuous or wicked deed in a past life to what happens in a present one, usually told by the Buddha to explain a situation in front of him. They are the neighbours of the Jataka stories and differ mainly in whose past lives are being told. The frame is the form: a present event, a past cause, an identification.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named narrative genre with a Sanskrit corpus and a stated structural frame; LCGFT files it directly under Literature.","sourceIds":["lcgft-avadana-stories","wp-avadana"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"biographies","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Biographies as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-avadana-stories"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-avadana-stories","title":"Avadana stories — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026109"},{"id":"wp-avadana","title":"Avadana — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avadana"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Azharot","description":"Hebrew liturgical poems versifying the 613 commandments, recited at Shavuot in several rites. The earliest known examples are anonymous and old, and Solomon ibn Gabirol wrote the best-known later ones. Putting law into verse is a mnemonic as much as a devotional act.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named liturgical verse genre with a fixed subject, named authors and a continuing place in the rite; LCGFT files it under Liturgical poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-azharot","wp-azharot"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"liturgical-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Liturgical poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-azharot"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-azharot","title":"Azharot — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026234"},{"id":"wp-azharot","title":"Azharot — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azharot"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Bad Painting","description":"A trend in American figurative painting named by the curator Marcia Tucker for her 1978 exhibition at the New Museum, gathering fourteen mostly unknown painters. The work is deliberately awkward, cartoonish and unrefined, made against the smoothness of Minimal and Conceptual art. The scare quotes are part of the name: the badness is the position.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-bad-painting","wd-q2878528","aat-300263413"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-bad-painting","title":"Bad Painting — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Painting"},{"id":"wd-q2878528","title":"Bad Painting (Q2878528) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2878528"},{"id":"aat-300263413","title":"Bad Painting — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300263413","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300263413"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Ballades (Poetry)","description":"A French fixed form of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries: three stanzas on the same rhymes, each ending in a refrain line, followed by a shorter envoy addressed to a patron or prince. Machaut set them to music, and the ballade was one of the three formes fixes most often sung between the late thirteenth and the fifteenth century. LCGFT keeps the ballade distinct from the ballad.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-ballades-poetry","wp-ballade"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-ballades-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-ballades-poetry","title":"Ballades (Poetry) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026235"},{"id":"wp-ballade","title":"Ballade (forme fixe) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_(forme_fixe)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Barbizon School","description":"The French painters who settled around the village of Barbizon from the 1830s and took the forest and the working countryside as their subject. They worked from studies made outdoors, kept the tonal range low and earthy, and treated an ordinary field or a stand of trees as sufficient without a narrative reason.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named school with a documented body of work.","sourceIds":["wp-barbizon","aat-barbizon"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"realism-art-movement","explanation":"The painters are described as part of an art movement advancing Realism, working inside the Romanticism then dominant.","sourceIds":["wp-barbizon"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"impressionism","label":"influenced","explanation":"The Impressionists took up working from outdoor studies of ordinary landscape and extended it to painting the whole picture outdoors.","sourceIds":["wp-barbizon"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-barbizon","title":"Barbizon school — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbizon_school"},{"id":"aat-barbizon","title":"Barbizon School — Getty AAT 300264658","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264658"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-01a068cd-9c07-7892-9b1a-0aef3c21939c","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Barbizon school\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-barbizon"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-01a068ce-425c-71a3-8d76-f6d7ea2ffd78","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Barbizon plein-air painting\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-barbizon"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-01a068cd-9e02-7e91-b9b6-ac3cf8fbe0e3","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Barbizon school\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-barbizon"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-01a068ce-4455-7d93-be52-e3809e59a41d","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Barbizon plein-air painting\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-barbizon"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Barong plays","description":"Balinese dance dramas staging the contest between Barong, a protective lion-like creature, and the witch Rangda, performed with gamelan and masks. {"version":3,"name":"Bay Area Figurative Movement","description":"A San Francisco Bay Area movement of the 1950s and 1960s in which painters trained in Abstract Expressionism turned back to the figure while keeping the loaded brush. David Park's break is its founding moment, and Diebenkorn, Bischoff and Joan Brown followed. The paint handling stays abstract while the subject returns.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-bay-area-figurative-movement","wd-q3577822"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"abstract-expressionism","explanation":"The painters trained in Abstract Expressionism and kept its handling when they returned to the figure, which is why the result is called a hybrid.","sourceIds":["wp-bay-area-figurative-movement"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-bay-area-figurative-movement","title":"Bay Area Figurative Movement — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Area_Figurative_Movement"},{"id":"wd-q3577822","title":"Bay Area Figurative Movement (Q3577822) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3577822"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Beast epics","description":"Long narrative poems in which animals hold court, plead, cheat and take revenge in a mirror of human society. The Reynard cycle in Dutch, French, German and English, and the Latin Ysengrimus behind it, are the main body, written from the twelfth century onward. The satire works because the animals keep their fixed characters across many separate poems.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named narrative tradition with a multilingual cycle, a dated corpus and a satirical purpose; LCGFT files it under Narrative poetry and Satirical literature.","sourceIds":["lcgft-beast-epics","wp-reynard-the-fox"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"satirical-literature","explanation":"LCGFT files Beast epics under Satirical literature; the animal court exists to ridicule the human one.","sourceIds":["lcgft-beast-epics","wp-reynard-the-fox"]},{"cellId":"narrative-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Narrative poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-beast-epics"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-beast-epics","title":"Beast epics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2020026038"},{"id":"wp-reynard-the-fox","title":"Reynard the Fox — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reynard_the_Fox"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Beijing East Village","description":"An avant-garde community that formed in 1993 in a cheap settlement on Beijing's eastern margin, where Zhang Huan, Ma Liuming and the photographer Rong Rong made and recorded extreme performance work. It was broken up by the authorities in 1994. Its record is largely photographic, which shapes how the work is known.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-beijing-east-village","wd-q4881125"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-beijing-east-village","title":"Beijing East Village — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_East_Village"},{"id":"wd-q4881125","title":"Beijing East Village (Q4881125) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q4881125"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Bengal School of Art","description":"An Indian movement originating in Calcutta and Santiniketan in the early twentieth century, which turned from British academic training to Mughal and Rajput miniature and to Japanese wash technique. {"version":3,"name":"Blogs","description":"Dated posts on a site, newest first, usually with one hand behind them. Print production fell in the 1990s as choice-based stories moved to screens.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A printed narrative form defined by its branching structure and second-person address.","sourceIds":["lcgft-choose-your-own-stories","wp-gamebook"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-choose-your-own-stories"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"hypertext-fiction","label":"influenced","explanation":"Gamebooks influenced hypertext fiction; the numbered branching page is the printed ancestor of the link.","sourceIds":["wp-gamebook"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-choose-your-own-stories","title":"Choose-your-own stories — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026259"},{"id":"wp-gamebook","title":"Gamebook — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamebook"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Choose-your-own-story comics","description":"Comics that branch, where the reader picks an option and is sent to another panel, page or link. Webcomics and print both use it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The branching-choice structure worked out in comics. {"version":3,"name":"Christmas pantomimes","description":"British Christmas stage entertainment built on a fairy tale, with a set of conventions that audiences enforce: a man playing the dame, a woman playing the principal boy, audience call and response, topical jokes and a slapstick routine. It grows out of the eighteenth-century harlequinade and settled into its present form in the Victorian theatre. The conventions are the form and are broken only deliberately.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named theatrical form with conventions an audience knows and enforces, and a documented history; LCGFT files it under Christmas plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-christmas-pantomimes","wp-pantomime"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"christmas-plays","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Christmas plays as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-christmas-pantomimes"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-christmas-pantomimes","title":"Christmas pantomimes — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026113"},{"id":"wp-pantomime","title":"Pantomime — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantomime"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

The Library of Congress files Christmas pantomimes under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A seasonal body of stage work reaching back to the thirteenth century; the Library of Congress files it under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-christmas-plays","wp-nativity-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"The Library of Congress record gives Drama as its broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-christmas-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-christmas-plays","title":"Christmas plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026061"},{"id":"wp-nativity-play","title":"Nativity play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nativity_play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Cinquains","description":"Five-line poems and stanzas, and in particular the form Adelaide Crapsey devised while reading Japanese verse and published in Verse (1915): five unrhymed lines of two, four, six, eight and two syllables. The word once meant any five-line stanza; the Crapsey cinquain gave it a fixed shape that classrooms and poets still use.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-cinquains","wp-cinquain"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-cinquains"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-cinquains","title":"Cinquains — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026260"},{"id":"wp-cinquain","title":"Cinquain — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinquain"},{"id":"wp-adelaide-crapsey","title":"Adelaide Crapsey — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide_Crapsey"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"City mysteries","description":"Popular nineteenth-century novels that take a reader down through the layers of a city to the crime, poverty and corruption underneath. Eugène Sue's Les Mystères de Paris, serialised from 1842, set off imitations in London, New York, Berlin and dozens of other cities within a decade. The form promises exposure: a guide, a descent, and a claim to be showing what respectable readers do not see.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named nineteenth-century genre with a founding text, a wave of imitations and a defined period; LCGFT files it under Detective and mystery fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-city-mysteries","wp-city-mysteries"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"detective-and-mystery-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files City mysteries under Detective and mystery fiction; the descent into the city's underside is organised as an uncovering.","sourceIds":["lcgft-city-mysteries","wp-city-mysteries"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-city-mysteries","title":"City mysteries — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2024026087"},{"id":"wp-city-mysteries","title":"City mysteries — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_mysteries"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Classical Prose Movement","description":"A Chinese movement of the Tang and Song dynasties, led by Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan and later by Ouyang Xiu, that rejected the ornamental parallel prose of the preceding centuries and argued for the plainer prose of the pre-Han classics. Its case was that rigid antithesis and rare allusion had put form ahead of what a sentence is for. It settled how literary Chinese prose was written for the next thousand years.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-classical-prose-movement","wd-q5128310"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-classical-prose-movement","title":"Classical Prose Movement — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Prose_Movement"},{"id":"wd-q5128310","title":"Classical Prose Movement (Q5128310) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q5128310"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Clerihews","description":"Four-line biographical jokes in two rhyming couplets, the first line being the subject's name and one half of a rhyme. Edmund Clerihew Bentley invented the form as a schoolboy in 1890 and it is named after him. The metre is deliberately lopsided, which is part of the joke.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with a dated invention, a named inventor and a stated set of rules; LCGFT files it under Humorous poetry, which pass 2 declined as a tone umbrella.","sourceIds":["lcgft-clerihews","wp-clerihew"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"humorous-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Humorous poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-clerihews"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-clerihews","title":"Clerihews — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026261"},{"id":"wp-clerihew","title":"Clerihew — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clerihew"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Climate fiction","description":"Fiction in which a changing climate is the condition the story takes place in, drawing on climate science for its premises. The shorthand cli-fi was coined by the journalist Dan Bloom around 2007 and picked up quickly by reviewers and by teaching. Its settings range from the near present to deep future, and it is often argued about as a form of persuasion.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named movement with a coined name, a critical literature and a fast-growing body of work; LCGFT files it under Ecofiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-climate-fiction","wp-climate-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"ecofiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Climate fiction under Ecofiction; it is the branch of ecofiction whose premise is climatic change.","sourceIds":["lcgft-climate-fiction","wp-climate-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-climate-fiction","title":"Climate fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2021026022"},{"id":"wp-climate-fiction","title":"Climate fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Closet drama","description":"Plays written to be read instead of staged, keeping dramatic form while giving up the stage's constraints. Seneca's tragedies are read this way, and the Romantic period produced them deliberately in Byron, Shelley and Goethe, whose Faust exceeds any theatre of its time. Freedom from staging is what the form is for: scale, interiority and length can go where performance could not follow.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named form defined by how the work is meant to be received, with a canon and a critical literature; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-closet-drama","wp-closet-drama"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-closet-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-closet-drama","title":"Closet drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2024026010"},{"id":"wp-closet-drama","title":"Closet drama — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closet_drama"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"CoBrA","description":"A European avant-garde group active from 1948 to 1951, its name assembled by Christian Dotremont from Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam. Asger Jorn, Karel Appel and Constant painted fast, bright and deliberately childlike, drawing on folk art, myth and children's drawing against what they saw as French formalism. It broke up quickly and its influence lasted much longer.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-cobra-art-movement","wd-q212611"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-cobra-art-movement","title":"COBRA (art movement) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COBRA_(art_movement)"},{"id":"wd-q212611","title":"COBRA (Q212611) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q212611"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Colab","description":"Collaborative Projects, a New York artists' group formed in the late 1970s out of open meetings, which organised exhibitions in disused buildings, ran a cable programme and worked without a hierarchy. The Times Square Show of 1980 is its best-known event. Self-organisation was the method and the point.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-colab","wd-q1107572"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-colab","title":"Colab — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colab"},{"id":"wd-q1107572","title":"Colab (Q1107572) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1107572"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Comédies-ballets","description":"A French Baroque form that alternates spoken comedy with sung and danced interludes, made for the court of Louis XIV. Molière and Lully invented it with Les Fâcheux in 1661 and refined it through Le Bourgeois gentilhomme in 1670. The interludes are written into the play's argument, so the dancing carries part of the plot.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named genre with a dated invention, named collaborators and a defined structural rule; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedies-ballets","wp-comedie-ballet"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedies-ballets"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-comedies-ballets","title":"Comédies-ballets — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2017026083"},{"id":"wp-comedie-ballet","title":"Comédie-ballet — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comédie-ballet"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Comedies of humours","description":"English comedy of the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries in which each character is ruled by one dominant trait, on the model of the four bodily humours. Ben Jonson made it a programme in Every Man in His Humour and Every Man out of His Humour, and the plots work by setting fixed obsessions against each other. Character is deliberately flat: the comedy is in the collision.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic genre with a programmatic author, a period and a stated method of characterisation; LCGFT files it under Comedy plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedies-of-humours","wp-comedy-of-humours"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comedy-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Comedies of humours under Comedy plays; they are comedies distinguished by how they build character.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedies-of-humours","wp-comedy-of-humours"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-comedies-of-humours","title":"Comedies of humours — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026262"},{"id":"wp-comedy-of-humours","title":"Comedy of humours — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_of_humours"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Comedies of manners","description":"Comedy that satirises the code of a particular society by putting its wit and its hypocrisies on stage. The English Restoration line of Etherege, Wycherley and Congreve is the classic case, revived by Sheridan, Wilde and Coward. Dialogue carries almost all of it: the plot exists to give the talk somewhere to happen.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic genre with a canon across three centuries and a stated reliance on dialogue; LCGFT files it under Comedy plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedies-of-manners","wp-comedy-of-manners"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comedy-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Comedies of manners under Comedy plays; the form satirises through comic action and wit.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedies-of-manners","wp-comedy-of-manners"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-comedies-of-manners","title":"Comedies of manners — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026263"},{"id":"wp-comedy-of-manners","title":"Comedy of manners — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_of_manners"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Comedy plays","description":"Drama with a light or humorous movement, in which the characters come through and the ending restores or remakes a community. It is one of the two Greek dramatic kinds and has been treated as a form with rules ever since, from Aristophanes and Menander through Roman comedy to the European traditions that follow them. The movement of the plot, more than the jokes, makes a play a comedy.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form root of drama with a continuous history and its own poetics; LCGFT files Commedia dell'arte, Comedies of manners, Comedy sketches and eleven more terms under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedy-plays","wp-comedy-drama"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedy-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-comedy-plays","title":"Comedy plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026264"},{"id":"wp-comedy-drama","title":"Comedy (drama) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_(drama)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Comedy sketches","description":"Short self-contained comic scenes, usually between one and ten minutes, performed as part of a longer bill. The form comes out of music hall, vaudeville and revue and moved into radio and television, where a troupe writes and plays a run of them in sequence. A sketch is built around one premise and ends when the premise is used up.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A performance form with a stated length, a stated structure and a documented line from music hall to broadcast; LCGFT files it under Comedy plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedy-sketches","wp-sketch-comedy"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comedy-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Comedy sketches under Comedy plays; a sketch is a short comic play.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comedy-sketches","wp-sketch-comedy"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-comedy-sketches","title":"Comedy sketches — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026265"},{"id":"wp-sketch-comedy","title":"Sketch comedy — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sketch_comedy"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Comics (Graphic works)","description":"Narrative made from sequences of images, usually with text in balloons and captions, read as a series of panels with gaps the reader fills. It has its own grammar of panel, gutter, page turn and lettering, worked out in newspaper strips, comic books, bande dessinée and manga. Will Eisner and Scott McCloud made that grammar explicit.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A narrative form with its own described grammar and a large body of work in several national traditions; LCGFT files thirty-eight terms under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comics-graphic-works","wp-comics"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-comics-graphic-works","title":"Comics (Graphic works) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026266"},{"id":"wp-comics","title":"Comics — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Comics journalism","description":"Reporting done in comics, built from interviews and observation, with the reporter usually drawn into the story. Joe Sacco's Palestine established the practice, and the drawn witness raises questions about evidence that the form takes on openly. Drawing lets a reporter show what a witness described.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named practice with a founding body of work, a stated method and an explicit argument about evidence; LCGFT files it under Nonfiction comics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comics-journalism","wp-comics-journalism"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"nonfiction-comics","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Nonfiction comics as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-comics-journalism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-comics-journalism","title":"Comics journalism — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026049"},{"id":"wp-comics-journalism","title":"Comics journalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comics_journalism"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Coming-of-age comics","description":"Comics following a young person into adulthood. The form can show a body and a face changing across pages, which is a resource prose does not have, and much of the strongest work is autobiographical. {"version":3,"name":"Coming-of-age fiction","description":"Novels that follow a protagonist's moral and psychological growth from youth into adulthood. The German Bildungsroman, dated from Goethe's Wilhelm Meister (1795–96) and named by Morgenstern in 1819, is the model; Carlyle's translation carried it into English. LCGFT lists Bildungsromane and Künstlerromane as variants.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A novel form with a defined structure and a documented history.","sourceIds":["lcgft-coming-of-age-fiction","wp-bildungsroman"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-coming-of-age-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-coming-of-age-fiction","title":"Coming-of-age fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026243"},{"id":"wp-bildungsroman","title":"Bildungsroman — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bildungsroman"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Commedia dell'arte","description":"Professional Italian comic theatre of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, played by touring companies from a scenario instead of a script. Masked stock characters, Arlecchino, Pantalone, Il Dottore and the rest, carry fixed traits, and rehearsed comic routines called lazzi are dropped into the improvisation. What survives on paper is the scenarios, the lazzi and the descriptions.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named theatrical tradition with companies, stock characters and a documented practice of improvisation from a scenario; LCGFT files it under Comedy plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-commedia-dellarte","wp-commedia-dellarte"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comedy-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Commedia dell'arte under Comedy plays; the companies played comedies and the form is built on comic types.","sourceIds":["lcgft-commedia-dellarte","wp-commedia-dellarte"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-commedia-dellarte","title":"Commedia dell'arte — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026267"},{"id":"wp-commedia-dellarte","title":"Commedia dell'arte — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commedia_dell'arte"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Commedia erudita","description":"Written Italian comedies of the sixteenth century, composed by scholars in imitation of Plautus and Terence and performed at courts and academies. Ariosto, Machiavelli and Bibbiena wrote in it. It is the learned half of the same century, opposite the improvised companies.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named body of written comedy with authors, models and a defined period; LCGFT files it under Comedy plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-commedia-erudita","wp-commedia-erudita"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comedy-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Commedia erudita under Comedy plays; the works are comedies built on the Roman comic plot.","sourceIds":["lcgft-commedia-erudita","wp-commedia-erudita"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-commedia-erudita","title":"Commedia erudita — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026060"},{"id":"wp-commedia-erudita","title":"Commedia erudita — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commedia_erudita"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Committed literature","description":"Writing that takes a stated ethical or political position and accepts responsibility for its effect in the world. The dispute is part of what the term names.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work.
