{"version":3,"name":"Computer art","description":"Art in which a computer does part of the making or the showing, from the plotter drawings and algorithmic compositions of the 1960s to installation, net and generative work now. Vera Molnár and Frieder Nake worked in the early period, when the machine time had to be borrowed from a laboratory. The instruction written for the machine is the work as much as the print is.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-computer-art","wd-q1376265","aat-300069478"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-computer-art","title":"Computer art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_art"},{"id":"wd-q1376265","title":"computer art (Q1376265) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1376265"},{"id":"aat-300069478","title":"Computer art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300069478","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300069478"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Computer-generated literature","description":"Poetry and prose produced by a procedure: rules, combinatorics, chance, and now language models. John Clark's Latin Verse Machine of the 1830s is the mechanical ancestor and Christopher Strachey's 1952 love-letter generator the first digital work; Scott Rettberg places the practice in the line of Dada, Surrealism, Oulipo and Fluxus. LCGFT names computer poetry as its narrower form.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A genre of electronic literature defined by how its text is produced.","sourceIds":["lcgft-computer-generated-literature","wp-generative-literature"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"electronic-literature","explanation":"The claim is the parent's: Wikipedia's Electronic literature article counts generated text among the capabilities that define the field and gives the generated poems of the 1950s as its first works. This cell's own pages do not say it.","sourceIds":["wp-electronic-literature"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"surrealism","label":"influenced by","explanation":"Rettberg connects generative literature to Dada, Surrealism, Oulipo and Fluxus.","sourceIds":["wp-generative-literature"]},{"cellId":"cut-ups-literature","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Both recombine existing text by rule or chance: the cut-up is an aleatory method and generative literature follows a combinatory, sometimes aleatory logic.","sourceIds":["wp-generative-literature","wp-cut-up-technique"]},{"cellId":"hypertext-fiction","label":"contrasted with","explanation":"Hannes Bajohr distinguishes generative literature, which foregrounds production, from hypertext, which foregrounds reception.","sourceIds":["wp-generative-literature"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-computer-generated-literature","title":"Computer-generated literature — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2024026018"},{"id":"wp-generative-literature","title":"Generative literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_literature"},{"id":"wp-cut-up-technique","title":"Cut-up technique — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cut-up_technique"},{"id":"wp-electronic-literature","title":"Electronic literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_literature"},{"id":"lcgft-computer-poetry","title":"Computer poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026269"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Conceptual Art","description":"Art in which the idea carries at least as much weight as the object, so that a work may exist as an instruction, a document, a proposition or a set of photographs. Sol LeWitt's 1967 Paragraphs on Conceptual Art put the term into circulation, and LeWitt, Kosuth, Weiner and Art & Language are its central figures. Dematerialisation is the argument: the object can be optional.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-conceptual-art","wd-q203209","aat-300264827"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-conceptual-art","title":"Conceptual art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_art"},{"id":"wd-q203209","title":"conceptual art (Q203209) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q203209"},{"id":"aat-300264827","title":"Conceptual Art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300264827","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264827"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Concrete Art","description":"Abstraction that refers to nothing outside itself, formulated by Theo van Doesburg in 1930 and taken up after his death by Max Bill. Its forms are geometric, planned in advance and conceived before execution, which is what the word concrete claims: the work is a real object in its own right. It carried into Latin America and produced its own movements there.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-concrete-art","wd-q10822316","aat-300021436"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"geometric-abstraction","explanation":"The movement rests on a strong emphasis on geometrical abstraction, in van Doesburg's formulation and in Max Bill's.","sourceIds":["wp-concrete-art"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-concrete-art","title":"Concrete art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete_art"},{"id":"wd-q10822316","title":"concrete art (Q10822316) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q10822316"},{"id":"aat-300021436","title":"Concrete Art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300021436","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300021436"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Concrete poetry","description":"Poems in which the typographical arrangement carries as much meaning as the words. The international movement of the 1950s, with the Noigandres group in Brazil and Gomringer, wrote manifestos for it and treated the page as a field. Reading it and looking at it are the same act.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named international movement with manifestos, dated groups and a stated compositional principle; LCGFT files it under Visual poetry and Experimental poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-concrete-poetry","wp-concrete-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"experimental-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Experimental poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-concrete-poetry"]},{"cellId":"visual-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Visual poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-concrete-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-concrete-poetry","title":"Concrete poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026270"},{"id":"wp-concrete-poetry","title":"Concrete poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Condorism","description":"The third phase of Brazilian Romanticism, running from the mid-1860s to the early 1880s, named for the condor as an image of height and liberty. Tobias Barreto created it and Castro Alves is its great poet, turning Romantic rhetoric onto abolition and social justice. It follows Indianism and Ultra-Romanticism in the standard Brazilian account.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Confessional poetry","description":"American poetry of the late 1950s and early 1960s that writes the private life directly: illness, sexuality, family, suicide, and the poet's own I. That heading has no cell, so the parent here is Lyric poetry. Add the other parent if Autobiographical poetry becomes a cell."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-confessional-poetry","title":"Confessional poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026272"},{"id":"wp-confessional-poetry","title":"Confessional poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessional_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Cookbooks","description":"Collections of recipes in book form, with the household matter around them: quantities, timings, costs, seasons, and what to do with what is left. Each entry runs in a fixed order, ingredients then method then yield. The prose between entries carries whatever the author wants to teach. Beeton's Book of Household Management set the English pattern in 1861 by adding cost and season to every dish. The register is imperative and unhurried. It assumes a reader standing up.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Library of Congress carries Cookbooks as a genre, and the form has centuries of work behind it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-cookbooks","wp-cookbook"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"handbooks-and-manuals","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Cookbooks under Instructional and educational works, which this collection declined as a cataloguing heading with no practice of its own. Handbooks and manuals names a practice and is the nearest cell to it, so this parent is a judgement and not LC's filing.","sourceIds":["lcgft-cookbooks"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Beeton's book is wider than a cookbook. It covers servants, budgets, medicine and dress, so if that whole practice needs its own cell then the household manual is the leaf still missing and this record should move again.","The parent here is not the one the Library of Congress gives. If Instructional and educational works becomes a cell, this link moves to it."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-cookbooks","title":"Cookbooks — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2011026169"},{"id":"wp-cookbook","title":"Cookbook — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cookbook"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-019f2ed1-8e18-7bc1-8b68-f88b86e693f5","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Household-manual tradition\" (UnderReview). {"version":3,"name":"Coppet group","description":"The circle around Germaine de Staël at Coppet Castle in Switzerland between 1804 and 1815, gathering Benjamin Constant, Sismondi, Schlegel and others in exile from Napoleon. Their conversation carried German Romantic thought into French. It was a working intellectual community with no doctrine.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-coppet-group","wd-q3117678"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-coppet-group","title":"Coppet group — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coppet_group"},{"id":"wd-q3117678","title":"Coppet group (Q3117678) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3117678"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Costumbrismo","description":"A nineteenth-century Hispanic tendency in writing and painting towards precise depiction of local customs, manners and everyday types. It draws on Romanticism and on realism together, taking the first's interest in the particular and the second's care for accuracy, and it is often satirical or moralising without offering an analysis. In prose it produced the sketch of manners and fed the novel of manners.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-costumbrismo","wd-q1136545"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-costumbrismo","wd-q1136545"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"realism-art-movement","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as a subclass of realism.","sourceIds":["wd-q1136545"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-costumbrismo","title":"Costumbrismo — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costumbrismo"},{"id":"wd-q1136545","title":"Costumbrismo (Q1136545) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1136545"},{"id":"wd-q5790162","title":"Literary costumbrismo (Q5790162) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q5790162"},{"id":"wp-literary-costumbrismo","title":"Literary costumbrismo — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_costumbrismo"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Counting-out rhymes","description":"Children's rhymes used to pick or eliminate a player, chanted while pointing round a circle. Eeny meeny miny moe and its many variants have been collected across languages, and the words often survive long after they stop meaning anything. The rhythm does the work: one stress per player is the whole mechanism.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A folk verse form with a stated function, a collected corpus and a defining rhythmic mechanism; LCGFT files it under Nursery rhymes.","sourceIds":["lcgft-counting-out-rhymes","wp-counting-out-game"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"nursery-rhymes","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Nursery rhymes as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-counting-out-rhymes"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-counting-out-rhymes","title":"Counting-out rhymes — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026273"},{"id":"wp-counting-out-game","title":"Counting-out game — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting-out_game"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Courtesy books","description":"Manuals of manners written for people who had to move at court: how to speak, defer, dress and hold a room. The genre starts in the thirteenth century. It runs through Castiglione and Peacham to Chesterfield's letters to his son, which the histories treat as the last traditional English one. Advice is given as worldly instruction to a named junior, with the reasons attached and no appeal to conscience. The tone is the tell. It is assured, particular, and interested in effect.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Courtesy literature has been written since the thirteenth century and its canon runs to the eighteenth.","sourceIds":["wp-courtesy-book"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"handbooks-and-manuals","explanation":"A manual that teaches a reader how to conduct themselves, arranged as instruction and consulted in the same way.","sourceIds":["wp-courtesy-book"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-courtesy-book","title":"Courtesy book — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtesy_book"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-019f2ed1-612b-78f2-88ac-fa97cb94e3b3","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Epistolary advice tradition\" (UnderReview). The reference names Chesterfield's Letters to His Son as the last traditional English courtesy book. These are real letters, written to a single reader and published as literature, which is what sets the record apart from the treatises the genre otherwise runs on.","sourceIds":["wp-courtesy-book"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Cowboy poetry","description":"Verse made by working cattle hands about that work, usually rhymed and metrical and meant to be recited aloud. It grew out of nineteenth-century trail-camp storytelling and has a living institution in the annual gathering at Elko, Nevada, which began in 1985. First-hand experience is treated inside the tradition as a condition of writing it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named occupational verse tradition with a documented origin, a living institution and its own internal standards; LCGFT files it under Folk poetry, which is already a live cell.","sourceIds":["lcgft-cowboy-poetry","wp-cowboy-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Cowboy poetry under Folk poetry; it is composed and carried within a working community and recited aloud.","sourceIds":["lcgft-cowboy-poetry","wp-cowboy-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-cowboy-poetry","title":"Cowboy poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026028"},{"id":"wp-cowboy-poetry","title":"Cowboy poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowboy_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Cozy mysteries","description":"Mystery fiction in which violence happens offstage, the detective is an amateur embedded in a small community, and the tone stays light. The pattern descends from the English between-the-wars puzzle novel and became an explicit publishing category in the United States from the 1990s. {"version":3,"name":"Creative nonfiction","description":"Factual prose written with the devices of fiction: scenes in order, dialogue, a point of view, and a narrator the reader can hear. The facts stay checkable and the shaping is deliberate, so a piece can be reported and still read as a story. The essay, the memoir, travel writing and reported narrative all fall inside it. Where the name came from is not known, though the field's main magazine and its first graduate programme both used it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Library of Congress files it as prose literature, and the Wikipedia article treats it as a genre of writing with its own history.","sourceIds":["lcgft-creative-nonfiction","wp-creative-nonfiction"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-creative-nonfiction","title":"Creative nonfiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026074"},{"id":"wp-creative-nonfiction","title":"Creative nonfiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_nonfiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Créolie","description":"A literary and musical movement in Réunion, named in 1970 and taken up by Bishop Gilbert Aubry in 1978, which places Réunionese identity inside a larger French one. It draws on island folklore and the French inheritance together. It is usually discussed against Créolité, which reads the same material through the history of slavery instead.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Créolité","description":"A Martinican movement launched by Patrick Chamoiseau, Jean Bernabé and Raphaël Confiant with Éloge de la créolité in 1989, arguing that Caribbean identity is composite and that Creole language and orality have a place in literature. It was written as an answer to Négritude, whose one African root the authors found too narrow. Its first sentence declares the writers neither European nor African nor Asian but Creole.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Cronicas","description":"Short prose pieces written for a newspaper or magazine column, hooked to something in the day's news and free to move into anecdote, memory or invention. {"version":3,"name":"Cyberpunk fiction","description":"Science fiction of high technology in low places: networks, implants and corporate power seen from the level of hustlers and outsiders. {"version":3,"name":"Cynical Realism","description":"A Chinese painting movement of the 1990s, named by the critic Li Xianting in 1992, using a satirical realist manner to register the disillusionment following 1989. Fang Lijun's shaven-headed grinning figures and Yue Minjun's laughing self-portraits are its emblems. The humour is defensive and the target is the official image of a confident nation.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-cynical-realism","wd-q3650833"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-cynical-realism","title":"Cynical realism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynical_realism"},{"id":"wd-q3650833","title":"Cynical realism (Q3650833) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3650833"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Dada","description":"An international movement begun in Zurich in 1916 as a response to the war and to the society that produced it, rejecting art's existing forms in favour of an anti-art of chance, collage, nonsense and provocation. It spread to Berlin, Hanover, Cologne, Paris and New York, each centre taking it differently. Its refusals became the working methods of most of what followed.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-dada","wd-q6034","aat-300021500"]},{"map":"writing","explanation":"The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. {"version":3,"name":"Dansaekhwa","description":"A retroactive grouping of Korean painting shown from the mid-1970s, usually translated monochrome painting, in which the canvas is worked by soaking, pushing, tearing or repeated marking. {"version":3,"name":"Danube school","description":"A circle of painters and printmakers in Bavaria and Austria in the first third of the sixteenth century, among the first to make pure landscape a subject in its own right. Their etchings are as important as their panels.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-danube-school","wd-q587691","aat-300263782"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-danube-school","title":"Danube school — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube_school"},{"id":"wd-q587691","title":"Danube school (Q587691) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q587691"},{"id":"aat-300263782","title":"Danube school — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300263782","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300263782"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Dau al Set","description":"The first Spanish artistic movement after the war, founded in Barcelona in September 1948 around the poet Joan Brossa, with Antoni Tàpies among its painters. The name means the seventh face of the die.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-dau-al-set","wd-q1172762"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-dau-al-set","title":"Dau al Set — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dau_al_Set"},{"id":"wd-q1172762","title":"Dau al Set (Q1172762) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1172762"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Der Blaue Reiter","description":"A Munich group and almanac created by Kandinsky and Franz Marc, which mounted two exhibitions in 1911 and 1912 and published its almanac in 1912. {"version":3,"name":"Descorts","description":"An Old Occitan troubadour genre whose stanzas differ from one another in metre, melody or even language, the discord of the form answering the discord of unrequited love. Mondrian and Van Doesburg argued it as a universal language of balance, and the programme ran straight into furniture, typography and architecture. Rietveld's chair and the Schröder House are the argument built.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-de-stijl","wd-q207445","aat-300021259"]},{"map":"design","explanation":"The movement worked in design as well as in the visual arts. {"version":3,"name":"Detective and mystery fiction","description":"Fiction organised around the investigation of a crime, usually murder, by a professional or amateur detective. {"version":3,"name":"Dialect drama","description":"Plays that write the speech of a region or a social group into the script, so that pronunciation, idiom and grammar are part of the text an actor is given. The same technique in prose and in verse has its own cells.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A technique applied to the writing of a play. {"version":3,"name":"Dialect fiction","description":"Fiction that renders the speech of a region or social group on the page through vocabulary, grammar and altered spelling. Writers use it in dialogue to place characters, and sometimes throughout the narration. Eye dialect, the respelling of standard pronunciations to signal a speaker's class or schooling, is one of its tools.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A technique of rendering speech in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-dialect-fiction","wp-eye-dialect"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-dialect-fiction"]},{"cellId":"dialect-literature","explanation":"Regional and social speech rendered in prose.","sourceIds":["wd-dialect-literature"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-dialect-fiction","title":"Dialect fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026283"},{"id":"wp-eye-dialect","title":"Eye dialect — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_dialect"},{"id":"wd-dialect-literature","title":"dialect literature (Q1208422) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1208422"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Dialect literature","description":"Writing that puts the speech of a region or a social group on the page — its vocabulary, its grammar and its sound — in place of a standard written variety. {"version":3,"name":"Dialect poetry","description":"Poems written in the speech of a region or a social group, its vocabulary, grammar and sound spelled onto the page. Proposed as its own cell because the verse tradition (Burns, Barnes, Dunbar) has its own history; the human may prefer one dialect cell across forms."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-dialect-poetry","title":"Dialect poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026284"},{"id":"wp-paul-laurence-dunbar","title":"Paul Laurence Dunbar — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Laurence_Dunbar"},{"id":"wd-dialect-literature","title":"dialect literature (Q1208422) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1208422"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Dialogues (Literature)","description":"Works written as a conversation between two or more speakers, used to test an argument or teach a doctrine. {"version":3,"name":"Diaries","description":"Dated entries written as the days pass, by someone who does not yet know how the story ends. Entries may be private or written for later readers, and the register shifts with that. Because the writing is serial it records changes of mind, boredom and detail that a retrospective account would drop.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Diaries under creative nonfiction, and diaries are read as literature as well as kept as records.","sourceIds":["lcgft-diaries","wp-diary"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"creative-nonfiction","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Diaries under Creative nonfiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-diaries"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"diary-fiction","label":"is imitated by","explanation":"Diary fiction borrows the dated entry and the writer who cannot see ahead, and applies them to invented material.","sourceIds":["wp-diary"]}],"questions":["Pepys, Woolf and Kafka are three unlike practices under one heading. Naming that leaf needs a source on the early modern English diary."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-diaries","title":"Diaries — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026085"},{"id":"wp-diary","title":"Diary — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-019f2ed1-3653-7fd3-8eb4-be2fd817a0b4","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Diary tradition\" (UnderReview). {"version":3,"name":"Diary fiction","description":"Fiction written as a character's dated diary or journal. Early printed examples include the Grossmiths' Diary of a Nobody; Dracula, Adrian Mole and Diary of a Wimpy Kid show the range from horror to comedy. {"version":3,"name":"Die Brücke","description":"A German Expressionist group founded in Dresden in 1905 by four architecture students, Bleyl, Heckel, Kirchner and Schmidt-Rottluff, later joined by Nolde, Pechstein and Mueller. They painted in harsh colour with cut, angular drawing, revived the woodcut, and lived and worked communally. The group dissolved in 1913.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-die-brucke","wd-q152778"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"german-expressionism","explanation":"Its own article opens by calling the group German expressionist artists formed in Dresden in 1905, so it sits under German Expressionism rather than under the wider Expressionism cell above it.","sourceIds":["wp-die-brucke"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-die-brucke","title":"Die Brücke — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Brücke"},{"id":"wd-q152778","title":"Die Brücke (Q152778) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q152778"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Dirty realism","description":"North American fiction that stays with ordinary and unglamorous life and reports it in spare, unadorned language. Bill Buford of Granta named it in 1983, and Raymond Carver, Tobias Wolff, Richard Ford and Ann Beattie wrote it. Sentences are short and declarative, adjectives are rationed, and interiority is left for the reader to infer from what people do and say. Stories end without resolving.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A literary movement named in 1983, with a canon.","sourceIds":["wp-dirty-realism"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"literary-realism","explanation":"It is a sub-category of realism, narrowed to the seamier and more mundane parts of ordinary life.","sourceIds":["wp-dirty-realism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-dirty-realism","title":"Dirty realism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirty_realism"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Documentary poetry","description":"Socially engaged poetry built from primary documents: news reports, legal transcripts, oral histories, letters and public records, arranged or quoted so the record itself speaks. Muriel Rukeyser's The Book of the Dead (1938), on the Hawks Nest Tunnel disaster, is an early landmark; docupoetry is its working name.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-documentary-poetry","pw-docupoetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-documentary-poetry"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"found-poetry","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Documentary poets quote and arrange non-literary source texts; found poetry is the wider practice of reframing such text.","sourceIds":["pw-docupoetry"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-documentary-poetry","title":"Documentary poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026067"},{"id":"pw-docupoetry","title":"Docupoetry — Poets & Writers","url":"https://www.pw.org/content/docupoetry"},{"id":"wp-muriel-rukeyser","title":"Muriel Rukeyser — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Rukeyser"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Dolce Stil Novo","description":"A school of Italian love poetry of the late thirteenth century, whose subject is a love that ennobles and whose lady is close to an angel. Its sweetness is a technical claim about diction as much as a subject.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Domestic drama","description":"Plays whose serious action falls on ordinary middle-class or working-class people in their own homes, against the older rule that tragedy required the fall of the great. Arden of Faversham and Lillo's The London Merchant establish the English line. The claim is that a household is a large enough stage for a catastrophe.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic genre that changed who tragedy could be about, with a canon and an explicit theoretical argument; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-domestic-drama","wp-domestic-tragedy"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-domestic-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline against the rule that declined Domestic fiction as subject-defined. {"version":3,"name":"Double dactyls","description":"A comic fixed form invented by Anthony Hecht and Paul Pascal in 1951 and spread by Hecht and John Hollander's anthology Jiggery-Pokery: two quatrains of dactylic dimeter, the first line a nonsense jingle, the second a proper name, one line of the second stanza a single six-syllable word, and the two stanzas' last lines rhymed.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-double-dactyls","wp-double-dactyl"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-double-dactyls"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-double-dactyls","title":"Double dactyls — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026296"},{"id":"wp-double-dactyl","title":"Double dactyl — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_dactyl"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Drama","description":"Writing made for performance: plays for the stage, and the radio, television and film scripts that carry the same form. {"version":3,"name":"Dramatic monologues (Poetry)","description":"Poems spoken by a character who is not the poet, to a listener who says nothing, and who gives away more than they intend. {"version":3,"name":"Dystopian fiction","description":"Fiction set in a society organised badly on purpose, where the arrangement itself is the antagonist. {"version":3,"name":"Ecofiction","description":"Fiction that treats the human and the non-human world as one system and follows what people do to it. {"version":3,"name":"Epistolary poetry","description":"Poems written as letters to a friend, patron or lover. Horace's Epistles (20 and 14 BC) set the familiar, moral kind that Renaissance and later poets imitated; Ovid's Heroides, letters in the voices of legendary women, set the romantic kind. LCGFT's variants are Verse epistles and Horatian epistles.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-epistolary-poetry","wp-epistle"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-epistolary-poetry"]},{"cellId":"epistolary-literature","explanation":"The verse side of the letter tradition, from Horace and Ovid to Pope; the prose novel is its sibling under the same parent.","sourceIds":["wd-epistolary-literature","wp-epistle","wp-epistles-horace"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"epistolary-fiction","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Both build the work out of letters; the verse epistle is older and addresses a real or imagined correspondent in the poet's own voice.","sourceIds":["wp-epistle"]}],"questions":["Stands apart from Epistolary fiction because the two have different histories and canons (Horace and Ovid against Richardson); if the human prefers one letter-form cell across prose and verse, this merges."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-epistolary-poetry","title":"Epistolary poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026315"},{"id":"wp-epistle","title":"Epistle — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle"},{"id":"wp-epistles-horace","title":"Epistles (Horace) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistles_(Horace)"},{"id":"wd-epistolary-literature","title":"epistolary literature (Q3491641) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3491641"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Epithalamia","description":"Poems written for a wedding, addressed to the couple and often following the day from morning to the bridal chamber. Sappho's fragments and Catullus's poems establish the classical form and Spenser's Epithalamion is the great English one. Its conventions are specific: the invocation, the procession, the blessing on the marriage.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named classical genre with a stated set of conventions and a continuous canon; LCGFT files it under Occasional verse and Commemorative works.","sourceIds":["lcgft-epithalamia","wp-epithalamium"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"occasional-verse","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Occasional verse as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-epithalamia"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-epithalamia","title":"Epithalamia — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026317"},{"id":"wp-epithalamium","title":"Epithalamium — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epithalamium"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Erasure poetry","description":"Poems made by removing words from an existing text so that what remains becomes the poem. Ronald Johnson's Radi os, cut out of Paradise Lost, and Mary Ruefle's whited-out books are worked examples, and the removal can be shown or hidden. What is taken away stays in the work, so the source text is always named.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named compositional technique with a canon and a stated rule about its source; LCGFT files it under Found poetry, which is already a live cell.","sourceIds":["lcgft-erasure-poetry","wp-blackout-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"found-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Erasure poetry under Found poetry; both make a poem out of language the poet did not write.","sourceIds":["lcgft-erasure-poetry","wp-blackout-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-erasure-poetry","title":"Erasure poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026017"},{"id":"wp-blackout-poetry","title":"Blackout poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackout_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Essays","description":"Short prose in which the writer makes an argument or sets down an observation, addressed to a reader who is being persuaded or given company. The form runs from Montaigne's trials of a thought through the periodical essay to the magazine and online essay. Any subject is allowed, and the movement of the argument gives the piece its order. The essayist's thinking is on the page and the reader follows it as it moves.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Essays under creative nonfiction, and the form has been written continuously since Montaigne.","sourceIds":["lcgft-essays","wp-essay"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"creative-nonfiction","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Essays directly under Creative nonfiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-essays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-essays","title":"Essays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026094"},{"id":"wp-essay","title":"Essay — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essay"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Etiquette books","description":"Books that set out what is done and what is not done in daily social life. They go event by event: the introduction, the invitation, the funeral, the table. They took over from the courtesy book once the audience stopped being courtiers. Emily Post's Etiquette of 1922 is the American one everyone cites. The writing is specific and unembarrassed, and it gives the reason as consideration for the other person. Rulings are short and stated without irony, to a reader who is mid-situation.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The books have named authors and dated editions, and people are still buying them.","sourceIds":["wp-etiquette"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"handbooks-and-manuals","explanation":"A manual consulted for the answer to a particular situation, which is how the handbook heading is defined.","sourceIds":["wp-etiquette"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"courtesy-books","label":"descends from","explanation":"Both instruct a reader in conduct. The courtesy book addressed the court, and this one addresses everyone.","sourceIds":["wp-etiquette"]}],"questions":["The reference calls these books of etiquette. The cell takes the plural form the rest of the collection uses. Rename it if the source phrasing should win."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-etiquette","title":"Etiquette — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etiquette"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-019f2eec-7ab9-7b80-9e8c-f00e6135186d","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Etiquette-manual tradition\" (UnderReview). Emily Post's Etiquette of 1922 is named in the reference, and it is the edition the record is built from.","sourceIds":["wp-etiquette"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Exempla","description":"Short moral anecdotes used by medieval preachers to drive a point home in a sermon, gathered into handbooks such as Jacques de Vitry's collection and the Gesta Romanorum. {"version":3,"name":"Explanatory journalism","description":"Reporting whose job is to make an ongoing story understandable by supplying the background a news item assumes. {"version":3,"name":"Fables","description":"Short narratives in prose or verse whose characters are animals, plants or objects that speak and act as people do, and which end in a moral. The Greek collection attributed to Aesop is the root of the European line, with the Sanskrit Panchatantra and the Arabic Kalila wa-Dimna as parallel traditions, and La Fontaine's verse fables in the seventeenth century as its most famous rewriting. The moral closes the form.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A tradition with a canon in several languages and a stated formal rule; LCGFT files it under Folk tales and Exempla.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fables","wp-fable"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-tales","explanation":"LCGFT files Fables under Folk tales; the fable travels by retelling and most of its texts have no single author.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fables","wp-fable"]},{"cellId":"exempla","explanation":"LCGFT files Fables under Exempla; a fable is a short narrative told to prove a moral point, which is what an exemplum does.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fables","wp-fable"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-fables","title":"Fables — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026327"},{"id":"wp-fable","title":"Fable — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fable"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Fabliaux","description":"Short comic verse tales written in France between about 1150 and 1400, usually in octosyllabic couplets, mostly anonymous and frankly obscene. Their world is one of tricked husbands, greedy clerics and quick-witted wives, and their attitudes run against courtly literature. Chaucer took the form directly into English.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named medieval verse form with a dated corpus, a stated metre and a consistent set of attitudes; LCGFT files it under Humorous poetry, which pass 2 declined as a tone umbrella.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fabliaux","wp-fabliau"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"humorous-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Humorous poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fabliaux"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-fabliaux","title":"Fabliaux — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026328"},{"id":"wp-fabliau","title":"Fabliau — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabliau"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Fairy tales","description":"Short folk narratives in which magic and enchanted beings work without needing explanation, and in which ordinary people meet them. The oral material was gathered and rewritten into the printed canon by Perrault in 1697 and by the Grimms from 1812, and Andersen wrote new ones in the same manner. Their construction is highly regular, and the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index numbers their plots.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A tradition with a collected canon and a formal structure that folklorists index; LCGFT files it under Folk tales.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fairy-tales","wp-fairy-tale"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-tales","explanation":"LCGFT files Fairy tales under Folk tales; the printed canon is a redaction of oral material collected from many tellers.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fairy-tales","wp-fairy-tale"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-fairy-tales","title":"Fairy tales — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026329"},{"id":"wp-fairy-tale","title":"Fairy tale — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_tale"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Familiar essay","description":"An essay addressed to one reader as if in conversation, about the writer and about a particular subject at the same time. Writers use it when a piece has to be personal without becoming a confession.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named manner of the English essay, described in the Wikipedia article on the essay form.","sourceIds":["wp-essay-familiar"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"essays","explanation":"It is a way of writing an essay, separated from the critical and the personal essay by how it balances thought and feeling.","sourceIds":["wp-essay-familiar"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Named from the section of the Wikipedia essay article that describes the form, which cites Anne Fadiman. A standalone reference on the familiar essay would be a better citation, and it should be added when one is found."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-essay-familiar","title":"Essay: Familiar — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essay#Familiar"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Fantasy fiction","description":"Fiction in which magic, the supernatural or invented worlds are part of the story's fabric. {"version":3,"name":"Farces","description":"Comedy that runs on improbable situations, mistaken identity, physical business and speed. It goes back to Roman comedy and the medieval French farce, and its nineteenth-century French form built the machinery of doors, hiding places and near-misses that later farce still uses. Timing is the craft: the plot has to accelerate past the point where anyone could stop it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A comic form with a continuous history and a stated method of construction; LCGFT files Antimasques, Atellanae and Drolls under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-farces","wp-farce"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comedy-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Farces under Comedy plays; farce is one of comedy's oldest and most defined kinds.","sourceIds":["lcgft-farces","wp-farce"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-farces","title":"Farces — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026335"},{"id":"wp-farce","title":"Farce — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farce"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Fastnachtsspiele","description":"Short amateur plays performed in German towns at Shrove Tuesday carnival in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, coarse and topical, played in the street or in an inn. Nuremberg has the fullest record, with Hans Rosenplüt, Hans Folz and later Hans Sachs writing for it. Carnival licence is built into the form: the plays say what is not said the rest of the year.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic form with a period, a place, named authors and an occasion that shapes what it may say; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fastnachtsspiele","wp-fastnachtspiel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-fastnachtsspiele"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-fastnachtsspiele","title":"Fastnachtsspiele — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026336"},{"id":"wp-fastnachtspiel","title":"Fastnachtspiel — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fastnachtspiel"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Flash fiction","description":"Very short fiction, usually under a thousand words, that still turns and still implies a larger story. {"version":3,"name":"Fluxus","description":"An international, interdisciplinary network of the 1960s and 1970s, named by George Maciunas in 1962, working in performance, event scores, small printed multiples and mail. Its scores are often one sentence telling someone what to do.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-fluxus","wd-q108908","aat-300022168"]},{"map":"writing","explanation":"The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. {"version":3,"name":"Folk Art","description":"Visual work made within a popular tradition, usually with a use as well as a look: painted furniture, quilts, signs, carvings, votive pictures. The category is contested at both edges, against naive art on one side and craft on the other. It is defined by how the maker learned as much as by what the object is.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-folk-art","wd-q1153484","aat-300056487"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-folk-art","title":"Folk art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_art"},{"id":"wd-q1153484","title":"folk art (Q1153484) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1153484"},{"id":"aat-300056487","title":"Folk Art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300056487","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300056487"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Folk drama","description":"Plays a community owns, performed by amateurs at fixed points in the year and passed on by custom instead of by a printed text. Mummers' plays, guising and their equivalents across Europe and Asia work this way, with variants recorded from village to village. The occasion, the performers and the transmission all define the form.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A family of made work defined by how it is transmitted and performed, in the same way the live cell Folk literature is; LCGFT files eleven regional traditions under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-folk-drama","wp-folk-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-literature","explanation":"LCGFT files Folk drama under Folk literature; both are composed and carried by a community rather than by named authors.","sourceIds":["lcgft-folk-drama","wp-folk-play"]},{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-folk-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-folk-drama","title":"Folk drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026341"},{"id":"wp-folk-play","title":"Folk play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Folk literature","description":"Stories, songs, sayings and drama composed and carried by word of mouth, with no fixed text and many tellers. Each performance varies, and versions accumulate across generations before folklorists write them down. The cell holds the oral traditions themselves and the collections made from them.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT places Folk literature under Literature; the practice is verbal composition transmitted by speech and song, later transcribed.","sourceIds":["lcgft-folk-literature","wp-oral-literature"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Is a mode of transmission a direction in the same sense as a movement? Proposed as the parent of Folk tales and Memorates; the human decides."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-folk-literature","title":"Folk literature — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026342"},{"id":"wp-oral-literature","title":"Oral literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_literature"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Folk poetry","description":"Poems composed and passed on by word of mouth, usually by people who do not write, each generation receiving them from the last. Their forms are many and never fixed, and they were mostly sung or recited before collectors wrote them down. LCGFT files cowboy poetry, toasts and hahiwang under it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-folk-poetry","wp-oral-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-literature","explanation":"LCGFT lists Folk poetry under Folk literature: it is the verse part of oral tradition.","sourceIds":["lcgft-folk-poetry"]},{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-folk-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-folk-poetry","title":"Folk poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026343"},{"id":"wp-oral-poetry","title":"Oral poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Folk tales","description":"Short anonymous narratives handed down orally, reshaped by each teller, and later collected in print. {"version":3,"name":"Forum Lingkar Pena","description":"An Indonesian writers' collective founded in 1997 by the sisters Helvy Tiana Rosa and Asma Nadia, which by 2008 had chapters in twenty-three provinces and eight other countries. {"version":3,"name":"Fotonovelas","description":"Comics made from photographs instead of drawings, laid out in panels with balloons and captions. {"version":3,"name":"Graveyard poetry","description":"An eighteenth-century tradition of meditative poems on death and the hope of a life beyond, set among tombs: Parnell's Night-Piece on Death, Blair's The Grave, Young's Night Thoughts and Gray's Elegy. {"version":3,"name":"Handbooks and manuals","description":"Writing that tells a reader how to do something, arranged so it can be entered at any point. {"version":3,"name":"Hardboiled","description":"Crime fiction told by or around a detective who is cynical, physically at risk, and no better than the system he works in. {"version":3,"name":"Heroic drama","description":"English Restoration plays in rhymed couplets about a noble hero torn between love and honour, staged with exotic settings and expensive scenery. The rhyme is the marker: the form argues that heroic action needs an elevated verse to carry it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named genre with a defined period, a theorist, a verse rule and a contemporary parody; LCGFT files it under Tragedies.","sourceIds":["lcgft-heroic-drama","wp-heroic-drama"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"tragedies-drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Tragedies (Drama) as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-heroic-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-heroic-drama","title":"Heroic drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026367"},{"id":"wp-heroic-drama","title":"Heroic drama — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroic_drama"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"High fantasy","description":"Fantasy set in a self-consistent invented world, where the outcome decides the whole of it. {"version":3,"name":"High Renaissance","description":"A short and intense period in Italian art from about 1490 or 1500 to about 1520, centred on Rome and Florence, in which Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael brought perspective, anatomy and composition to a settled balance. {"version":3,"name":"Kyōgen plays","description":"Japanese comic plays performed between the acts of a nō programme, in ordinary speech and without masks for most roles. {"version":3,"name":"Lakhō̜n chātrī plays","description":"Fast, lightly staged Thai dance drama from the central region, closely related to the Nora of the south and often performed to discharge a vow made to a shrine. {"version":3,"name":"Language poetry","description":"An American avant-garde of the late 1960s onward, named after the magazine L=A=N=G=U=A=G=E: Bernstein, Silliman, Hejinian, Howe, Armantrout and others who treated the poem as a construction in language, broke syntax and reference, and gave the reader the work of making meaning. {"version":3,"name":"Linked stories","description":"A collection of stories that each stand alone but are arranged so that reading them together produces something one story could not. Joyce's Dubliners is a standard case, and the recurrence may be place, family, narrator or motif. Criticism calls the same form the short-story cycle.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A structural technique for assembling a book, with a critical literature under the name short-story cycle; LCGFT files it under Novels and Short stories.","sourceIds":["lcgft-linked-stories","wp-short-story-cycle"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"short-stories","explanation":"LCGFT files Linked stories under Short stories; the parts are self-contained short stories.","sourceIds":["lcgft-linked-stories","wp-short-story-cycle"]},{"cellId":"novels","explanation":"LCGFT files Linked stories under Novels; the assembled whole is read as one book-length work.","sourceIds":["lcgft-linked-stories","wp-short-story-cycle"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-linked-stories","title":"Linked stories — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026126"},{"id":"wp-short-story-cycle","title":"Short-story cycle — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-story_cycle"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Linked verse","description":"Poems composed in turns by two or more poets, each adding a stanza that links to the last. Japan built the great tradition: the court renga of Sōgi, the renku that Bashō brought to its height, and renshi since the 1980s; a Chinese linked verse, lianju, is older and may have shaped renga. The ideal is range, so poets avoid narrative and keep changing the scene.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-linked-verse","wp-renga"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-linked-verse"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-linked-verse","title":"Linked verse — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026413"},{"id":"wp-renga","title":"Renga — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renga"},{"id":"wp-renku","title":"Renku — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renku"},{"id":"wp-renshi","title":"Renshi — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renshi"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Linklog","description":"A blog made of links out, where the post title is the link and the writer's note is the post. The note does the work: it says why to click, or argues with the thing, or supplies the sentence the original left out. Length runs from a clause to a paragraph and the pace is high, so the voice comes through in accumulation across many entries. This is the filter-style weblog of the early 2000s, still written.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named blog form with a described structure, the title linking out and the body complementing it, and two decades of practice.","sourceIds":["wp-linklog"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"blogs","explanation":"The reference defines it as a type of blog whose posts are primarily links out, with the post title linking directly to the external page.","sourceIds":["wp-linklog"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"liveblogging","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Both run short dated entries at pace, and the linklog points outward where the liveblog reports what is in front of it.","sourceIds":["wp-linklog"]}],"questions":["The classic link roundup newsletter is the same manner delivered by email. If that reading holds, this cell serves Newsletters as well and the relation should be added."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-linklog","title":"Linklog — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linklog"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Listicle","description":"An article built as a numbered list, with the count in the title and a subheading for each entry. A ranked one puts its judgement in the order and counts down to the best. An unranked one groups by theme and lets the reader enter anywhere. Each entry has to earn its own heading, so the form rewards writers who can make a point in a paragraph and punishes padding. The count is a promise about length, which is most of why readers open it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named form with a described structure, a count in the title and a subheading per entry, and an enormous body of work in journalism and blogging.","sourceIds":["wp-listicle"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"journalism","explanation":"The reference places it in journalism, as an article whose structure is a list.","sourceIds":["wp-listicle"]},{"cellId":"blogs","explanation":"The reference places it equally in blogging, where the form is as common as it is in the press.","sourceIds":["wp-listicle"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Two parents, because the reference names journalism and blogging together and neither is the senior one. {"version":3,"name":"Literary realism","description":"Writing that keeps to ordinary life and reports it without heightening. It began in mid-nineteenth-century French and Russian literature and spread through the novel, the story and reported nonfiction. {"version":3,"name":"LitRPG (Fiction)","description":"Fiction in which the rules of a computer role-playing game are real inside the story, so characters gain levels, read stat blocks and see interface text on the page. {"version":3,"name":"Liturgical drama","description":"Medieval sung dramatic performances staged inside the Roman Catholic liturgy, most famously the Quem quaeritis exchange at the Easter sepulchre. {"version":3,"name":"Liveblogging","description":"Rolling coverage of an event as it happens, posted in short timestamped updates, newest first. {"version":3,"name":"Living newspapers","description":"Documentary theatre that stages current events from press reports, statistics and official records, usually to argue for action. {"version":3,"name":"Logbooks","description":"A running record of a vessel's working day, kept in a fixed order: time, position, wind, sail, work done, anything that went wrong. The form began at sea, where the master was required to keep one. It moved into aircraft and plant operation with its conventions intact. Entries are short, dated, impersonal, and written to be read by someone checking. Whatever a log has of a voice comes from what its writer chose to enter.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Logs are written to required conventions and survive in large numbers.","sourceIds":["wp-logbook"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"diaries","explanation":"Dated serial entries made as the days pass by someone who cannot see ahead, which is what a diary does, put to operational use.","sourceIds":["wp-logbook"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["A log is kept under an obligation and a diary is not, so this may be a record instead of a direction.
