{"version":3,"name":"Manga","description":"Japanese comics, with a set of conventions that travel with them: black and white art, right-to-left reading, stylised faces, shaped speech balloons, speed lines and sound words drawn into the picture. Serialisation in weekly and monthly magazines shapes the pacing, and the industry's editorial categories organise the whole field. Its modern form is usually dated to Tezuka in the postwar decades.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A national comics tradition with a described set of formal conventions and its own publishing structure; LCGFT files Shōjo, Shōnen, Seinen, Yuri and Isekai manga under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-manga","wp-manga"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"LCGFT files Manga under Comics; it is the Japanese branch of the form.","sourceIds":["lcgft-manga","wp-manga"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-manga","title":"Manga — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2022026036"},{"id":"wp-manga","title":"Manga — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manga"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Manhwa","description":"Korean comics, read left to right unlike manga, with a history shaped by colonial censorship, postwar rental libraries and, since about 2003, the vertical-scrolling webtoon. The webtoon format changed the drawing: full colour, one long strip, pacing controlled by how far a reader scrolls. It is now a major export.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A national comics tradition with its own reading direction, publishing history and a format that changed its drawing; LCGFT files it under Comics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-manhwa","wp-manhwa"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"LCGFT files Manhwa under Comics; it is the Korean branch of the form.","sourceIds":["lcgft-manhwa","wp-manhwa"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-manhwa","title":"Manhwa — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2024026083"},{"id":"wp-manhwa","title":"Manhwa — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhwa"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Mannerism","description":"A style in European art from about 1520 to the end of the sixteenth century, following the High Renaissance, in which figures are elongated, poses are strained, space is unstable and colour is acidic. It begins in Rome and Florence with Pontormo, Rosso and Parmigianino and spreads north. It is a knowing response to a settled classical order.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-mannerism","wd-q131808","aat-300021144"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"renaissance-art","explanation":"Its own article places it in European art from about 1520 to the end of the sixteenth century, emerging in the later years of the High Renaissance and ending when the Baroque replaced it, so it falls inside the span this cell covers. It sits at that span's edge and is the weakest of the three Renaissance placements.","sourceIds":["wp-mannerism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-mannerism","title":"Mannerism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannerism"},{"id":"wd-q131808","title":"Mannerism (Q131808) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q131808"},{"id":"aat-300021144","title":"Mannerism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300021144","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300021144"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Man page","description":"The Unix manual page: a fixed sequence of sections, NAME, SYNOPSIS, DESCRIPTION, OPTIONS and the rest, written for a reader at a terminal who needs one fact. The register is terse, declarative and present-tense, with no narrative and no encouragement. Completeness counts for more than order, because the reader arrives searching for one thing. Pages written today use the same section order as pages from the 1970s.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A software documentation form with published conventions and fifty years of pages behind it.","sourceIds":["wp-man-page","man7-man-pages"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"handbooks-and-manuals","explanation":"The name is short for manual page, and Wikipedia describes it as a form of software documentation.","sourceIds":["wp-man-page"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-man-page","title":"Man page — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_page"},{"id":"man7-man-pages","title":"man-pages(7) — conventions for writing Linux man pages","url":"https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/man-pages.7.html"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Maqāmāt","description":"Medieval Arabic tales in rhymed prose with verse inserted, told by a narrator who keeps meeting the same eloquent trickster in a new disguise. Al-Hamadhani invented the form in the tenth century and al-Hariri's collection became a school text across the Islamic world. The trickster wins by speaking well, and the display of language is what a reader comes for.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named prosimetric form with a dated invention, a canonical collection and imitations in Hebrew and Persian; LCGFT files it under Prose poems.","sourceIds":["lcgft-maqamat","wp-maqama"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"prose-poems","explanation":"LCGFT files Maqāmāt under Prose poems; the form is built in rhymed prose using poetic technique.","sourceIds":["lcgft-maqamat","wp-maqama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-maqamat","title":"Maqāmāt — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026425"},{"id":"wp-maqama","title":"Maqama — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqama"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Masnavis","description":"Long poems in rhyming couplets (aa, bb, cc), the Persian form for epic, romance and didactic verse, written also in Arabic, Turkish, Kurdish and Urdu; Rumi's Masnavi is the most famous and has a special place in Sufism. The couplets are independent, so the poem has no fixed length.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Poetry, and it is a way of building a poem.","sourceIds":["lcgft-masnavis","wp-mathnawi"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-masnavis"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-masnavis","title":"Masnavis — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026427"},{"id":"wp-mathnawi","title":"Mathnawi — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathnawi"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Masques","description":"Courtly entertainments of the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries in which poetry, music, dance and costly stage effects are built around a slight mythological or allegorical plot, and the court itself dances in it. In England Ben Jonson wrote the words and Inigo Jones designed the machines, and they quarrelled in public over which of the two mattered more. The audience is also the cast, which is what the form is for.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named courtly form with a defined period, named collaborators, a documented staging practice and a surviving textual corpus; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-masques","wp-masque"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-masques"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-masques","title":"Masques — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026428"},{"id":"wp-masque","title":"Masque — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masque"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Maximalism","description":"An aesthetic of excess and abundance, defined against minimalism, in which more is held to be more. In writing it names the long, digressive, encyclopedic novel of Pynchon, Wallace and Bolaño, and the term is used in music, design and visual art on the same principle. It is a tendency named in criticism, with no membership.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-maximalism","wd-q2246318"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-maximalism","wd-q2246318"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline: a tendency named by critics rather than a movement anyone joined. Kept because the encyclopedic novel is a recognisable body of work discussed under this name; strike it if a critics' label without members should not be a cell."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-maximalism","title":"Maximalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximalism"},{"id":"wd-q2246318","title":"maximalism (Q2246318) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2246318"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Medieval art","description":"Over a thousand years of Western art between antiquity and the Renaissance, taking in Early Christian, Byzantine, Insular, Carolingian, Romanesque and Gothic work across painting, manuscript, metal, glass and stone. Much of it is anonymous, made for the church, and organised by workshop. It is a span of time, and the conditions of making are what its work has in common.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-medieval-art","wd-q3624153"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-medieval-art","title":"Medieval art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_art"},{"id":"wd-q3624153","title":"medieval art (Q3624153) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3624153"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Melic poetry","description":"Ancient Greek lyric composed to be sung to the lyre, in monody by Sappho and Alcaeus or by a chorus in Pindar and Bacchylides. Its metres are quantitative and were built for music that is now lost, so much of what survives reads as fragments of something larger. The Alexandrian canon of nine lyric poets defines the body.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named ancient body of work with a fixed canon, its own metres and a documented performance practice; LCGFT files it under Lyric poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-melic-poetry","wp-greek-lyric"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"lyric-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Melic poetry under Lyric poetry; it is the Greek origin of the lyric and gives the category its name.","sourceIds":["lcgft-melic-poetry","wp-greek-lyric"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-melic-poetry","title":"Melic poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026431"},{"id":"wp-greek-lyric","title":"Greek lyric — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_lyric"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Melodramas (Drama)","description":"Drama that puts plot, incident and strong feeling ahead of shaded character, with music originally underscoring the action. It dominates the nineteenth-century popular stage in France and Britain and hands its machinery to early cinema. Its moral world is legible on sight, which is a technique and not an accident.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic mode with a dated dominance, a described machinery and a documented descent into film; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-melodramas-drama","wp-melodrama"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-melodramas-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-melodramas-drama","title":"Melodramas (Drama) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026432"},{"id":"wp-melodrama","title":"Melodrama — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Memoirs","description":"An account of one part of a life: a job, an illness, a marriage, a few years. It has autobiography's first person and claim to fact in a narrower frame, so the writing can slow down and stay inside scenes. In voice it is close to the personal essay, and in construction close to the novel. A memoirist settles what the period was about before settling what goes in.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Library of Congress separates it from autobiography by its narrower focus, and the modern form is written and published in quantity.","sourceIds":["lcgft-memoirs","wp-memoir"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"autobiographies","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Memoirs under Autobiographies, as autobiographies covering one event, period or theme.","sourceIds":["lcgft-memoirs"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-memoirs","title":"Memoirs — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2025026019"},{"id":"wp-memoir","title":"Memoir — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoir"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Memorates","description":"First-person accounts of an encounter with something uncanny, told as true by the person it happened to. Carl Wilhelm von Sydow introduced the term in the 1930s to separate these personal testimonies from legends that have settled into shared, traditional form. Russian bylichki are the best-known regional body of them.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A narrative form of oral tradition, collected and transcribed by folklorists.","sourceIds":["lcgft-memorates","wp-memorate"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-literature","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Memorates directly under Literature and relates it to Personal narratives. Placing it under Folk literature is our judgement, on what the record describes: first-person testimony of an uncanny encounter, collected and studied by folklorists. It refines the authority's filing and does not report it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-memorates"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Is a folklorists' classification of oral testimony a direction? Proposed because the manner (a sworn first-person account of the uncanny) is distinct and imitable.","The genre/form authority files Memorates under Literature; the LCSH subject heading relates it to folk literature, which is a different vocabulary. This cell relies on the genre/form record and states its own placement as a refinement. Re-point it to a Literature cell if one is ever written and the filing should be shown as well."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-memorates","title":"Memorates — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026433"},{"id":"wp-memorate","title":"Memorate — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorate"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Memory plays","description":"Plays narrated by a character who is remembering the events being staged, so the scenes are admittedly partial and shaped by the teller. Tennessee Williams coined the term in his production notes for The Glass Menagerie in 1944 and gave it its licence: sentiment, distortion and unrealistic staging are permitted because memory works that way. The narrator's presence inside and outside the action is the form's structure.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic form with a dated coinage by its own practitioner and a stated licence for how it may be staged; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-memory-plays","wp-memory-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-memory-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-memory-plays","title":"Memory plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2017026073"},{"id":"wp-memory-play","title":"Memory play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Memphis Group","description":"The Milan design collective founded by Ettore Sottsass in 1981. Laminate patterns, saturated unmixed colour, asymmetric stacked geometry and legs that do not match. The objects work as furniture and abandon the reduced palette and rectilinear discipline of the modernism they came out of.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named collective with a documented body of work.","sourceIds":["wp-memphis","aat-memphis"]},{"map":"design","explanation":"It is a design movement, and design languages take from its objects and graphics.","sourceIds":["wp-memphis"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-memphis","title":"Memphis Group — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Group"},{"id":"aat-memphis","title":"Memphis — Getty AAT 300265730","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300265730"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019f8af1-3605-75c2-b564-4c4448c79aa9","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Memphis Group (Milan, 1981)\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-memphis"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-01a05fe0-f91a-7ac0-9487-f3e614166313","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Memphis-era functional geometry\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-memphis"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-019f157e-8f8e-7f70-8847-e6da360aa900","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Memphis Group (Ettore Sottsass et al.)\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-memphis"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Mennonite literature","description":"Writing by and about Mennonites that emerged in the mid to late twentieth century and is discussed as both a movement and a genre. Rudy Wiebe, Di Brandt, Miriam Toews and Patrick Friesen are among the Canadian writers usually named, and much of it works at the friction between a pacifist religious community and the writer who leaves it. Conferences and journals treat it as a field.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-mennonite-literature","wd-q85851417"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline against the rule that declines community and identity labels. Kept because its own scholarship treats it as a movement with a shared argument about community and dissent; strike it if that reads as a subject."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-mennonite-literature","title":"Mennonite literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonite_literature"},{"id":"wd-q85851417","title":"Mennonite literature (Q85851417) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q85851417"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Metadramas","description":"Drama that points at its own theatricality, most often through a play within the play, a character who addresses the audience, or actors who discuss the performance they are in. Hamlet and Pirandello's Six Characters in Search of an Author are standing cases, and Lionel Abel gave the practice the name metatheatre in 1963. The device turns the audience's position into the argument.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic technique with a coined critical name, a canon and a described set of devices; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-metadramas","wp-metatheatre"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-metadramas"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-metadramas","title":"Metadramas — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026434"},{"id":"wp-metatheatre","title":"Metatheatre — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metatheatre"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Mexican Muralism","description":"A public painting programme funded by the Mexican state after the Revolution, in which Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros covered the walls of public buildings with the country's history. The murals are didactic by design, addressed to a largely non-reading public, and they place Indigenous Mexico at the centre of the national story. Fresco technique was revived and taught to make them.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-mexican-muralism","wd-q938864","aat-300107850"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"social-realism","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as a subclass of social realism.","sourceIds":["wd-q938864"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-mexican-muralism","title":"Mexican muralism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_muralism"},{"id":"wd-q938864","title":"Mexican muralism (Q938864) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q938864"},{"id":"aat-300107850","title":"Mexican Muralism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300107850","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300107850"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Mezzotint","description":"An intaglio process worked from dark to light. The plate is roughened all over with a rocker so that it would print solid black, and the image is then burnished and scraped back into it, which gives deep velvety shadows and soft gradation. It was the reproductive process of choice for painting in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A printmaking process with its own canon of reproductive and original prints.","sourceIds":["wp-mezzotint","aat-mezzotint"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"intaglio-printmaking","explanation":"The rocked and burnished plate is inked in its recesses and printed under press, like every intaglio process.","sourceIds":["wp-mezzotint"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-mezzotint","title":"Mezzotint — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mezzotint"},{"id":"aat-mezzotint","title":"mezzotint (process) — Getty AAT 300053233","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300053233"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019f4929-b02b-7bc1-b2d6-d48f3a1c05c9","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Mezzotint printmaking\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-mezzotint"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-01a03f5c-182a-7743-9baf-77edd4597a07","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Mezzotint\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-mezzotint"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019efd19-7805-7fb0-9543-c19fd9f65537","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Mezzotint printmaking tradition\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-mezzotint"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-01a05fe4-7b5d-7751-b00b-4081ec559558","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Manière noire (mezzotint)\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-mezzotint"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Microblogs","description":"Posts short enough to read at a glance, without titles, shown in a stream. The service fixes the length and the reply, so writers compress, front-load, and write for someone who is scrolling. Threads and quote-posts are how a longer argument gets made inside the form. Readers judge a post in the stream, by whether they answer it or pass it on.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Microblogs under Blogs, and an enormous amount of writing is published this way.","sourceIds":["lcgft-microblogs","wp-microblogging"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"blogs","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Microblogs under Blogs, as blogging in short untitled posts.","sourceIds":["lcgft-microblogs"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["The leaf under this cell is Tweetstorm, found in the trade press where criticism had named nothing. Practitioner sources name manners critics have not yet written up.","The same reservation as Blogs applies here. This may be a medium and not a direction."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-microblogs","title":"Microblogs — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026172"},{"id":"wp-microblogging","title":"Microblogging — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microblogging"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Mime plays","description":"Performances carried entirely by gesture and body, without speech and often with music. The line runs from Roman pantomimus through commedia's physical business to the twentieth-century schools of Decroux, Barrault and Marceau, who codified it as a technique to be taught. The absence of words is the discipline: everything has to be made visible.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A performance form with codified twentieth-century technique, named schools and a long history; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-mime-plays","wp-mime-artist"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-mime-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-mime-plays","title":"Mime plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026117"},{"id":"wp-mime-artist","title":"Mime artist — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mime_artist"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Mingei","description":"The Japanese folk-craft movement Yanagi Soetsu named in the 1920s, which argued that the ordinary handmade object of an unnamed maker is beautiful. Its objects are unsigned, made for use in quantity, and finished in local materials with the marks of the process left visible.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named movement with a documented body of work and its own museums.","sourceIds":["wp-mingei","aat-mingei"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-art","explanation":"Its Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus record gives folk art as its broader concept; mingei is the Japanese folk-craft movement named by Yanagi.","sourceIds":["aat-mingei","wp-mingei"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-mingei","title":"Mingei — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingei"},{"id":"aat-mingei","title":"mingei — Getty AAT 300260035","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300260035"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019f9a3b-f328-7722-b884-31027d19d2a7","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Mingei folk-craft movement\" (Draft).","sourceIds":["wp-mingei"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019f7079-05df-7ea1-a013-1947675a78d5","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Japanese mingei folk-craft pottery\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-mingei"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-019f9a3b-f56e-7d21-b4cd-e2f1d8c00a58","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Mingei folk-craft movement\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-mingei"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Minimalism","description":"Art reduced to its essentials, with the object and the viewer's experience of it in the room left as the whole content and the artist's hand withdrawn. {"version":3,"name":"Mummers' plays","description":"English folk plays performed at fixed seasons by amateur troupes in disguise, turning on a combat, a death and a comic revival by a doctor. {"version":3,"name":"Muwashshaḥāt","description":"Strophic Arabic poems of five to seven stanzas developed in al-Andalus in the tenth and eleventh centuries, each stanza in two parts with differing rhyme patterns and a closing kharja that may be in another language. {"version":3,"name":"Naturalism (theatre)","description":"A movement in European theatre from the late nineteenth century that set out to produce the illusion of real life on stage, with real objects, ordinary speech and the fourth wall kept closed. {"version":3,"name":"Noir fiction","description":"Crime fiction told from inside the wrongdoing, where the protagonist is compromised and the ending closes off escape. {"version":3,"name":"Noir plays","description":"Plays of crime in which the line between criminal and hero is not drawn and the protagonist's decision closes off escape. Its material overlaps detective drama, and its structure does not.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The compromised-protagonist structure worked out in dramatic form. {"version":3,"name":"Nonfiction comics","description":"Non-fiction told in the comics medium, in formats from the newspaper strip to the trade paperback. It grew out of literary journalism and the illustrated reporting that preceded photography. The Library of Congress files comics journalism and biographical comics under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Drawn panels used for reporting and record, with a body of work from Joe Sacco onward; the Library of Congress files it under Comics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-nonfiction-comics","wp-nonfiction-comics"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"The Library of Congress record gives Comics (Graphic works) as its broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-nonfiction-comics"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-nonfiction-comics","title":"Nonfiction comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026453"},{"id":"wp-nonfiction-comics","title":"Non-fiction comics — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction_comics"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Nonfiction novels","description":"Books that tell real events about real people with the techniques of a novel: scene construction, dialogue, point of view. John Hersey's Hiroshima (1946) set the pattern that Capote, Mailer and Didion followed, and the New Journalism of the 1960s and 1970s carried it into reporting. Faction is the slang name.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A technique of narrative treatment applied to factual material; LCGFT files it under both Fiction and Creative nonfiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-nonfiction-novels","wp-non-fiction-novel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"creative-nonfiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Creative nonfiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-nonfiction-novels"]},{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-nonfiction-novels"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-nonfiction-novels","title":"Nonfiction novels — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026454"},{"id":"wp-non-fiction-novel","title":"Non-fiction novel — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction_novel"},{"id":"wp-new-journalism","title":"New Journalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Journalism"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Nō plays","description":"Japanese classical theatre performed since the fourteenth century, in which music, dance and poetry are held to a very slow, fixed ceremony. Zeami's treatises set out its aesthetics and much of its repertoire, and its plays commonly turn on a ghost who returns to complete something. Masks, a bare stage and a chorus carry the whole of it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named theatrical tradition with a written poetics, a fixed repertoire and six centuries of continuous practice; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-no-plays","wp-noh"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-no-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-no-plays","title":"Nō plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026450"},{"id":"wp-noh","title":"Noh — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noh"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Northern Renaissance","description":"The Renaissance north of the Alps, beginning in earnest in the last years of the fifteenth century and taking a different form in each country. Oil technique, minute observed detail and a Christian subject matter distinguish it, in Van Eyck, Dürer, Bruegel and Bosch. Printing and the Reformation formed it as much as Italian example did.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-northern-renaissance","wd-q610877","aat-300252246"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"renaissance-art","explanation":"Its own article calls it the Renaissance that occurred in Europe north of the Alps, and this cell covers the period as it begins in Italy and spreads north.","sourceIds":["wp-northern-renaissance"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-northern-renaissance","title":"Northern Renaissance — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Renaissance"},{"id":"wd-q610877","title":"Northern Renaissance (Q610877) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q610877"},{"id":"aat-300252246","title":"Northern Renaissance — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300252246","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300252246"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Norwegian new realism","description":"The dominant tendency in Norwegian literature in the first half of the twentieth century, returning to realist narration with a heavier psychological and moral weight. Sigrid Undset, the later Knut Hamsun, Johan Falkberget and Olaf Bull worked in it, and two of them took the Nobel Prize. It follows the modernist and neo-romantic 1890s and answers them.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-norwegian-new-realism","wd-q10744336"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-norwegian-new-realism","title":"Norwegian new realism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_new_realism"},{"id":"wd-q10744336","title":"Norwegian new realism (Q10744336) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q10744336"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Nouveau Réalisme","description":"A movement declared in Milan in 1960 by the critic Pierre Restany with Yves Klein, whose manifesto proposed new ways of perceiving the real. Its artists took the material of the city directly into the work: torn posters, crushed cars, accumulations of objects, the blue monochrome. It is the French answer to Neo-Dada and Pop art and reaches the same street from another direction.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-nouveau-realisme","wd-q276308","aat-300112105"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-nouveau-realisme","title":"Nouveau réalisme — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouveau_réalisme"},{"id":"wd-q276308","title":"Nouveau réalisme (Q276308) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q276308"},{"id":"aat-300112105","title":"Nouveau Réalisme — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300112105","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300112105"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Novellas","description":"Prose fiction of middle length, longer than a short story and shorter than a novel, usually holding one situation to its conclusion without subplot. The word comes from the Italian novella, a short tale. German criticism treated the Novelle as a form with rules of its own, and the length has its own canon in Melville, James, Conrad and Mann.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form category defined by length with its own criticism and canon; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-novellas","wp-novella"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-novellas"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["A form defined by length. {"version":3,"name":"Novels","description":"Extended prose fiction published as a book, long enough to carry several lines of action and to change a reader's sense of a life over time. The European form settles in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries with Cervantes, Defoe and Richardson, though long prose fiction is older in Japan and in the Hellenistic world. Length is what makes its characteristic moves available: digression, subplot, and the slow accumulation of a milieu.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form category kept as a nesting parent: LCGFT files Cell phone novels, Sentimental novels, Novels in verse and eleven more terms under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-novels","wp-novel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-novels"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Kept as a nesting parent, in the same way Lyric poetry was kept in B8. {"version":3,"name":"Novels in verse","description":"Novel-length narratives written as poetry, carrying the scale and character work of a novel in metrical or free verse. Pushkin's Eugene Onegin and Browning's The Ring and the Book are the nineteenth-century cases; the form returns strongly in contemporary writing for young readers. {"version":3,"name":"Novels of manners","description":"Realistic fiction that describes in detail the customs, habits, values and expectations of a particular society, and lets judgment of its people arise from how they speak and behave. {"version":3,"name":"Novísimos","description":"A group of young Spanish poets gathered in Josep Maria Castellet's 1970 anthology Nueve novísimos poetas españoles, culturally allusive, media-saturated and deliberately at a distance from the social poetry that preceded them. The anthology made the group.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Nursery rhymes","description":"Short traditional rhymes and songs for children, carried orally and printed from the eighteenth century onward, when Mother Goose collections fixed many of the texts. Their sound stays exact while their sense goes, and they outlast changes in the language. Iona and Peter Opie's collecting made them a documented body.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A folk verse tradition with a collected corpus and its own scholarship; LCGFT files Counting-out rhymes, Cumulative rhymes and Jump rope rhymes under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-nursery-rhymes","wp-nursery-rhyme"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-nursery-rhymes"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-nursery-rhymes","title":"Nursery rhymes — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026459"},{"id":"wp-nursery-rhyme","title":"Nursery rhyme — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nursery_rhyme"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Occasional verse","description":"Poems written for a particular occasion: a wedding, a death, a coronation, a departure. The occasion sets the form and the audience, and the poem is often made to be spoken aloud. The Library of Congress files epithalamia under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Verse tied to performance and patronage, with named forms for birth, marriage and death; the Library of Congress files it under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-occasional-verse","wp-occasional-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"The Library of Congress record gives Poetry as its broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-occasional-verse"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-occasional-verse","title":"Occasional verse — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026460"},{"id":"wp-occasional-poetry","title":"Occasional poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occasional_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Odes","description":"Formal lyric poems of praise or elevated reflection, built in elaborate stanzas. The Greek line divides into the public Pindaric ode with its triadic structure and the private Horatian ode in repeated stanzas, and English poetry adds an irregular kind used by Wordsworth and Keats. The stanza's difficulty is part of the ceremony.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named lyric genre with described sub-forms, a stated formal difficulty and a canon in several languages; LCGFT files it under Lyric poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-odes","wp-ode"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"lyric-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Odes under Lyric poetry; the ode speaks in a single voice at high formal pitch.","sourceIds":["lcgft-odes","wp-ode"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-odes","title":"Odes — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026461"},{"id":"wp-ode","title":"Ode — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ode"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Offbeat generation","description":"A loose association of British writers named by Andrew Gallix in 3:AM Magazine in 2006, united less by style than by working outside a publishing industry driven by marketing. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-offbeat-generation","wd-q7079030"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-offbeat-generation","title":"Offbeat generation — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offbeat_generation"},{"id":"wd-q7079030","title":"Offbeat generation (Q7079030) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q7079030"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"One-act plays","description":"Plays complete in one act, running roughly twenty to forty minutes and following one situation without an interval. The form became a serious one with the little-theatre and art-theatre movements at the end of the nineteenth century, and festivals and competitions have kept it alive since. The one unbroken span is the constraint: there is no interval to reset an audience.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form defined by a structural constraint, with its own festivals, competitions and canon; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-one-act-plays","wp-one-act-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-one-act-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-one-act-plays","title":"One-act plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026462"},{"id":"wp-one-act-play","title":"One-act play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-act_play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Onirism","description":"A Romanian literary school of the 1960s built on the dream as a structure, using automatic writing and other Surrealist techniques under a communist state that soon suppressed it. Dumitru Țepeneag and Leonid Dimov are its central figures. Its programme was explicitly aesthetic, which was itself the political problem.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-onirism","wd-q3306247"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-onirism","title":"Onirism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onirism"},{"id":"wd-q3306247","title":"Onirism (Q3306247) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3306247"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Op Art","description":"Abstraction built to act on the eye, using precise geometric pattern, high contrast and colour interaction to produce flicker, movement and after-images. Bridget Riley and Victor Vasarely are its central figures, and the term dates from 1964 and the Responsive Eye exhibition that followed. The picture is completed in the viewer's perception, which is the claim the work makes.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-op-art","wd-q182331","aat-300022195"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"geometric-abstraction","explanation":"Its own article defines the term as a form of abstract art working through manipulated geometrical patterns.","sourceIds":["wp-op-art"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-op-art","title":"Op art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Op_art"},{"id":"wd-q182331","title":"op art (Q182331) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q182331"},{"id":"aat-300022195","title":"Op Art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300022195","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300022195"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Op-ed","description":"A short signed argument by someone outside the publication, on one issue, usually 500 to 700 words. The New York Times made the modern form when it opened the page opposite its editorials. The piece states its position early and runs one line of argument, and the writer's standing on the subject is part of the case. Length constrains everything else.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A newspaper form with fixed conventions, written by many hands since 1970.","sourceIds":["wp-op-ed"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"editorials","explanation":"It is opinion writing on the editorial pages, signed and written from outside the publication.","sourceIds":["wp-op-ed"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-op-ed","title":"Op-ed — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Op-ed"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-01a08456-0162-70d0-9637-848b9972097f","explanation":"The record's credits name the register \"Op-ed\" (Draft). Its corpus is four passages the pipeline wrote in register, so no columnist's prose was used.","sourceIds":["wp-op-ed"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Orientalism","description":"The Western depiction of Eastern subjects, a nineteenth-century academic speciality in painting of West Asia and North Africa, full of harems, bazaars and desert light. Edward Said's 1978 book turned the term into a critique of how that depiction served empire. Both senses are now in use and the cell holds the practice and the argument about it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-orientalism","wd-q42865","aat-300055784"]},{"map":"writing","explanation":"The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-orientalism","wd-q42865","aat-300055784"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-orientalism","title":"Orientalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orientalism"},{"id":"wd-q42865","title":"Orientalism (Q42865) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q42865"},{"id":"aat-300055784","title":"Orientalism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300055784","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300055784"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Orphism (art)","description":"An offshoot of Cubism towards pure abstraction and bright colour, named by Guillaume Apollinaire in 1912 after Orpheus. Robert and Sonia Delaunay are its central figures, working from simultaneous colour contrast. It is Cubism with the colour turned back up.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-orphism-art","wd-q519443","aat-300134101"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"cubism","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as part of cubism.","sourceIds":["wd-q519443"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-orphism-art","title":"Orphism (art) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orphism_(art)"},{"id":"wd-q519443","title":"Orphism (Q519443) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q519443"},{"id":"aat-300134101","title":"Orphism (art) — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300134101","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300134101"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Outdoor literature","description":"First-person prose about being out in country that is indifferent to you: sailing, climbing, walking, exploring, surviving. The interest is in what the place demanded and what the writer did about it. That makes the detail practical before it is scenic. Slocum's Sailing Alone Around the World is named in the reference as a classic of it, and the sea end of the genre is where this collection's voyage records sit. The register stays level under strain, and the drama comes from what is reported.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The reference names the subgenres and lists the canon, and all of it is prose.","sourceIds":["wp-outdoor-literature"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"travel-writing","explanation":"The reference says travel literature is similar with considerable overlap, and separates the two by whether the writing is out of doors.","sourceIds":["wp-outdoor-literature"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"nature-writing","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Both put a first-person observer in a real place. Nature writing reflects, and this one records what the place required.","sourceIds":["wp-outdoor-literature"]}],"questions":["Dana's Two Years Before the Mast is attached here and the cited article does not name it. The placement rests on the record's own credits instead of on the reference. A source naming the book in this genre would settle it."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-outdoor-literature","title":"Outdoor literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outdoor_literature"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-019f38cf-311b-7c21-985c-5cc0ec5448f2","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Sea-narrative tradition\" (UnderReview). It is built from Two Years Before the Mast of 1840, a first-person account of a voyage worked from the forecastle.","sourceIds":["wp-outdoor-literature"]},{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-019f38cf-6c62-7e00-9a97-d8bb19a6867b","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Voyage-narrative tradition\" (UnderReview). It is built from Sailing Alone Around the World of 1900, which the reference names as a classic of this genre.","sourceIds":["wp-outdoor-literature"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Outsider Art","description":"Work by self-taught makers standing outside art training and the art world, often produced under psychiatric care or in isolation and only later collected and exhibited. Roger Cardinal coined the English term in 1972 as a translation of Dubuffet's art brut. The category is contested from inside: as the work enters museums, the outside it names moves.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-outsider-art","wd-q594150","aat-300056472"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-outsider-art","title":"Outsider art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outsider_art"},{"id":"wd-q594150","title":"outsider art (Q594150) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q594150"},{"id":"aat-300056472","title":"Outsider Art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300056472","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300056472"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Palinodes","description":"Poems in which the poet takes back something said in an earlier poem. Stesichorus wrote the first recorded one in the seventh century BC, retracting an attack on Helen, and Chaucer's retraction works the same way. The form needs the earlier poem to exist, so it is always a second act.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named genre defined by its relation to another work, with a documented origin and a canon; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-palinodes","wp-palinode"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-palinodes"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-palinodes","title":"Palinodes — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026465"},{"id":"wp-palinode","title":"Palinode — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palinode"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Panchatantra stories","description":"Retellings of the Sanskrit Panchatantra, a collection of animal fables set inside a frame story and framed again as a prince's education in worldly conduct. The text moved into Middle Persian in the sixth century, into Arabic as Kalila wa-Dimna, and from there into Hebrew, Latin and most European languages, gathering changes at every step. This cell covers that retelling tradition, which many writers extended over many centuries.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Retold across many languages instead of copied from a fixed text, and LCGFT files it under Fables.","sourceIds":["lcgft-panchatantra-stories","wp-panchatantra"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fables","explanation":"LCGFT files Panchatantra stories under Fables; the collection is the Sanskrit branch of the animal fable.","sourceIds":["lcgft-panchatantra-stories","wp-panchatantra"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline: the tradition is named after a single text. Proposed as a cell because the retellings are by many hands in many languages and each is a different work; strike it if a cell named for one text is a study inside Fables instead."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-panchatantra-stories","title":"Panchatantra stories — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026143"},{"id":"wp-panchatantra","title":"Panchatantra — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panchatantra"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pantoums","description":"Poems in quatrains where the second and fourth lines of each stanza become the first and third of the next, so every line is heard twice. It comes into French from the Malay pantun berkait and was taken up by Baudelaire and later by English poets. The repetition drags the poem backwards as it advances, which is the effect the form exists for.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with a stated repetition rule, a documented transmission from Malay verse and a canon; LCGFT files it under Quatrains.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pantoums","wp-pantoum"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"quatrains","explanation":"LCGFT files Pantoums under Quatrains; the form is built entirely from interlocking four-line stanzas.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pantoums","wp-pantoum"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pantoums","title":"Pantoums — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026466"},{"id":"wp-pantoum","title":"Pantoum — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantoum"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Parables","description":"Short plain stories about people that carry a lesson the hearer has to draw out. The Gospel parables are the best-known body in English, and the form appears across the wisdom traditions; unlike the fable it keeps its characters human. The lesson is usually left unstated, so the story does the arguing.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named narrative form with a stated structural rule and a canon across several traditions; LCGFT files it under Exempla, which is already a live cell.","sourceIds":["lcgft-parables","wp-parable"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"exempla","explanation":"LCGFT files Parables under Exempla; a parable is a short narrative told to make a moral point.","sourceIds":["lcgft-parables","wp-parable"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-parables","title":"Parables — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026467"},{"id":"wp-parable","title":"Parable — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Paranormal comics","description":"Comics in which the supernatural is real and ordinary characters deal with it: spirits, possession, witchcraft, second sight. Hellblazer is a standing case in the English-language tradition and the material is old in manga. Drawing a spirit settles the question of whether it is there, so the tension has to come from elsewhere.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The supernatural premise worked out in comics. The cell Paranormal fiction works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-comics","wp-supernatural-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Comics; the direction is worked out through the form's own panel grammar.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-comics","wp-supernatural-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Paranormal fiction, Paranormal drama, Paranormal poetry and Paranormal comics. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-paranormal-comics","title":"Paranormal comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026468"},{"id":"wp-supernatural-fiction","title":"Supernatural fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Paranormal drama","description":"Plays in which the supernatural is real inside the story and ordinary characters deal with it: spirits, possession, witchcraft, second sight. The stage has carried this since the mystery cycles and it remains a working popular form. What is offstage does much of the work.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The supernatural premise worked out in dramatic form. The cell Paranormal fiction works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-drama","wp-supernatural-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Paranormal fiction and Paranormal drama. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-paranormal-drama","title":"Paranormal drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2017026044"},{"id":"wp-supernatural-fiction","title":"Supernatural fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Paranormal fiction","description":"Fiction in which the supernatural is real inside the story: ghosts, spirits, witchcraft, possession and second sight act on ordinary characters and are treated as fact. It descends from folk belief and from the Gothic, and it separates from horror by aim, since a supernatural story may be elegiac or comic. Wikipedia and most criticism call the same body of work supernatural fiction.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A family of made work organised around a shared premise, with a long history and many hands; LCGFT files Ghost stories, Vampire fiction and Witch fiction under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-fiction","wp-supernatural-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Its LCGFT parent Monster fiction was declined in pass 1 as subject-defined. This one is kept because the supernatural is a premise the story is built on rather than a topic it covers, but the two calls sit close together."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-paranormal-fiction","title":"Paranormal fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026469"},{"id":"wp-supernatural-fiction","title":"Supernatural fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Paranormal poetry","description":"Poems in which the supernatural is real and acts on the speaker or the characters: spirits, second sight, witchcraft, the dead who answer. Ballads carry much of the older material and the Romantic and Gothic revivals took it up deliberately. Verse suits the material because a poem need not explain what it shows.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The supernatural premise worked out in verse. The cell Paranormal fiction works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-poetry","wp-supernatural-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Paranormal fiction, Paranormal drama and Paranormal poetry. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-paranormal-poetry","title":"Paranormal poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026065"},{"id":"wp-supernatural-fiction","title":"Supernatural fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Paranormal romance fiction","description":"Romance fiction in which one of the lovers, or the world they meet in, is supernatural: vampires, shapeshifters, ghosts or the fae. It emerged as a distinct publishing category in the 1990s and became one of the largest in the 2000s. The two sets of conventions constrain each other, since the romance must resolve while the supernatural rules must hold.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A crossover genre with its own publishing category, conventions and body of work; LCGFT files it under Romance fiction and Paranormal fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-romance-fiction","wp-paranormal-romance"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"romance-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Paranormal romance under Romance fiction; the love relationship carries the plot and the ending resolves it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-romance-fiction","wp-paranormal-romance"]},{"cellId":"paranormal-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Paranormal romance under Paranormal fiction; the supernatural is real inside the story.","sourceIds":["lcgft-paranormal-romance-fiction","wp-paranormal-romance"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-paranormal-romance-fiction","title":"Paranormal romance fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2024026063"},{"id":"wp-paranormal-romance","title":"Paranormal romance — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranormal_romance"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Parnassianism","description":"A French poetic movement of roughly the 1860s to the 1890s, between Romanticism and Symbolism, which wanted exact form, impersonality and finish, taking Gautier's art for art's sake as its principle. Leconte de Lisle, Heredia and the young Mallarmé published in the anthology Le Parnasse contemporain. The metaphor is sculpture: the poem is worked until it is cold and hard.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-parnassianism","wd-q335652"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-parnassianism","title":"Parnassianism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parnassianism"},{"id":"wd-q335652","title":"parnassianism (Q335652) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q335652"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Parodies (Literature)","description":"Imitations that exaggerate the manner of a writer, school, genre or work in order to mock it or comment on it. Critics place parody between pastiche, which imitates in tribute, and burlesque, which drags high material to low ends. LCGFT lists burlesques as its narrower form.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A literary technique with anthologies of its own; parody in other arts is a separate membership once cited.","sourceIds":["lcgft-parodies-literature","wp-parody"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[{"cellId":"satirical-literature","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Parody is one of satire's standing instruments, and much parody is written to satirical ends.","sourceIds":["wp-parody"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-parodies-literature","title":"Parodies (Literature) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026470"},{"id":"wp-parody","title":"Parody — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Participatory drama","description":"Plays built so that the audience joins the performance. Boal's forum theatre, in which spectators stop a scene and replace a character, is the most fully theorised form; work for very young audiences and immersive productions use the same principle differently. The script has to leave room for what the audience does.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A dramatic practice with a theorised method and a documented range of applications; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-participatory-drama","wp-participatory-theatre"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-participatory-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-participatory-drama","title":"Participatory drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026471"},{"id":"wp-participatory-theatre","title":"Participatory theatre — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Participatory_theatre"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Passion plays","description":"Plays staging the trial, suffering, death and resurrection of Jesus, performed at Lent and Easter and often by a whole community. The Oberammergau play, vowed in 1633 and performed each decade since, is the most continuous instance. Their history includes a record of antisemitic representation that later productions have had to confront.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic tradition with a continuous performance history, a communal production practice and its own contested reception; LCGFT files it under Bible plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-passion-plays","wp-passion-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"bible-plays","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Bible plays as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-passion-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-passion-plays","title":"Passion plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026472"},{"id":"wp-passion-play","title":"Passion Play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_Play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pastiches (Literature)","description":"Works assembled in the manner of another writer, or stitched from borrowed passages of several, as homage or play. The word comes from the Italian pasticcio, a pie of mixed ingredients, and since postmodernism the practice has been read as deliberate, witty imitation. LCGFT lists centos, poems made from other poets' lines, as a narrower form.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A literary technique of stylistic imitation; the same word names practices in art, music and architecture.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastiches-literature","wp-pastiche"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[{"cellId":"parodies-literature","label":"contrasted with","explanation":"Pastiche imitates in tribute where parody imitates to mock; the two share the technique and differ in intent.","sourceIds":["wp-pastiche"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pastiches-literature","title":"Pastiches (Literature) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026049"},{"id":"wp-pastiche","title":"Pastiche — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastiche"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pastoral drama","description":"Plays set among shepherds and country people that hold rural life up as a standard. The Italian Renaissance made it a major form with Tasso's Aminta in 1573 and Guarini's Il pastor fido, and it passes into English through Fletcher and Jonson. Its artificiality is deliberate: nobody mistook these shepherds for farmers.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The pastoral mode worked out in dramatic form. The cell Pastoral fiction works the same direction out in prose, and the Italian Renaissance gave it its own canon.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-drama","wp-pastoral"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Pastoral fiction and Pastoral drama. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pastoral-drama","title":"Pastoral drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026473"},{"id":"wp-pastoral","title":"Pastoral — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pastoral elegies","description":"Elegies that mourn through the pastoral convention, making the dead person a shepherd and the landscape a mourner. Theocritus and Virgil supply the machinery, and Milton's Lycidas and Shelley's Adonais are the great English instances. The convention holds the grief at a distance where it can be handled.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named genre combining two named traditions, with a classical origin and a canonical English corpus; LCGFT files it under Pastoral poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-elegies","wp-pastoral-elegy"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"pastoral-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Pastoral elegies under Pastoral poetry; the mourning is carried entirely by the pastoral convention.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-elegies","wp-pastoral-elegy"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pastoral-elegies","title":"Pastoral elegies — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026474"},{"id":"wp-pastoral-elegy","title":"Pastoral elegy — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral_elegy"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pastoral fiction","description":"Fiction that sets country life against the world that reads about it and makes rural simplicity the standard. The mode descends from Theocritus and Virgil through Renaissance prose romance to the regional novel, and it is usually written by and for people who are not shepherds. Its recurring move is the retreat: a character leaves the centre, learns something, and the return is the argument.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A mode with a continuous history from classical poetry to the modern novel and a large critical literature; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-fiction","wp-pastoral"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pastoral-fiction","title":"Pastoral fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026475"},{"id":"wp-pastoral","title":"Pastoral — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pastoral poetry","description":"Short poems that set country life up as a standard, with shepherds who have leisure enough to sing and argue. Theocritus's Idylls and Virgil's Eclogues found the tradition and the Renaissance revives it across Europe. Its artificiality is open: the shepherds are a convention both poet and reader agree to.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A mode with a founding classical canon and a continuous European history; LCGFT files Pastoral elegies and Pastourelles under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-poetry","wp-pastoral"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastoral-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Pastoral fiction, Pastoral drama and Pastoral poetry. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pastoral-poetry","title":"Pastoral poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026476"},{"id":"wp-pastoral","title":"Pastoral — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pastourelles","description":"Old French lyric poems in which a knight meets a shepherdess and tries to seduce her, and she refuses him, outwits him or does not escape. The situation is fixed and the poems are read against each other for how they handle it. It is a pastoral form with the coercion left visible.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named lyric genre with a fixed situation, a defined Old French corpus and a body of criticism about how the situation is handled; LCGFT files it under Pastoral poetry and Lyric poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastourelles","wp-pastourelle"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"pastoral-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Pastourelles under Pastoral poetry; the encounter takes place in the pastoral world and uses its conventions.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastourelles","wp-pastourelle"]},{"cellId":"lyric-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Lyric poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pastourelles"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pastourelles","title":"Pastourelles — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026477"},{"id":"wp-pastourelle","title":"Pastourelle — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastourelle"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pattern and Decoration","description":"An American movement of the mid-1970s to early 1980s that made ornament, textile and the decorative into serious painting, against Minimalism's austerity. It drew on Islamic, African and folk pattern and on feminist arguments about which crafts had been dismissed as women's work. {"version":3,"name":"Pattern poetry","description":"Poems set on the page in the shape of the thing they are about: wings, an altar, a bottle, a cross.
