The shape illustrates the poem, which is what separates it from concrete poetry, where the typography carries the meaning itself.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named visual form with an ancient origin and a continuous canon; LCGFT files it under Visual poetry and keeps it apart from Concrete poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pattern-poetry","wp-calligram"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"visual-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Visual poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-pattern-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-pattern-poetry","title":"Pattern poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026478"},{"id":"wp-calligram","title":"Calligram — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calligram"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Performance art","description":"Work in which the artist is present and what they do is the material, made in front of an audience or recorded for one. It gathered as a named practice in the 1960s, and its terms are time, space, the body, the artist's presence, and the relation to the public. Usually only a photograph or a film is left afterwards, and how much of the work that carries is argued about inside the practice.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A practice in the visual arts with its own literature, museums and canon since the 1960s.","sourceIds":["wp-performance-art"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Fluxus, Gutai and Body Art are all made by doing something in front of people, and all three are left as roots or placed elsewhere; whether any of them sits under this cell needs a reading of their own sources."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-performance-art","title":"Performance art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance_art"},{"id":"wd-q213156","title":"performance art (Q213156) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q213156"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pittura Metafisica","description":"An Italian style developed by Giorgio de Chirico from 1910 and joined by Carlo Carrà, painting empty arcaded squares, long shadows, mannequins and incongruous objects in a hard, still light. {"version":3,"name":"Plain English","description":"Writing meant to be understood on one reading by someone with no background in the subject: common words, short sentences, the reader's question answered first. Government letters, contracts, forms and internal operational writing are where it is used. The difficulty is keeping the precision after the technical vocabulary goes.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A prescriptive register with a movement behind it and a shelf of published guidance.","sourceIds":["wp-plain-english","digitalgov-plain-language"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"style-manuals","explanation":"Its body of work is a shelf of guides setting how institutional writing is done, which is what the style manual heading covers.","sourceIds":["digitalgov-plain-language"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-plain-english","title":"Plain English — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plain_English"},{"id":"digitalgov-plain-language","title":"Plain language guide — Digital.gov (the United States federal plain language guidelines)","url":"https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Plough Monday plays","description":"English folk plays performed on the first Monday after Epiphany, when the ploughing year began and ploughmen went about the parish with a decorated plough. {"version":3,"name":"Popular science","description":"Science written or spoken for people outside it, by researchers or by writers who report on them. The cited history runs from Greek and Roman antiquity, through a handbook tradition that survived into print, to Fontenelle's Conversations on the Plurality of Worlds in 1686 and the popularisations that followed Newton. By 1830 John Herschel was arguing in a letter to Whewell that the public needed digests of what was known in each branch. The working problem has not changed: explain the thing without the mathematics that makes it exact, and stop short of a claim the work does not support.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Its practitioners are named and its body of work is continuous, in print and in the lecture hall.","sourceIds":["wp-popular-science"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"popular-works","explanation":"Writing for a reader without the training, narrowed to science.","sourceIds":["wp-popular-science"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-popular-science","title":"Popular science — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_science"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Popular works","description":"Writing that explains a specialist subject to a reader who has none of the training. The writer decides what can be assumed, what has to be built up first, and what to leave out. Those three decisions set everything after them. It covers science, law, medicine and history alike, and the Library of Congress carries it as one heading. The difficulty is in the subject, and the sentences do not add to it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The Library of Congress carries it as a genre for works written for the layperson.","sourceIds":["lcgft-popular-works"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["No parent yet. The Library of Congress files it under Informational works, a cataloguing heading with no practice of its own."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-popular-works","title":"Popular works — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2025026092"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Portal fantasy fiction","description":"Fantasy in which a character crosses from an ordinary world into a separate one and the crossing is one of its events. Carroll's Alice, Baum's Oz and Lewis's Narnia are the standing examples, and the crossing lets the strange world be explained to the visitor and so to the reader. Farah Mendlesohn's taxonomy of fantasy made portal-quest fantasy a working critical category.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A structural device with a critical taxonomy behind it and a large canon; LCGFT files it under Fantasy fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-portal-fantasy-fiction","wp-portal-fantasy"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fantasy-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Portal fantasy fiction under Fantasy fiction; the world crossed into is a secondary world.","sourceIds":["lcgft-portal-fantasy-fiction","wp-portal-fantasy"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-portal-fantasy-fiction","title":"Portal fantasy fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026057"},{"id":"wp-portal-fantasy","title":"Portal fantasy — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portal_fantasy"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Post-Impressionism","description":"The French painting of roughly 1886 to 1905 that came after Impressionism and turned from recording light towards structure, symbol and personal expression. Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin and Seurat are its four principal figures, alike only in what they rejected. Roger Fry coined the term for a London exhibition in 1910, well after the fact.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-post-impressionism","wd-q166713","aat-300021508"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-post-impressionism","title":"Post-Impressionism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionism"},{"id":"wd-q166713","title":"Post-impressionism (Q166713) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q166713"},{"id":"aat-300021508","title":"Post-Impressionism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300021508","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300021508"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Post-Internet","description":"A loosely defined movement of the 2010s made when the internet had stopped being a novelty and became the condition everything is made in. Marisa Olson coined the term in 2006 for her own work, and the art it names often circulates as an image of an object as much as an object. Its subject is what constant circulation does to a thing.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-post-internet","wd-q17299972"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"net-art","explanation":"The movement grew out of earlier internet art.","sourceIds":["wp-post-internet"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-post-internet","title":"Post-Internet — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Internet"},{"id":"wd-q17299972","title":"post-internet (Q17299972) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q17299972"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Postminimalism","description":"Work of the late 1960s and early 1970s that took Minimalism's clarity and let process, gravity, softness and chance back in. Poor and unstable materials are used deliberately, against the fabricated box.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-postminimalism","wd-q2394116","aat-300112731"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"minimalism","explanation":"Pincus-Witten coined the term for work influenced by Minimalism, or attempting to develop and go beyond it.","sourceIds":["wp-postminimalism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-postminimalism","title":"Postminimalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postminimalism"},{"id":"wd-q2394116","title":"postminimalism (Q2394116) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2394116"},{"id":"aat-300112731","title":"Postminimalism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300112731","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300112731"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Post-Painterly Abstraction","description":"A term Clement Greenberg used for his 1964 Los Angeles exhibition, naming abstraction that dropped Abstract Expressionism's loaded gesture for flat, clear colour and open composition. The name is a critic's construction and carries his argument with it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-post-painterly-abstraction","wd-q1962478"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"abstract-art","explanation":"Greenberg's term names abstract painting that had dropped the loaded gesture for flat colour, so it names a strand inside abstraction.","sourceIds":["wp-post-painterly-abstraction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-post-painterly-abstraction","title":"Post-painterly abstraction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-painterly_abstraction"},{"id":"wd-q1962478","title":"Post-painterly Abstraction (Q1962478) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1962478"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Precisionism","description":"An American movement after the First World War that painted grain elevators, factories, bridges and skyscrapers as clean geometry in flat planes of light, with detail removed. Charles Demuth and Charles Sheeler are its principal painters, drawing on Cubism, Purism and Futurism. Its subject is industry and its manner is admiring and impersonal.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-precisionism","wd-q1578378"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"american-modernism","explanation":"Its own article opens by calling it a modernist art movement that emerged in the United States after the First World War.","sourceIds":["wp-precisionism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-precisionism","title":"Precisionism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precisionism"},{"id":"wd-q1578378","title":"Precisionism (Q1578378) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1578378"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood","description":"A secret brotherhood of seven English painters, poets and critics founded in 1848 by Hunt, Millais and Rossetti, who rejected the academic tradition that ran from Raphael onward. Ruskin's defence made their reputation.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-pre-raphaelite-brotherhood","wd-q184814","aat-300021225"]},{"map":"writing","explanation":"The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. {"version":3,"name":"Priamels","description":"Poems built as a list of alternatives that turn out to be foils for the real subject, revealed at the end. The list has to seem arbitrary for the ending to work.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named rhetorical form with a stated structure, a classical instance and a medieval German corpus; LCGFT files it under Epigrams and Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-priamels","wp-priamel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"epigrams","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Epigrams as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-priamels"]},{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-priamels"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-priamels","title":"Priamels — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026486"},{"id":"wp-priamel","title":"Priamel — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priamel"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Printmaking","description":"Making artworks by printing them, normally on paper, from a matrix the artist prepares by hand: a cut block, a bitten plate, a drawn stone, a stencil. The image exists as an edition rather than as one object, and the working of the matrix is part of the picture. Wikipedia's account names woodcut, etching, engraving, lithography and screenprinting as the traditional techniques, and includes risograph where hand and machine printing meet.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A technique family with its own body of work, its own editions and its own history separate from painting.","sourceIds":["wp-printmaking","aat-printing"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["The name is Wikipedia's; the Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus files these processes under 'printing (process)', which reads as a manufacturing term rather than an art practice. Rename if 'Printing' is the better label.","Halftone printing, dye transfer printing and xerox art are reproduction processes rather than printmaking as Wikipedia defines it, so they keep no parent here. Say if they belong under this cell."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-printmaking","title":"Printmaking — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printmaking"},{"id":"aat-printing","title":"printing (process) — Getty AAT 300053319","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300053319"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Problem plays","description":"Plays that put a contested social question on stage and expect the audience to argue with it afterwards. The form emerges with nineteenth-century realism and Ibsen, and Shaw wrote and defended it as a theatre of discussion. The convention it broke is that a play should settle its own question by the final curtain.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic genre with a dated emergence, a theorist who defended it and a canon; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-problem-plays","wp-problem-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-problem-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-problem-plays","title":"Problem plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026487"},{"id":"wp-problem-play","title":"Problem play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problem_play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Process Art","description":"Work in which the making is the subject: gathering, sorting, pouring, folding, letting a material do what it does. Morris's felt pieces and Serra's verb list are its statements. The finished object is a residue of the making.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-process-art","wd-q545851","aat-300022209"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-process-art","title":"Process art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process_art"},{"id":"wd-q545851","title":"process art (Q545851) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q545851"},{"id":"aat-300022209","title":"Process Art — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300022209","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300022209"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Progressive Artists' Group","description":"A group of modern Indian artists formed in Bombay in 1947, in the year of independence, setting out to make an Indian modernism that owed nothing to the Bengal School's revivalism. Souza, Raza, Husain, Ara and Gade were its founders, and it had no shared style, only a shared refusal. Its members went on to define post-independence Indian painting.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-bombay-progressive-artists-group","wd-q4940574"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-bombay-progressive-artists-group","title":"Bombay Progressive Artists' Group — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay_Progressive_Artists'_Group"},{"id":"wd-q4940574","title":"Bombay Progressive Artists' Group (Q4940574) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q4940574"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Proletarian fiction","description":"Fiction written from a working-class position about working-class life, usually with an explicit political aim. It is organised as a movement in the Soviet Union in the 1920s, in Japan as puroretaria bungaku, and in the United States and Britain in the 1930s, with journals, conferences and arguments about what the writing owed the movement. Writers inside it disagreed in public about whether the political aim helped the work.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named movement with organisations, journals and a dated history in several countries; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-proletarian-fiction","wp-proletarian-literature"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-proletarian-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-proletarian-fiction","title":"Proletarian fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026138"},{"id":"wp-proletarian-literature","title":"Proletarian literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proletarian_literature"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Prose poems","description":"Poems written in continuous prose, using image, rhythm and compression while giving up the line. Baudelaire's Petits poèmes en prose in the 1860s made the case for it in French, and the form runs on through Rimbaud, Stein and much contemporary writing. Dropping the line break is a formal decision and the poems are read as such.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named form with a founding argument, a canon and an explicit formal decision at its centre; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry and files Maqāmāt and Haibun under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-prose-poems","wp-prose-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-prose-poems"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-prose-poems","title":"Prose poems — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026488"},{"id":"wp-prose-poetry","title":"Prose poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prose_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Psalms","description":"Hebrew sacred poems of praise, lament, thanksgiving and complaint, built on parallel lines. The biblical collection is the model, and the form was rewritten continuously afterwards in metrical psalters, in devotional imitations and in modern poetry. Parallelism is what carries across every translation.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named poetic form with a defining structural principle, a founding corpus and a long tradition of imitation; LCGFT files it under Religious poetry and Sacred music texts.","sourceIds":["lcgft-psalms","wp-psalms"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"religious-poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Religious poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-psalms"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["The independent reference is Wikipedia's article on the biblical Book of Psalms, which is the founding collection rather than the form. A page on psalm as a genre would be better if one exists."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-psalms","title":"Psalms — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2015026079"},{"id":"wp-psalms","title":"Psalms — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalms"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Psychological comics","description":"Comics in which the interior of a character carries as much weight as the events. The form has its own means for it: the caption as inner voice, the panel that shows what is remembered instead of what is happening, the layout that comes apart as a mind does. Shōjo manga developed much of that vocabulary.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The interior emphasis worked out in comics. The cell Psychological fiction works the same direction out in prose, and the form has developed its own devices for it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-psychological-comics","wp-psychological-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"LCGFT files it under Comics; the direction is worked out through the form's own panel grammar.","sourceIds":["lcgft-psychological-comics","wp-psychological-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Psychological fiction and Psychological comics. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-psychological-comics","title":"Psychological comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026048"},{"id":"wp-psychological-fiction","title":"Psychological fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Psychological fiction","description":"Fiction in which the interior of a character carries as much weight as the events, so the narration follows thought, feeling and motive. The line runs from Richardson through James and Dostoevsky and opens into the modernist interior monologue. Its technique is a narrative position close enough to a mind to report what has not been said aloud.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A mode defined by where the narration stands, with a continuous canon; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction and files Stream of consciousness fiction under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-psychological-fiction","wp-psychological-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-psychological-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-psychological-fiction","title":"Psychological fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026492"},{"id":"wp-psychological-fiction","title":"Psychological fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Puppet plays","description":"Plays performed by manipulated figures. The traditions are distinct and old: Japanese bunraku with three visible operators to a figure, Sicilian opera dei pupi, Punch and Judy, Indonesian and Chinese shadow figures. Writing for puppets has its own constraints, because a figure's expression is fixed and movement carries what a face would.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A performance form with distinct named traditions, its own writing constraints and a long documented history; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-puppet-plays","wp-puppetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-puppet-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-puppet-plays","title":"Puppet plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026493"},{"id":"wp-puppetry","title":"Puppetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puppetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Purim plays","description":"Comic plays performed at Purim, dramatising the Book of Esther and licensed by the festival to be irreverent about it. The Yiddish purimshpil is documented from the fifteenth century and was often played by amateurs going house to house. The occasion licenses the mockery.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named folk dramatic tradition with a documented history, a fixed source narrative and an occasion that licenses its manner; LCGFT files it under Folk drama and Bible plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-purim-plays","wp-purim-spiel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-drama","explanation":"LCGFT files Purim plays under Folk drama; they are amateur community performances carried by custom.","sourceIds":["lcgft-purim-plays","wp-purim-spiel"]},{"cellId":"bible-plays","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Bible plays as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-purim-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-purim-plays","title":"Purim plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026494"},{"id":"wp-purim-spiel","title":"Purim spiel — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purim_spiel"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Purism","description":"A movement of 1918 to 1925 founded by Amédée Ozenfant and Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, later Le Corbusier, which set out to purify Cubism of what they considered its arbitrary and decorative turn. It paints ordinary objects, bottles, guitars, glasses, reduced to clear elementary forms in muted colour. Its argument passes directly into Le Corbusier's architecture.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-purism","wd-q478774","aat-300122664"]},{"map":"design","explanation":"The movement worked in design as well as in the visual arts. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-purism","wd-q478774","aat-300122664"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"cubism","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as part of cubism.","sourceIds":["wd-q478774"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-purism","title":"Purism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purism"},{"id":"wd-q478774","title":"purism (Q478774) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q478774"},{"id":"aat-300122664","title":"Purism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300122664","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300122664"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Pyreneanism","description":"A nineteenth-century culture of exploring the Pyrenees to write and draw them, named by Henri Beraldi in 1898 with the formula that the ideal Pyreneist knows how to climb, write and feel. It draws on mountaineering, science and literature together, and it produced a substantial body of narrative and description. The requirement that the climber also write is what makes it a literary movement.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-pyreneanism","wd-q3411437"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline: a sporting culture with a literature attached. Kept because its own defining formula requires the writing; strike it if the mountaineering is the real subject."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-pyreneanism","title":"Pyreneanism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyreneanism"},{"id":"wd-q3411437","title":"Pyreneanism (Q3411437) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3411437"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Qaṣīdas","description":"The long monorhymed Arabic ode, running through a fixed sequence: the poet stops at an abandoned campsite and remembers a lost love, then describes a journey or desert life, then praises a patron. It is pre-Islamic in origin and passed into Persian, Turkish and Urdu poetry. The sections are conventional and the art lies in the handling of them.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named form with a stated sequence of parts, a pre-Islamic origin and a canon across many languages; LCGFT files it under Lyric poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-qasidas","wp-qasida"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"lyric-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Qaṣīdas under Lyric poetry; the poem is a single voice sustained through its sections.","sourceIds":["lcgft-qasidas","wp-qasida"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-qasidas","title":"Qaṣīdas — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026495"},{"id":"wp-qasida","title":"Qasida — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qasida"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Quantum aesthetics","description":"A Spanish movement launched by Gregorio Morales at the end of the 1990s with El cadáver de Balzac, which borrows from quantum physics an argument for mystery and difference against realist description. It has a manifesto, a group and a journal. It is small and its scientific borrowing is contested.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-quantum-aesthetics","wd-q7269008"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-quantum-aesthetics","wd-q7269008"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Thin: a small movement with a manifesto and a founder but a modest body of work, and a contested use of physics. Strike it if that is too slight."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-quantum-aesthetics","title":"Quantum aesthetics — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_aesthetics"},{"id":"wd-q7269008","title":"Quantum aesthetics (Q7269008) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q7269008"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Quatrains","description":"Poems or stanzas of four lines, the commonest unit in European verse and in much verse elsewhere. The rhyme may be crossed, enclosed or paired, and the ballad stanza, the heroic quatrain and the Persian ruba'i are all particular settlings of it. Four lines is enough for a statement and a turn.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A structural unit kept as a nesting parent, with named settlings across several traditions; LCGFT files Pantoums under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-quatrains","wp-quatrain"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-quatrains"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline: a quatrain is a stanza shape rather than a direction. Kept as a nesting parent, as Lyric poetry and Novels were; strike it if a stanza should not be a cell."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-quatrains","title":"Quatrains — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026497"},{"id":"wp-quatrain","title":"Quatrain — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quatrain"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Quipu","description":"The Andean record kept in knotted cord. A main cord carries pendant cords, and the knot types, their positions, the ply direction and the colour together encode the record. Inka administrators kept the state's accounts in it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named recording tradition with surviving artefacts and a scholarly literature.","sourceIds":["wp-quipu","aat-quipu"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-quipu","title":"Quipu — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu"},{"id":"aat-quipu","title":"khipus — Getty AAT 300264828","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300264828"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019efda5-c4e0-7470-b703-81a71856c66d","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Quipu (Andean khipu cord-record tradition)\" (Archived).","sourceIds":["wp-quipu"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019efe17-a8c5-7883-a823-267268fa0784","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Andean quipu khipu textile record traditions\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-quipu"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-019efe17-ad31-7323-9780-f659cb3a1b7b","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Andean quipu khipu record traditions\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-quipu"]},{"entitySet":"PaletteSystems","entityId":"en-019efe17-ab2d-7801-bc60-f566a1262b09","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Andean quipu khipu textile record traditions\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-quipu"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Qu (Poetry)","description":"Classical Chinese verse written to fixed tone patterns derived from existing song tunes, with lines of uneven length. It becomes the dominant poetic form of the Yuan dynasty, in the sanqu lyric and in the arias of Yuan drama. The tune name at the head of a poem states its metrical pattern.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named classical form with a stated metrical rule tied to named tunes and a dated period of dominance; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-qu-poetry","wp-qu-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-qu-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-qu-poetry","title":"Qu (Poetry) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026496"},{"id":"wp-qu-poetry","title":"Qu (poetry) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qu_(poetry)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Radio plays","description":"Drama written for sound alone, where dialogue, music and effects have to build everything a listener sees. The form was made by broadcasting from the 1920s and produced its own writers, from Welles and MacNeice to Beckett and Under Milk Wood. Its constraint is strict and productive: a character who is silent is not there.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form defined by its medium's constraint, with its own writers, canon and technique; LCGFT files it under Radio scripts and Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-radio-plays","wp-radio-drama"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-radio-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-radio-plays","title":"Radio plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026499"},{"id":"wp-radio-drama","title":"Radio drama — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_drama"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Rāsalīlā drama","description":"Devotional dance drama on the childhood and youth of Krishna, combining poetry, music and dance, performed in the Braj region and beyond. The material comes from the Bhagavata Purana and the Gita Govinda, and the performance is an act of worship as much as a show. Boys usually take the divine roles.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named devotional performance tradition with a fixed textual source, a region and a documented practice; LCGFT files it under Dance drama and Religious drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-rasalila-drama","wp-raslila"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"dance-drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Dance drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-rasalila-drama"]},{"cellId":"religious-drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Religious drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-rasalila-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-rasalila-drama","title":"Rāsalīlā drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026035"},{"id":"wp-raslila","title":"Raslila — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raslila"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Realism (art movement)","description":"A French movement of the 1840s that rejected Romanticism and set out to paint ordinary contemporary people and situations at the scale history painting had reserved for gods and kings. Courbet is its proponent and A Burial at Ornans its provocation, with Millet and Daumier alongside him. The scandal was as much about who was being painted as about how.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-realism-art-movement","wd-q2642826","aat-300172861"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-realism-art-movement","title":"Realism (art movement) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_(art_movement)"},{"id":"wd-q2642826","title":"French Realism (Q2642826) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2642826"},{"id":"aat-300172861","title":"Realism (art movement) — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300172861","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300172861"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Recluse literature","description":"Japanese writing by men who withdrew from court and capital into religious retirement, at its height in the late Heian and early Kamakura periods. Kamo no Chōmei's Hōjōki is its central work, written from a hut and turning impermanence into a manner as much as a theme. The withdrawal is the condition of the writing.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-recluse-literature","wd-q7302589"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-recluse-literature","title":"Recluse literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recluse_literature"},{"id":"wd-q7302589","title":"Recluse literature (Q7302589) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q7302589"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Regulated verse","description":"The tonally regulated form of classical Chinese shi poetry, perfected in the Tang dynasty: lines of five or seven characters, one rhyme on the even lines, a controlled pattern of level and oblique tones, and parallel inner couplets. It has three types, the eight-line lü shi, the four-line jue ju, and the longer pai lü.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The parent form of Lü shi and Jue ju; LCGFT has no heading for it, so the Wikipedia name is used, as pass 0 did for Literary nonsense.","sourceIds":["wp-regulated-verse"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Not an LCGFT heading. Proposed only so that Jue ju and Lü shi share their obvious parent; drop it and both stand disconnected."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-regulated-verse","title":"Regulated verse — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulated_verse"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Relational aesthetics","description":"A tendency of the 1990s in which the work is a situation people take part in: a meal cooked, a room arranged for conversation, a service offered. Nicolas Bourriaud defined the term in 1998, taking human relations and their social context as the material. {"version":3,"name":"Renga","description":"Japanese collaborative linked verse in which poets alternate stanzas of 5-7-5 and 7-7, each linking to the one before and turning away from the one before that. {"version":3,"name":"Renku","description":"The popular, comic form of Japanese linked verse, also called haikai no renga, which loosened the courtly rules and admitted ordinary language and everyday material. {"version":3,"name":"Renshi","description":"Collaborative linked poetry in free verse, developed by Ōoka Makoto in the 1980s, where each poet contributes a whole poem instead of a stanza and drops the classical rules on length and season. {"version":3,"name":"Revenge tragedies","description":"Elizabethan and Jacobean tragedy in which a character sets out to avenge a murder, often prompted by the victim's ghost, and is destroyed by the attempt. Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy sets the pattern, Hamlet complicates it, and Webster and Middleton push it further. {"version":3,"name":"Rhopalic verse","description":"Verse in which each word is one syllable longer than the word before it, so the line widens as it goes. {"version":3,"name":"Rhyme royal","description":"A seven-line stanza rhyming ababbcc, brought into English by Chaucer for Troilus and Criseyde and used heavily through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Its conventions are unusually explicit, to the point that publishers and readers state them as rules.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A broad genre root with stated conventions and a continuous body of work; LCGFT files Paranormal romance fiction under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-romance-fiction","wp-romance-novel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-romance-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-romance-fiction","title":"Romance fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026516"},{"id":"wp-romance-novel","title":"Romance novel — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_novel"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Romances","description":"Verse and prose narratives of the medieval and early modern courts: a knight's quest through marvels, with love and courtly manners at the centre. They grew out of the epics, moved from verse into prose in the thirteenth century, and were out of fashion by 1600, when Cervantes burlesqued them. LCGFT reserves this heading for the chivalric tradition and sends love stories to Romance fiction.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A narrative genre of the high medieval and early modern courts, in verse and prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-romances","wp-chivalric-romance"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["The LCGFT heading is the bare word Romances; its listed variant Chivalric romances is clearer. Which name?"],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-romances","title":"Romances — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026517"},{"id":"wp-chivalric-romance","title":"Chivalric romance — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalric_romance"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Romans à clef","description":"Fiction in which real people, places or events appear under invented names, so that a reader with the key reads two stories at once. The form is named in seventeenth-century France, where Madeleine de Scudéry's novels circulated with keys, and it recurs wherever a writer needs both distance and recognition. The technique is the doubling itself, and the works often outlive the people they encode.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named technique with a French critical name and a long body of work; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-romans-a-clef","wp-roman-a-clef"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-romans-a-clef"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-romans-a-clef","title":"Romans à clef — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026518"},{"id":"wp-roman-a-clef","title":"Roman à clef — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_à_clef"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Romanticism","description":"A movement that began in Europe at the end of the eighteenth century and argued for subjectivity, imagination and nature against the Enlightenment and the industrial order. In literature it turns to the isolated speaker, to sensibility, to the past and to the supernatural; in painting and music it makes feeling the organising principle. Almost every later movement in this collection is positioned for or against it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-romanticism","wd-q37068","aat-300172863"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-romanticism","wd-q37068","aat-300172863"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-romanticism","title":"Romanticism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism"},{"id":"wd-q37068","title":"Romanticism (Q37068) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q37068"},{"id":"aat-300172863","title":"Romanticism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300172863","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300172863"},{"id":"wd-q5977111","title":"Romantic literature (Q5977111) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q5977111"},{"id":"wp-romantic-literature","title":"Romantic literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_literature"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Rondeaux","description":"A medieval and Renaissance French fixed form of about fifteen lines on two rhymes, with the opening words returning as an unrhymed refrain. It is one of the three formes fixes alongside the ballade and the virelai and was set to music as often as it was read. The refrain's return is the whole architecture.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with a stated rhyme and refrain rule, a defined period and a musical as well as a poetic history; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-rondeaux","wp-rondeau-forme-fixe"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-rondeaux"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-rondeaux","title":"Rondeaux — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026520"},{"id":"wp-rondeau-forme-fixe","title":"Rondeau (forme fixe) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rondeau_(forme_fixe)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Rondels","description":"Thirteen or fourteen lines in two or three stanzas on two rhymes, with a two-line refrain that returns in the middle and at the end. The form comes from fourteenth-century French lyric, alongside the rondeau it is related to, and Charles d'Orléans wrote many. The refrain pair is the fixed part and everything else works around it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with a stated refrain rule, a defined period and a canon; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-rondels","wp-rondel-poem"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-rondels"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-rondels","title":"Rondels — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026521"},{"id":"wp-rondel-poem","title":"Rondel (poem) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rondel_(poem)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Roundels","description":"An eleven-line English form on two rhymes, with a refrain taken from the opening words of the first line and returning in the fourth and eleventh. Swinburne devised it as an English answer to the French rondeau and published a hundred of them in 1883. It is a deliberate invention with a named author and a fixed rule.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with a stated rule, a named inventor and a dated founding collection; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-roundels","wp-roundel-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-roundels"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-roundels","title":"Roundels — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026074"},{"id":"wp-roundel-poetry","title":"Roundel (poetry) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundel_(poetry)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Royal Institution Christmas Lectures","description":"Lectures on one scientific subject, given to a general audience at the Royal Institution every year since 1825. The demonstration on the bench is the argument. The register is spoken and direct: an object, a question put to the room, a thing done in front of everyone, then what it means. Many of the series were published, so the written form keeps the address to a listener. Faraday gave nineteen of them.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The series has run since 1825, delivered by many hands and published as text.","sourceIds":["wp-ri-christmas-lectures"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"popular-science","explanation":"The reference says the lectures present scientific subjects to a general audience, which is what this parent covers, in the specific form the Royal Institution fixed.","sourceIds":["wp-ri-christmas-lectures"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["The Faraday record is built from lectures published in 1861. The reference names Faraday and the number he gave, and does not date the individual series, so the year is left to the record."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-ri-christmas-lectures","title":"Royal Institution Christmas Lectures — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Institution_Christmas_Lectures"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"WritingStyles","entityId":"en-019f2ed1-06ca-7702-a044-c84561480e36","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Public lecture-demonstration tradition\" (UnderReview). It is built from Faraday's lectures published in 1861, which are the 1860 Christmas Lectures on the chemical history of a candle.","sourceIds":["wp-ri-christmas-lectures"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sagas","description":"Prose narratives written in Iceland and Scandinavia from the twelfth century on, about settlers, feuds, kings, saints and legendary heroes. They were composed in Old Norse and Icelandic at a time when Latin was Europe's language of history, and verse stanzas are embedded in the prose. The sagas of Icelanders are the best-known group.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A vernacular prose tradition with a recognisable manner and a defined body of texts.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sagas","wp-saga"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[{"cellId":"romances","label":"absorbed","explanation":"Chivalric romances were translated into Old Norse and composed locally as sagas, so the two traditions overlap.","sourceIds":["wp-saga"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sagas","title":"Sagas — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026522"},{"id":"wp-saga","title":"Saga — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saga"},{"id":"wp-sagas-of-icelanders","title":"Sagas of Icelanders — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagas_of_Icelanders"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sandae drama","description":"Korean masked dance drama from the Seoul region, satirising the aristocracy and the clergy through fixed masked types. Some scholars treat it as the root form from which other Korean mask dramas developed, and it was originally managed by a state office before passing to village troupes. Satire aimed upward is what the masks license.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named masked tradition with a documented institutional history, fixed types and a satirical function; LCGFT files it under Folk drama, Satirical literature and Dance drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sandae-drama","wp-sandae-nori"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-drama","explanation":"LCGFT files Sandae drama under Folk drama; it passed from a state office to village troupes and is carried by performance.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sandae-drama","wp-sandae-nori"]},{"cellId":"satirical-literature","explanation":"LCGFT files Sandae drama under Satirical literature; the masked types exist to ridicule the nobility and clergy.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sandae-drama","wp-sandae-nori"]},{"cellId":"dance-drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Dance drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sandae-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sandae-drama","title":"Sandae drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026036"},{"id":"wp-sandae-nori","title":"Sandae-nori — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandae-nori"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sapphics","description":"Four-line stanzas in the Aeolic pattern Sappho used: three long lines of a fixed quantitative shape and a short fourth. Catullus and Horace wrote it in Latin, and imitations since the Middle Ages usually reproduce the syllable count instead of the quantities. The short fourth line is the signature.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named stanza form with a named originator, a fixed metrical pattern and a long line of imitation; LCGFT files it under Quatrains.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sapphics","wp-sapphic-stanza"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"quatrains","explanation":"LCGFT files Sapphics under Quatrains; the stanza is four lines with a fixed internal shape.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sapphics","wp-sapphic-stanza"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sapphics","title":"Sapphics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026523"},{"id":"wp-sapphic-stanza","title":"Sapphic stanza — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphic_stanza"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

Its writers work in Italian and in Sardinian and take the island's history and language as their material. The term gathers a generation with no programme.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Sastra wangi","description":"A body of Indonesian writing by young urban women that appeared after 1998, taking on politics, religion and sexuality directly. Ayu Utami's Saman, published two weeks before Suharto fell, began it, and Djenar Maesa Ayu and Dewi Lestari followed. The label, meaning fragrant literature, was applied from outside and the writers have largely rejected it as a way of talking about their looks instead of their books.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. {"version":3,"name":"Satirical literature","description":"Writing that holds vices, follies and institutions up to ridicule, usually with the aim of shaming them into reform. Irony is its main instrument, backed by parody, exaggeration and juxtaposition. LCGFT gathers satirical fiction, drama, verse satire, beast epics and satirical comics under it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A mode of writing with a continuous history from Roman verse satire onward.","sourceIds":["lcgft-satirical-literature","wp-satire"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Satire spans the visual and performing arts too; should this cell also wear the art map once a cited visual source is added?"],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-satirical-literature","title":"Satirical literature — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026525"},{"id":"wp-satire","title":"Satire — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire"},{"id":"lcgft-satirical-comics","title":"Satirical comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026071"},{"id":"lcgft-satirical-drama","title":"Satirical drama — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026106"},{"id":"lcgft-satirical-fiction","title":"Satirical fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026105"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Satyr plays","description":"Short Athenian plays with a chorus of satyrs, performed after a tragic trilogy on mythical material treated coarsely. Euripides' Cyclops is the only one to survive whole, with a long fragment of Sophocles' Ichneutae. The place in the programme is the form: the same myths are replayed in a register the tragedies could not use.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named ancient dramatic form with a fixed place in the festival programme, a surviving text and its own scholarship; LCGFT files it under Burlesques and Bawdy plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-satyr-plays","wp-satyr-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"bawdy-plays","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Bawdy plays as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-satyr-plays"]},{"cellId":"burlesques-literature","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Burlesques (Literature) as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-satyr-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-satyr-plays","title":"Satyr plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026526"},{"id":"wp-satyr-play","title":"Satyr play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyr_play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sayings","description":"Short fixed expressions carried by repetition rather than by an author: proverbs, maxims, adages, apothegms. The Library of Congress files gnomic poetry and epigrams under the heading.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A compact form with collections in every written tradition, worked in prose and in verse alike.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sayings","wp-saying"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["The Library of Congress files Sayings under Reference works, a cataloguing container that is not a cell, so this cell has no parent."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sayings","title":"Sayings — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026170"},{"id":"wp-saying","title":"Saying — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saying"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Scar literature","description":"Chinese fiction of the late 1970s and early 1980s that wrote directly about the suffering of the Cultural Revolution, taking its name from Lu Xinhua's 1978 story Scar. It appeared as soon as it was permitted to and was read as a national reckoning, then gave way to the root-seeking writing that followed it. The movement is tightly dated, which is part of what makes it legible.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named national movement with a founding story, a short defined period and a critical literature; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-scar-literature","wp-scar-literature"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-scar-literature"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-scar-literature","title":"Scar literature — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026104"},{"id":"wp-scar-literature","title":"Scar literature — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scar_literature"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"School of London","description":"A loose group of London-based painters through the later twentieth century who kept working from the figure while abstraction, Minimalism and Conceptual art dominated. Bacon, Freud, Auerbach, Kossoff, Andrews and Kitaj are usually named, and Kitaj coined the label for a 1976 exhibition. They share a subject and a stubbornness.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-school-of-london","wd-q55780244"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-school-of-london","title":"School of London — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_London"},{"id":"wd-q55780244","title":"School of London (Q55780244) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q55780244"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"School of Paris","description":"The French and émigré artists who worked in Paris while the city was the centre of Western art. Before the war the term named the foreign-born painters of Montparnasse, Modigliani, Chagall and Soutine among them, and widened to take in nearly all progressive work made in the city. After 1945 it named a second Paris, where Matisse and Picasso returned and a new international generation worked in lyrical abstraction, Art Brut and kinetic art. A run of exhibitions in the 1950s fixed an informal membership list for the public.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-school-of-paris","wd-q273506"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":["Artsy splits this into a pre-war and a post-war gene. {"version":3,"name":"Science fiction","description":"Fiction that imagines a change in what is technically or scientifically possible and follows what that change does to people and societies. It runs from Shelley's Frankenstein and Verne through the American pulp magazines of the 1920s, which gave it its name and its readership, to the New Wave and after. Its conventions are argumentative: a premise is proposed and the story tests it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A broad genre root with a continuous body of work and its own conventions; LCGFT files Cyberpunk, Dystopian, Apocalyptic, Steampunk and eleven more terms under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-science-fiction","wp-science-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-science-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-science-fiction","title":"Science fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026529"},{"id":"wp-science-fiction","title":"Science fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Science fiction poetry","description":"Poetry that works from science-fictional and fantastic premises, also called speculative poetry, with its own magazines, awards and anthologies since the 1970s. The Science Fiction and Fantasy Poetry Association and the Rhysling Award give it an institutional footing. Compression suits the premise: a poem can propose a world and leave it unexplained.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The speculative premise worked out in verse. {"version":3,"name":"Sensation fiction","description":"British fiction of roughly 1855 to 1890 that put bigamy, forgery, madness and murder inside respectable domestic settings.
