{"version":3,"name":"Sentimental novels","description":"Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century novels that treat strong feeling as evidence of virtue and ask the reader to weep with the sufferer. Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa, Sterne's A Sentimental Journey and Goethe's Werther establish it, and it is bound up with the period's arguments about sensibility and moral perception. The tears are the point: feeling is the proof the book offers.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named genre with a dated period, a canon and a philosophical argument behind it; LCGFT files it under Novels.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sentimental-novels","wp-sentimental-novel"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"novels","explanation":"LCGFT files Sentimental novels under Novels; the works are book-length prose fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sentimental-novels","wp-sentimental-novel"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sentimental-novels","title":"Sentimental novels — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026536"},{"id":"wp-sentimental-novel","title":"Sentimental novel — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_novel"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Serapion Brothers","description":"A group of writers formed in Petrograd in 1921 and named after Hoffmann's storytelling circle, insisting that literature owed nothing to any party programme. Zoshchenko, Kaverin, Shklovsky, Slonimsky and Fedin belonged to it, and they came together in the seminars of Tynyanov, Zamyatin and Shklovsky. Their declaration of independence made them a target as Soviet cultural policy hardened.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-serapion-brothers","wd-q1389156"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-serapion-brothers","title":"Serapion Brothers — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serapion_Brothers"},{"id":"wd-q1389156","title":"Serapion Brothers (Q1389156) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1389156"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Serialized fiction","description":"Fiction published in installments in a newspaper, magazine or other periodical, so that it is written and read against a schedule. Dickens made it the dominant English publishing form of the nineteenth century, and the form shows in the writing: recurring cliffhangers, recapitulation, and plots that could still respond to readers between numbers. The practice returns with pulp magazines, with Japanese manga weeklies, and with subscription platforms.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A publishing practice that shapes how the fiction is made, in the same way the live cell Cartonera books is a publishing practice; LCGFT files Cronicas under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-serialized-fiction","wp-serial-literature"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-serialized-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-serialized-fiction","title":"Serialized fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026537"},{"id":"wp-serial-literature","title":"Serial (literature) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_(literature)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Service journalism","description":"Reporting written to be acted on, which the trade calls news you can use. It answers a practical question and stops when the reader could act. What to buy, where to go, what a rule change means for them this month. The register is direct and second person, and the test is whether a reader finishes better equipped than they started. It runs from the serious to the frivolous and it is the register most topic newsletters are written in.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named newsroom register with a working definition, news you can use, and a large body of work across the consumer press.","sourceIds":["wp-service-journalism"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"journalism","explanation":"Reporting for a general reader, narrowed to the case where the reader is meant to act on it.","sourceIds":["wp-service-journalism"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"newsletters","label":"is practised in","explanation":"Most topic newsletters are written in this register, which is the nearest thing the Newsletters cell has to a manner of its own.","sourceIds":["wp-service-journalism"]}],"questions":["The Newsletters cell still has no leaf. This register is the closest thing to one. It is a journalism register, so it is linked from the Newsletters cell instead of parented under it."],"sources":[{"id":"wp-service-journalism","title":"Service journalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_journalism"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sestets","description":"Poems or stanzas of six lines. The name is also used for the second part of an Italian sonnet, where the sestet answers the octave, and the unit appears on its own in many traditions. Six lines allows a statement, a qualification and a close.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A structural unit kept as a nesting parent alongside Quatrains; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sestets","wp-sestet"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sestets"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline, as Quatrains was: a sestet is a stanza shape rather than a direction. Strike both together if a stanza should not be a cell."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sestets","title":"Sestets — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026538"},{"id":"wp-sestet","title":"Sestet — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sestet"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sestinas","description":"Thirty-nine-line poems in six six-line stanzas and a three-line envoi, where the same six end words return in each stanza in a fixed rotating order. Arnaut Daniel invented it among the troubadours and Dante and Petrarch carried it into Italian. The rotation is mechanical and the difficulty is making it sound inevitable.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with a stated permutation rule, a named inventor and a canon across several languages; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sestinas","wp-sestina"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sestinas"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sestinas","title":"Sestinas — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026539"},{"id":"wp-sestina","title":"Sestina — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sestina"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sewamono","description":"Japanese plays of contemporary life, written for bunraku and kabuki about townspeople, merchants and courtesans instead of warriors and nobles. Chikamatsu's love-suicide plays are the central works, some taken from events days old. The category exists against the period plays, jidaimono, and the division shapes both.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named category of the Japanese repertoire with a central author, a defined social material and a formal opposition that organises the whole repertoire; LCGFT files it under Kabuki plays and Domestic drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sewamono","wp-sewamono"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"kabuki-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Sewamono under Kabuki plays; the category names one half of the kabuki and bunraku repertoire.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sewamono","wp-sewamono"]},{"cellId":"domestic-drama","explanation":"LCGFT files Sewamono under Domestic drama; its subjects are ordinary townspeople in their own households.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sewamono","wp-sewamono"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sewamono","title":"Sewamono — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026540"},{"id":"wp-sewamono","title":"Sewamono — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewamono"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sfumato","description":"Modelling by gradation so fine that no edge is visible, with the transitions from light to shadow laid in translucent layers until they read as continuous. Contours dissolve into their surroundings and the softness describes the form.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A painting technique with a documented body of work and a long literature.","sourceIds":["wp-sfumato","aat-sfumato"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"renaissance-art","explanation":"One of the canonical painting modes of the Renaissance, one of four available to Italian High Renaissance painters.","sourceIds":["wp-sfumato"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"chiaroscuro","label":"shares a technique","explanation":"Both build form from the arrangement of light and dark; sfumato names the handling of the transition between them.","sourceIds":["wp-sfumato"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-sfumato","title":"Sfumato — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sfumato"},{"id":"aat-sfumato","title":"sfumato — Getty AAT 300053421","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300053421"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019f47ba-7109-7db3-b3c8-79a0e7033a20","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Sfumato\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-sfumato"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019f9641-e595-7bf3-92ee-817bda9ea6b2","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Sfumato\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-sfumato"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Shadow plays","description":"Plays performed with flat cut-out figures held between a lamp and a translucent screen, so the audience watches the shadows. Javanese and Balinese wayang kulit, Chinese piying, Turkish Karagöz and Greek Karagiozis are separate living traditions with their own repertoires and puppeteers. The screen is a rule: everything must read as a silhouette.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A performance form with several distinct living traditions and a defining technical constraint; LCGFT files it under Puppet plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-shadow-plays","wp-shadow-play"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"puppet-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Shadow plays under Puppet plays; the figures are puppets and the performance is by manipulation.","sourceIds":["lcgft-shadow-plays","wp-shadow-play"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-shadow-plays","title":"Shadow plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026541"},{"id":"wp-shadow-play","title":"Shadow play — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_play"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Shin-hanga","description":"A Japanese print movement of the Taishō and Shōwa periods that revived ukiyo-e by keeping its collaborative division of labour between artist, carver, printer and publisher, while taking in Western light and perspective. The publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō organised it and much of the audience was Western. It runs alongside sōsaku-hanga, which insisted the artist do everything.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-shin-hanga","wd-q842183","aat-300262954"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"ukiyo-e","explanation":"The movement revived ukiyo-e and kept its division of labour between artist, carver, printer and publisher.","sourceIds":["wp-shin-hanga"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-shin-hanga","title":"Shin-hanga — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shin-hanga"},{"id":"wd-q842183","title":"shin-hanga (Q842183) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q842183"},{"id":"aat-300262954","title":"Shin-hanga — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300262954","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300262954"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Shinkankakuha","description":"A prewar Japanese literary group led by Yokomitsu Riichi and Kawabata Yasunari, usually translated as the New Perception school, which set out to write sensation directly and to strip away what habit had made of things. Its prose is compressed, figurative and abrupt, and it drew on European modernism and on film. Yokomitsu's own statements are the clearest account of its programme.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-shinkankakuha","wd-q11082779"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-shinkankakuha","title":"Shinkankakuha — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkankakuha"},{"id":"wd-q11082779","title":"Shinkankakuha (Q11082779) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q11082779"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Shōjo manga","description":"Manga published for adolescent girls and young women, one of the industry's four editorial categories. It developed a visual language of its own in the 1970s under the Year 24 Group: broken panel borders, floating figures, interior monologue running across the page, large eyes carrying feeling. The category is a magazine's market, and the style grew inside it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A publishing category that produced a distinct and much-described visual language; LCGFT files it under Manga.","sourceIds":["lcgft-shojo-manga","wp-shojo-manga"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"manga","explanation":"LCGFT files Shōjo manga under Manga; it is one of the industry's four editorial categories.","sourceIds":["lcgft-shojo-manga","wp-shojo-manga"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline against the rule that declines audience-defined labels. Kept because shōjo manga developed a documented visual grammar of its own, which is a manner and not a readership; strike it if the market category should decide."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-shojo-manga","title":"Shōjo manga — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026060"},{"id":"wp-shojo-manga","title":"Shōjo manga — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shōjo_manga"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Shōnen manga","description":"Manga published for adolescent boys, the largest of the four editorial categories, carried by weeklies such as Shōnen Jump. Its serialised long-form action storytelling, with escalating opponents, training sequences and a reader-poll pressure on the plot, is a working method. The magazine's ranking system shapes what gets written.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A publishing category with a documented working method and a described effect of its own institutions on the writing; LCGFT files it under Manga.","sourceIds":["lcgft-shonen-manga","wp-shonen-manga"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"manga","explanation":"LCGFT files Shōnen manga under Manga; it is one of the industry's four editorial categories.","sourceIds":["lcgft-shonen-manga","wp-shonen-manga"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Borderline for the same reason as Shōjo manga: kept for the method rather than the readership."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-shonen-manga","title":"Shōnen manga — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2023026061"},{"id":"wp-shonen-manga","title":"Shōnen manga — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shōnen_manga"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Short stories","description":"Prose fiction short enough to be read at one sitting, built around one incident or a small run of linked ones. Poe's review of Hawthorne in 1842 argued that the form's power comes from that one sitting, and the magazine markets of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries made it a working writer's staple. Compression is the technique: what a novel establishes, a short story implies.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form category kept as a nesting parent; LCGFT files Flash fiction and Linked stories under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-short-stories","wp-short-story"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-short-stories"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-short-stories","title":"Short stories — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026542"},{"id":"wp-short-story","title":"Short story — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_story"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Shunga","description":"Japanese erotic art, mostly woodblock prints and illustrated books in the ukiyo-e manner, produced from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries by nearly every major print artist. The name means picture of spring. It circulated widely and was periodically banned, and its exclusion from the ukiyo-e canon was a later editorial decision.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-shunga","wd-q1048478","aat-300041555"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"ukiyo-e","explanation":"Its Wikidata item files it as a subclass of ukiyo-e.","sourceIds":["wd-q1048478"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-shunga","title":"Shunga — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shunga"},{"id":"wd-q1048478","title":"shunga (Q1048478) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1048478"},{"id":"aat-300041555","title":"Shunga — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300041555","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300041555"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Signalism","description":"A neo-avant-garde movement founded in Yugoslavia by Miroljub Todorović in the mid-1960s, working across poetry, visual art and the sciences, with manifestos, a journal and a body of computer-generated and visual poetry. It gathered participants well beyond Yugoslavia in the late 1960s and 1970s. Its programme treats the sign itself, in any medium, as the material.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-signalism","wd-q3483628"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-signalism","wd-q3483628"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-signalism","title":"Signalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signalism"},{"id":"wd-q3483628","title":"Signalism (Q3483628) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3483628"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sijo","description":"Korean lyric poems of three lines averaging forty-five syllables, each line built of four phrase groups, with a twist expected at the start of the third. It emerged under Goryeo, flourished under Joseon and is still written. The third-line turn is required, which makes the form an argument as much as a picture.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with a stated structural rule, a documented history from the Goryeo dynasty and a living practice; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sijo","wp-sijo"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sijo"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sijo","title":"Sijo — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026544"},{"id":"wp-sijo","title":"Sijo — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sijo"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Silverpoint","description":"Drawing with a metal stylus on a prepared abrasive ground, which leaves a faint grey line that tarnishes warm over time. Nothing can be erased and the line has one weight, so tone is built entirely by hatching and the drawing has to be right the first time.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A drawing technique with a documented body of work from the fifteenth century onward.","sourceIds":["wp-silverpoint","aat-silverpoint"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-silverpoint","title":"Silverpoint — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverpoint"},{"id":"aat-silverpoint","title":"silverpoint (technique) — Getty AAT 300404634","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300404634"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-01a03f5c-80c6-7db2-b609-40f954290f91","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Silverpoint drawing\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-silverpoint"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019efaf5-f6b5-7ab0-a205-870106e5d867","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Old Master silverpoint and graphite draughtsmanship\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-silverpoint"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-01a03f5c-8287-74f1-9549-714830566a93","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Silverpoint drawing\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-silverpoint"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sirventes","description":"Old Occitan troubadour poems of satire, invective and political comment, as against the love song. The convention was to borrow the metre and often the tune of an existing canso, so the attack arrived in a familiar shape. Bertran de Born is the best-known practitioner.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named troubadour genre with a stated compositional convention and identified poets; LCGFT files it under Lyric poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sirventes","wp-sirventes"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"lyric-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Sirventes under Lyric poetry; the poem is a single sustained voice in a lyric metre.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sirventes","wp-sirventes"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sirventes","title":"Sirventes — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026545"},{"id":"wp-sirventes","title":"Sirventes — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirventes"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Skaldic poetry","description":"Old Norse court poetry composed by named poets for kings and chieftains, in elaborate alliterative metres and dense with kennings. Its syntax is deliberately tangled and the standard metre, dróttkvætt, counts syllables, alliteration and internal rhyme at once. It is the counterpart of the anonymous Eddic verse.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named body of work with identified authors, described metres and a documented social function; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-skaldic-poetry","wp-skald"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-skaldic-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-skaldic-poetry","title":"Skaldic poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026527"},{"id":"wp-skald","title":"Skald — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skald"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Skeltonic verse","description":"Short irregular lines that run on the same rhyme for as long as the poet can hold it, thick with alliteration and parallelism, named after John Skelton, who wrote it around 1500. The effect is headlong and deliberately rough, and it was written for satire and invective. Later poets take it up when they want that tumbling speed.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named verse manner with a named originator, a stated set of traits and later imitators; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-skeltonic-verse","wp-john-skelton-poet"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-skeltonic-verse"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["The independent reference is Wikipedia's article on Skelton himself, which describes the verse under his name. A page on the form would be better if one exists."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-skeltonic-verse","title":"Skeltonic verse — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026546"},{"id":"wp-john-skelton-poet","title":"John Skelton (poet) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Skelton_(poet)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Slapstick comedy plays","description":"Comedy built on exaggerated physical action: falls, blows, chases and collisions carried past what would really be survivable. The name comes from the batacchio, the hinged stick the commedia companies used to make a loud crack with a light blow. The violence is stylised and the audience is meant to know it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named comic technique with a documented origin in its own stage property and a continuous practice from commedia to film; LCGFT files it under Farces.","sourceIds":["lcgft-slapstick-comedy-plays","wp-slapstick"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"farces","explanation":"LCGFT files Slapstick comedy plays under Farces; physical business and accelerating collision are the farce's own machinery.","sourceIds":["lcgft-slapstick-comedy-plays","wp-slapstick"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-slapstick-comedy-plays","title":"Slapstick comedy plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026044"},{"id":"wp-slapstick","title":"Slapstick — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slapstick"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Slice-of-life comics","description":"Comics about ordinary people doing ordinary things, built from vignettes and small incidents instead of a driving plot. The mode is a staple of manga and of autobiographical comics, and its interest is in accumulation and in what is noticed. Nothing much happening is the formal choice.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named narrative mode with a stated structural choice and a large body of work in comics; LCGFT files it under Comics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-slice-of-life-comics","wp-slice-of-life"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"LCGFT files Slice-of-life comics under Comics; the vignette structure is worked out in the form's own pacing.","sourceIds":["lcgft-slice-of-life-comics","wp-slice-of-life"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-slice-of-life-comics","title":"Slice-of-life comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2022026062"},{"id":"wp-slice-of-life","title":"Slice of life — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slice_of_life"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Socialist Realism","description":"The official doctrine of Soviet culture from 1932 until the state's end, requiring art to be realist in manner, optimistic in tone and instructive about the building of socialism. It was proclaimed for literature at the 1934 Writers' Congress and applied to every art, and its enforcement is inseparable from the work. {"version":3,"name":"Social problem fiction","description":"Fiction written to put a named social wrong in front of readers who could act on it: factory conditions, slavery, sanitation, imprisonment. {"version":3,"name":"Social Realism","description":"Work in painting, photography, print and film that draws attention to the conditions of working life to criticise the arrangements that produce them. It is distinguished from Socialist Realism by not being an official doctrine.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-social-realism","wd-q837024","aat-300061066"]},{"map":"writing","explanation":"The movement worked in writing as well as in the visual arts. {"version":3,"name":"Society verse","description":"Light, polished, epigrammatic verse about the manners and small troubles of polite society, written to be amusing without being trivial. The English line runs through Prior and Praed to Locker-Lampson and later Betjeman and Larkin. Its restraint is deliberate: strong feeling would break the form's contract.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named genre with a French critical name, a defined English canon and a stated tonal contract; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-society-verse","wp-vers-de-societe"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-society-verse"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-society-verse","title":"Society verse — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026547"},{"id":"wp-vers-de-societe","title":"Vers de société — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vers_de_société"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Solarpunk","description":"Speculative fiction and art that imagines a future in which the climate problem was solved, and works out what daily life there would be like. The term appeared in 2008 and the body of work is mostly online and recent. The conflicts are about maintenance, community and who does the work. It borrows from utopian writing, Afrofuturism and do-it-yourself culture.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A speculative genre that appeared in 2008, with an identifiable body of work.","sourceIds":["wp-solarpunk"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction","explanation":"It is a genre of speculative fiction turning on ecologically sustainable futures.","sourceIds":["wp-solarpunk"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"cyberpunk-fiction","label":"reacted against","explanation":"Wikipedia calls solarpunk the inverse of cyberpunk, keeping the countercultural stance and dropping the dystopia.","sourceIds":["wp-solarpunk"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-solarpunk","title":"Solarpunk — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solarpunk"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Soliloquies","description":"Speeches in which a character alone on stage, or believing themselves alone, thinks aloud for the audience. The convention gives a play direct access to a mind without a narrator, and Elizabethan drama makes it structural. It differs from a monologue addressed to others in exactly who is supposed to be listening.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named dramatic convention with a defined rule about its audience and a long technical literature; LCGFT files it under Monologues.","sourceIds":["lcgft-soliloquies","wp-soliloquy"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"monologues-drama","explanation":"LCGFT files Soliloquies under Monologues; a soliloquy is the variety spoken while alone.","sourceIds":["lcgft-soliloquies","wp-soliloquy"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-soliloquies","title":"Soliloquies — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026548"},{"id":"wp-soliloquy","title":"Soliloquy — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soliloquy"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sonnets","description":"Fourteen-line poems on a set rhyme scheme, invented in thirteenth-century Sicily and carried through Petrarch into every European literature. The Italian form turns between an octave and a sestet; the English form saves the turn for a closing couplet. The turn is the argument, and the form has lasted eight centuries on it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with two described variants, a dated invention and a canon in most European languages; LCGFT files it under Lyric poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sonnets","wp-sonnet"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"lyric-poetry","explanation":"LCGFT files Sonnets under Lyric poetry; the sonnet is a single voice working one thought to a turn.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sonnets","wp-sonnet"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sonnets","title":"Sonnets — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026549"},{"id":"wp-sonnet","title":"Sonnet — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonnet"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sound poetry","description":"Poetry made for performance in which the sounds of speech carry the work and semantic meaning is set aside. Hugo Ball's Dada recitations in 1916 and Kurt Schwitters's Ursonate are the founding line, and the tape recorder extended it. It is literature and music at once, and recordings are how it is documented.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named movement with a dated founding, a canon and a stated compositional principle; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sound-poetry","wp-sound-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-sound-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-sound-poetry","title":"Sound poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026550"},{"id":"wp-sound-poetry","title":"Sound poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Southern Gothic","description":"Gothic fiction relocated to the American South, where what haunts the characters is the region's own history of slavery, poverty and violence. Its subjects are violence, cruelty, disability, race and sexual difference, seen through characters the social order has already marked. Faulkner, O'Connor, McCullers and Welty are its canon. Exact regional speech sits next to grotesque incident, and the incident is played straight.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A literary subgenre written in and about the American South, with a canon of its own.","sourceIds":["wp-southern-gothic"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"gothic-fiction","explanation":"It is fiction heavily influenced by Gothic elements and set in the American South, where the persistence of social trauma replaces the Gothic past.","sourceIds":["wp-southern-gothic"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-southern-gothic","title":"Southern Gothic — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Gothic"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Soviet nonconformist art","description":"Soviet art made outside state control and outside Socialist Realism, from the Stalin years to the end of the union, shown in apartments and studios. The 1974 Bulldozer Exhibition, broken up by the authorities in a Moscow field, is its emblem. Moscow Conceptualism and Sots Art are inside it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-soviet-nonconformist-art","wd-q1134449"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-soviet-nonconformist-art","title":"Soviet nonconformist art — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_nonconformist_art"},{"id":"wd-q1134449","title":"nonconformist art (Q1134449) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q1134449"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Space operas (Fiction)","description":"Large-scale adventure fiction set across inhabited space, where faster-than-light travel is assumed and the stakes are worlds or empires. Wilson Tucker coined the name in 1941 as an insult, on the model of horse opera and soap opera, and the form took it as a badge. {"version":3,"name":"Spatialism","description":"A movement founded in Milan in 1947 by Lucio Fontana, which proposed an art combining colour, sound, space, movement and time, appropriate to an age of flight and broadcast. Its most famous result is the cut and punctured canvas, which opens the picture into actual space. The manifestos are as much of the work as the paintings.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-spatialism","wd-q2297997"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-spatialism","title":"Spatialism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spatialism"},{"id":"wd-q2297997","title":"Movimento Spaziale (Q2297997) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2297997"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Spiral (arts alliance)","description":"A collective of African American artists formed in New York on 5 July 1963 by Romare Bearden, Charles Alston, Norman Lewis and Hale Woodruff, meeting to argue what a Black artist owed the civil rights movement. It held one exhibition, in black and white only. It disbanded within a few years and has been reassessed since.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-spiral-arts-alliance","wd-q7577721"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-spiral-arts-alliance","title":"Spiral (arts alliance) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiral_(arts_alliance)"},{"id":"wd-q7577721","title":"Spiral (Q7577721) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q7577721"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Spoken word poetry","description":"Poetry written to be performed aloud, strongly stressed and rhythmic, with improvisation and wordplay expected. {"version":3,"name":"Spy fiction","description":"Fiction about espionage, built on secrecy, betrayal and divided loyalty. It forms in the years before 1914 with Erskine Childers and John Buchan and splits after 1945 into the adventure line of Fleming and the bureaucratic line of Le Carré and Deighton. Its recurring technique is withheld information: the reader is kept at the same disadvantage as the agent.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A genre with a dated formation, two well-described lines and a stated narrative technique; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-spy-fiction","wp-spy-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-spy-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-spy-fiction","title":"Spy fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026555"},{"id":"wp-spy-fiction","title":"Spy fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Steampunk fiction","description":"Science fiction that reasons forward from nineteenth-century steam technology, so the future arrives in brass, gears and coal. K. W. {"version":3,"name":"Strambotti","description":"Italian poems of six or eight eleven-syllable lines, common in late medieval popular verse and often sung. {"version":3,"name":"Stream of consciousness fiction","description":"Fiction that renders a character's perceptions, thoughts and memories as they arrive, by association and often against conventional grammar and punctuation. {"version":3,"name":"Street art","description":"Visual work made in public places for a public that did not ask for it, growing out of New York and Philadelphia graffiti writing in the 1970s and widening into stencil, paste-up, mural and installation. {"version":3,"name":"Street Photography","description":"Photography of unmediated chance encounters in public places, framed and timed as they happen. {"version":3,"name":"Style manuals","description":"Books that set how writing in a house or a field is done: spelling, punctuation, citation, usage, and what counts as a good sentence. The Chicago Manual of Style and the AP guide are the standard book-length ones, and a short one is called a style sheet. The register is prescriptive and terse: rule, reason, example. A style manual is written to be consulted, and readers take its own prose as a demonstration of what it asks for.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Books that prescribe how writing is done, with a shelf of standard works behind them.","sourceIds":["lcgft-style-manuals","wp-style-guide"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"handbooks-and-manuals","explanation":"The Library of Congress files Style manuals under Handbooks and manuals.","sourceIds":["lcgft-style-manuals"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Fowler and Strunk and White are the other standard usage books and the cited article names neither, so they are left out. {"version":3,"name":"Subterranean fiction","description":"Fiction set underground, in caverns, tunnels or a hollow earth holding its own world. Ludvig Holberg's Niels Klim in 1741 and Verne's Journey to the Centre of the Earth in 1864 are the standing cases, and Edmond Halley's hollow-earth hypothesis gave nineteenth-century writers a scientific pretext. The descent works as a frame: a separate society can be found underground.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A premise-defined tradition with a documented eighteenth- and nineteenth-century body of work; LCGFT files it under Science fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-subterranean-fiction","wp-subterranean-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Subterranean fiction under Science fiction; the underground world is reasoned from a scientific hypothesis of its day.","sourceIds":["lcgft-subterranean-fiction","wp-subterranean-fiction"]},{"cellId":"action-and-adventure-fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Action and adventure fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-subterranean-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-subterranean-fiction","title":"Subterranean fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2017026147"},{"id":"wp-subterranean-fiction","title":"Subterranean fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subterranean_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Superhero comics","description":"Comics about costumed figures with extraordinary powers, the dominant North American comic-book genre since Superman in 1938. Its conventions are unusually explicit and unusually persistent: the secret identity, the origin retold, the shared universe, the fight that resets. Serial continuity across decades and many writers is itself a feature of the form.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A genre with a dated origin, persistent stated conventions and a shared-continuity practice specific to the form; LCGFT files it under Comics.","sourceIds":["lcgft-superhero-comics","wp-superhero-comics"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comics-graphic-works","explanation":"LCGFT files Superhero comics under Comics; the genre was made in the form and its conventions are the form's own.","sourceIds":["lcgft-superhero-comics","wp-superhero-comics"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Superhero fiction and Superhero comics. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-superhero-comics","title":"Superhero comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026562"},{"id":"wp-superhero-comics","title":"Superhero comics — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superhero_comics"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Superhero fiction","description":"Fiction about costumed figures with extraordinary powers and the criminals who match them. The form is fixed by American comic books from Superman in 1938 and carries a set of conventions that later prose works assume: the secret identity, the origin, the recurring antagonist, the city that needs defending. Prose superhero fiction is written against that comics grammar.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A genre with a dated origin and conventions explicit enough that later works are read against them; LCGFT files it under Science fiction and Fantasy fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-superhero-fiction","wp-superhero-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Superhero fiction under Science fiction; many origins are given a technological or scientific explanation.","sourceIds":["lcgft-superhero-fiction","wp-superhero-fiction"]},{"cellId":"fantasy-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Superhero fiction under Fantasy fiction; many powers are magical or mythological in origin.","sourceIds":["lcgft-superhero-fiction","wp-superhero-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-superhero-fiction","title":"Superhero fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026073"},{"id":"wp-superhero-fiction","title":"Superhero fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superhero_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Suprematism","description":"Kazimir Malevich's abstraction, declared in 1915, built from a few geometric shapes in a limited palette and grounded in what he called the supremacy of pure artistic feeling. The Black Square is its founding statement, hung in the corner where an icon would go. It is an argument that painting can be about nothing outside itself and still be about everything.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-suprematism","wd-q191970","aat-300021405"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"geometric-abstraction","explanation":"Malevich built it from circles, squares and rectangles in a limited palette, which is the geometric case of abstraction.","sourceIds":["wp-suprematism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-suprematism","title":"Suprematism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suprematism"},{"id":"wd-q191970","title":"Suprematism (Q191970) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q191970"},{"id":"aat-300021405","title":"Suprematism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300021405","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300021405"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Sword and sorcery","description":"Fantasy about a fighter in immediate danger, where the stakes are personal and the world does not need saving. Robert E. Howard's Conan stories in the early 1930s started it and the name has been in use since the early 1960s. The pace is fast, the episodes are self-contained, and the hero's morals are as grey as everyone else's. The prose is physical and the magic is dangerous.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"Howard's Conan stories started it in the early 1930s and it has been written continuously since.","sourceIds":["wp-sword-and-sorcery"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fantasy-fiction","explanation":"It is a subgenre of fantasy built on sword-wielding heroes in violent adventures.","sourceIds":["wp-sword-and-sorcery"]}],"relations":[{"cellId":"high-fantasy","label":"defined against","explanation":"The two are separated by scale, and sword and sorcery keeps to personal battles.","sourceIds":["wp-sword-and-sorcery"]}],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-sword-and-sorcery","title":"Sword and sorcery — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword_and_sorcery"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Symbolism","description":"A late nineteenth-century movement of French and Belgian origin that set out to reach absolute truths through symbol and suggestion, against naturalism and realism. Moréas published its manifesto in 1886, Mallarmé, Verlaine and Rimbaud are its poets, and it passed into painting, music and theatre and into Russian and other literatures. Its principle is indirection: to name a thing is to destroy most of the poem.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-symbolism-movement","wd-q164800","aat-300021514"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-symbolism-movement","wd-q164800","aat-300021514"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-symbolism-movement","title":"Symbolism (movement) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbolism_(movement)"},{"id":"wd-q164800","title":"Symbolism (Q164800) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q164800"},{"id":"aat-300021514","title":"Symbolism — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300021514","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300021514"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Synchromism","description":"An American movement founded in 1912 by Stanton Macdonald-Wright and Morgan Russell, which built abstract paintings from colour scales analogised to music. Their synchromies were among the first abstract paintings by Americans, and the movement was short-lived and small. Its colour theory is worked out explicitly and published as such.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-synchromism","wd-q2615798"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"abstract-art","explanation":"The synchromies were among the first abstract paintings made by American artists.","sourceIds":["wp-synchromism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-synchromism","title":"Synchromism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchromism"},{"id":"wd-q2615798","title":"Synchromism (Q2615798) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q2615798"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tall tales","description":"Stories of impossible feats told straight, as though the teller expected to be believed. The American frontier cycle around Paul Bunyan, Pecos Bill and Mike Fink is the best-known body, and the form works by escalation against a deadpan delivery. The joke is in the telling: the audience is invited to catch the exaggeration.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named oral form with a collected canon and a stated technique of deadpan escalation; LCGFT files it under Humorous fiction, which pass 1 declined as a tone umbrella.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tall-tales","wp-tall-tale"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"humorous-fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Humorous fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tall-tales"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-tall-tales","title":"Tall tales — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026565"},{"id":"wp-tall-tale","title":"Tall tale — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tall_tale"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tan ci","description":"Chinese narrative singing alternating verse and prose, performed by one or two people in local dialect with pipa and sanxian. The verse runs mostly in seven-syllable lines, and long tanci narratives were also written to be read, many by women in the Qing period. It comes out of the southern storytelling traditions of Suzhou and its region.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named narrative performance form with a stated verse rule, its own instruments and a written as well as a performed corpus; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tan-ci","wp-tanci"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tan-ci"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-tan-ci","title":"Tan ci — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026038"},{"id":"wp-tanci","title":"Tanci — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanci"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tanka","description":"Japanese poems in five lines of five, seven, five, seven and seven syllables, the central form of classical Japanese poetry for more than a thousand years. It was the court's shared language, exchanged as letters and judged in competitions, and it is the parent of both renga and haiku. The break after the third line is where the poem usually turns.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named fixed form with more than a millennium of continuous practice and a documented social use; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tanka","wp-tanka"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tanka"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-tanka","title":"Tanka — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026566"},{"id":"wp-tanka","title":"Tanka — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanka"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Taʻziyah","description":"Shia passion drama reenacting the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala, performed in the month of Muharram in Iran and elsewhere. It is the major indigenous dramatic form of Iran.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named religious dramatic tradition with a fixed narrative, conventional staging and a documented ritual function; LCGFT files it under Religious drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-taziyah","wp-taziyeh"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"religious-drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Religious drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-taziyah"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-taziyah","title":"Taʻziyah — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026567"},{"id":"wp-taziyeh","title":"Ta'ziyeh — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta'ziyeh"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tenebrism","description":"Chiaroscuro taken to its limit: most of the picture is held in darkness and a narrow shaft of light picks out the action. Figures emerge from the dark with no described setting around them. It follows Caravaggio, and Spanish and Dutch painters carried it through the seventeenth century.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A manner in Baroque painting with a named body of work.","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism","aat-tenebrism"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"chiaroscuro","explanation":"Tenebrism is the extreme case of chiaroscuro's light-and-dark modelling, with almost the whole picture in darkness.","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-tenebrism","title":"Tenebrism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenebrism"},{"id":"aat-tenebrism","title":"tenebrism — Getty AAT 300343524","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300343524"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-01a03f5d-ffcd-71b0-9222-f8b3b62892ba","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Tenebrism\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019ff79f-a3b8-7142-90ff-a1ebb1c78566","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Tenebrism\" (Draft).","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019fd7b4-0e60-7161-bc60-6fc7ddeb847e","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Baroque tenebrism and chiaroscuro\" (Draft).","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019f8af8-a5a6-7ad3-ad0b-df3daf196b24","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Tenebrism\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-019fd7b4-10d8-7aa2-8013-1206eb6b488c","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Baroque tenebrism and chiaroscuro\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism"]},{"entitySet":"DesignLanguages","entityId":"en-01a03f5e-0284-77c0-830d-6367b3193737","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Tenebrism\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-tenebrism"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Terza rima","description":"Tercets interlocked so that the middle line of each supplies the rhyme for the outer lines of the next, giving a chain that can run indefinitely. Dante invented it for the Commedia, and Shelley, Byron and later English poets took it up despite the shortage of English rhymes. The interlock pulls the poem forward, which is what the form is for.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named rhyme structure with a named inventor, a founding work and a documented afterlife in other languages; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-terza-rima","wp-terza-rima"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-terza-rima"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-terza-rima","title":"Terza rima — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026570"},{"id":"wp-terza-rima","title":"Terza rima — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terza_rima"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"The Papelipolas","description":"A group of writers and artists formed in 1958 in Huila, Colombia, working in poetry above all but also in theatre, narrative, drawing, film and television. It dissolved in the mid-1960s and its members went on writing separately. Its work is still circulated and studied regionally decades later.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-the-papelipolas","wd-q3334809"]},{"map":"art","explanation":"The movement worked in the visual arts as well as in writing. One cell covers both, and this is its second map membership.","sourceIds":["wp-the-papelipolas","wd-q3334809"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-the-papelipolas","title":"The Papelipolas — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Papelipolas"},{"id":"wd-q3334809","title":"The Papelipolas (Q3334809) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q3334809"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"The Pictures Generation","description":"American artists who came up in the later 1970s and 1980s working by appropriating images from film, television and advertising, and examining what those images do. Douglas Crimp's 1977 exhibition Pictures at Artists Space named them, and Sherman, Levine, Prince, Kruger and Longo are its best-known figures. The 2009 Metropolitan Museum survey fixed the term.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-the-pictures-generation","wd-q115045796"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-the-pictures-generation","title":"The Pictures Generation — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pictures_Generation"},{"id":"wd-q115045796","title":"The Pictures Generation, 1974-1984 (Q115045796) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q115045796"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Thơ mới","description":"The New Poetry movement of 1930s colonial Vietnam, which abandoned the fixed Chinese-derived forms written in Hán-Nôm for free verse in the Latin-alphabet Quốc ngữ. Xuân Diệu and Hàn Mặc Tử are among its poets, and the change of script and of form arrived together. It is the founding moment of modern Vietnamese poetry.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named literary movement with a period, identified members and a body of work. Wikipedia lists it in Category:Literary movements.","sourceIds":["wp-tho-moi","wd-q7799938"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-tho-moi","title":"Thơ mới — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C6%A1_m%E1%BB%9Bi"},{"id":"wd-q7799938","title":"Thơ mới (Q7799938) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q7799938"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Thriller plays","description":"Plays built to hold an audience in apprehension, with a threat established early and a structure that keeps tightening. The stage thriller has its own machinery of dark scenes, sudden entrances and a confined set, and it was a West End staple for decades. Presence raises the stakes: the audience is in the room with the threat.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The engineered-suspense construction worked out in dramatic form. The cell Thrillers works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-thriller-plays","wp-thriller-genre"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-thriller-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Thrillers and Thriller plays. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-thriller-plays","title":"Thriller plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2017026045"},{"id":"wp-thriller-genre","title":"Thriller (genre) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_(genre)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Thrillers (Fiction)","description":"Fiction built to sustain apprehension, where a threat is established early and the plot keeps the reader ahead of, or behind, the characters. It overlaps crime, espionage and horror by material and separates from them by construction: pace, cross-cutting and a deadline. Suspense is engineered, and critics discuss its technique.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A genre defined by narrative construction, with a very large body of work; LCGFT files it directly under Fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-thrillers-fiction","wp-thriller-genre"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"fiction","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Fiction as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-thrillers-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-thrillers-fiction","title":"Thrillers (Fiction) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026571"},{"id":"wp-thriller-genre","title":"Thriller (genre) — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_(genre)"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Time-travel comics","description":"Comics in which movement through time is possible and the consequences are worked out. Long-running serials use it to revise their own histories, which makes the device an editorial tool as much as a plot one. A page can show two times at once, which prose has to do in sequence.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"The time-travel device worked out in comics. The cell Time-travel fiction works the same direction out in prose.","sourceIds":["lcgft-time-travel-comics","wp-time-travel-in-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction-comics","explanation":"LCGFT files Time-travel comics under Science fiction comics; the mechanism is treated as a physical possibility.","sourceIds":["lcgft-time-travel-comics","wp-time-travel-in-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":["Under D36 this wants a shared parent above Time-travel fiction and Time-travel comics. The parent is left for an insertion batch."],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-time-travel-comics","title":"Time-travel comics — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2019026008"},{"id":"wp-time-travel-in-fiction","title":"Time travel in fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_travel_in_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Time-travel fiction","description":"Fiction in which movement through time is possible and the story works out what follows. Wells's The Time Machine in 1895 fixed the device, and the tradition since has developed its own rule sets around paradox, fixed timelines and branching histories. The device is formal: it lets a plot fold back on itself in ways no other premise allows.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A device-defined family with worked-out internal rules that writers argue about; LCGFT files it under Science fiction.","sourceIds":["lcgft-time-travel-fiction","wp-time-travel-in-fiction"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"science-fiction","explanation":"LCGFT files Time-travel fiction under Science fiction; the mechanism is treated as a technology or a physical possibility.","sourceIds":["lcgft-time-travel-fiction","wp-time-travel-in-fiction"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-time-travel-fiction","title":"Time-travel fiction — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026573"},{"id":"wp-time-travel-in-fiction","title":"Time travel in fiction — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_travel_in_fiction"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Togatae","description":"Roman comedy set in Italy among Roman characters in the toga, as against the Greek-dress comedies. Afranius and Titus Quinctius Atta are the known writers, and only fragments survive. The change of setting is the whole claim: comedy about Romans, played in Roman clothes.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named Roman dramatic genre with known authors, a surviving fragmentary corpus and a defining formal contrast with its neighbour genre; LCGFT files it under Comedy plays.","sourceIds":["lcgft-togatae","wp-fabula-togata"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"comedy-plays","explanation":"LCGFT files Togatae under Comedy plays; they are Roman comedies distinguished by their setting and dress.","sourceIds":["lcgft-togatae","wp-fabula-togata"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-togatae","title":"Togatae — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2024026076"},{"id":"wp-fabula-togata","title":"Fabula togata — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabula_togata"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tonalism","description":"American landscape painting of roughly 1880 to 1915 held in a narrow band of closely related values. A single dominant hue carries the whole canvas, edges dissolve into atmosphere, and the subject is usually dusk, mist or a wooded interior rather than a described place.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named movement in painting with a documented body of work.","sourceIds":["wp-tonalism","aat-tonalism"]}],"broader":[],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-tonalism","title":"Tonalism — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonalism"},{"id":"aat-tonalism","title":"Tonalist — Getty AAT 300132908","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300132908"}],"manifestations":[{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019efb4b-df31-7181-b06a-d4679c052936","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Tonalism\" (Published).","sourceIds":["wp-tonalism"]},{"entitySet":"ArtStyles","entityId":"en-019eff61-648c-72c2-8237-d1661e642fdf","explanation":"The record's credits name \"James McNeill Whistler / Tonalism\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-tonalism"]},{"entitySet":"PaletteSystems","entityId":"en-019eff62-c74f-76c1-b8c4-5cb5e3db0c35","explanation":"The record's credits name \"Tonalism\" (UnderReview).","sourceIds":["wp-tonalism"]}],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tongue twisters","description":"Phrases built to be hard to say, from runs of similar consonants that the mouth keeps confusing. They are folk material, collected in every language, and they are used as a game and as speech training. The form has no content to speak of: the difficulty is the whole work.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A folk verbal form with a collected corpus in many languages and a stated compositional principle; LCGFT files it under Folk literature and Humor.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tongue-twisters","wp-tongue-twister"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"folk-literature","explanation":"LCGFT files Tongue twisters under Folk literature; they are anonymous and carried by speech.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tongue-twisters","wp-tongue-twister"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-tongue-twisters","title":"Tongue twisters — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026575"},{"id":"wp-tongue-twister","title":"Tongue twister — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue_twister"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Topeng plays","description":"Indonesian masked dance drama in which one or several performers take fabled kings, heroes and myths, accompanied by gamelan. In the Balinese solo form one dancer changes masks to become each character in turn. The mask sets both the character and the movement vocabulary that goes with it.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named masked performance tradition with its own repertoire, music and technique; LCGFT files it under Dance drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-topeng-plays","wp-topeng-dances"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"dance-drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Dance drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-topeng-plays"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-topeng-plays","title":"Topeng plays — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2016026039"},{"id":"wp-topeng-dances","title":"Topeng dances — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topeng_dances"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Topographical poetry","description":"Poems that describe and usually praise a particular place, moving from what is seen to what it prompts the poet to think. Denham's Cooper's Hill in 1642 established the English genre, which peaked in the eighteenth century and includes Pope's Windsor Forest and Wordsworth's Tintern Abbey. The place has to be a real and named one.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named genre with a founding poem, a dated peak and a stated structural movement from prospect to reflection; LCGFT files it directly under Poetry.","sourceIds":["lcgft-topographical-poetry","wp-topographical-poetry"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"poetry","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Poetry as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-topographical-poetry"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-topographical-poetry","title":"Topographical poetry — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2018026132"},{"id":"wp-topographical-poetry","title":"Topographical poetry — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographical_poetry"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tragedies (Drama)","description":"Drama in which suffering falls on a central figure and is followed to its end. It is the older of the two Greek dramatic kinds, and Aristotle's account of it in the Poetics has been argued with ever since, through Seneca, the Elizabethans, French neoclassicism and the modern reworkings that ask whether ordinary people can be tragic subjects. The form carries a theory with it, which is unusual.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A form root of drama with a continuous history and a poetics that is still disputed; LCGFT files Revenge tragedies, Heroic drama and Social tragedies under it.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tragedies-drama","wp-tragedy"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tragedies-drama"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-tragedies-drama","title":"Tragedies (Drama) — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026576"},{"id":"wp-tragedy","title":"Tragedy — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Tragicomedies","description":"Plays that mix the two kinds, either by lightening a tragic action or by letting a comic one carry real danger. Plautus used the word for Amphitryon, Guarini defended the mixture in the sixteenth century, and Shakespeare's late plays are read through it. The mixing is deliberate and was contested, which is what makes it a form and not an accident.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"writing","explanation":"A named form with a defended theory and a canon on both sides of the mixture; LCGFT files it directly under Drama.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tragicomedies","wp-tragicomedy"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"drama","explanation":"Its Library of Congress record gives Drama as a broader term.","sourceIds":["lcgft-tragicomedies"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"lcgft-tragicomedies","title":"Tragicomedies — Library of Congress Genre/Form Terms","url":"https://id.loc.gov/authorities/genreForms/gf2014026577"},{"id":"wp-tragicomedy","title":"Tragicomedy — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragicomedy"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Transavanguardia","description":"The Italian branch of Neo-Expressionism, named by the critic Achille Bonito Oliva around 1979, which returned to figuration, myth and quotation after Arte Povera's austerity. Chia, Clemente, Cucchi and Paladino are its painters. Its programme is an explicit refusal of the avant-garde's forward march.","provenance":{"basis":"cited"},"maps":[{"map":"art","explanation":"A named style or movement in the visual arts.","sourceIds":["wp-transavantgarde","wd-q224885","aat-300022218"]}],"broader":[{"cellId":"neo-expressionism","explanation":"Its own article opens by calling it the Italian version of Neo-Expressionism.","sourceIds":["wp-transavantgarde"]}],"relations":[],"questions":[],"sources":[{"id":"wp-transavantgarde","title":"Transavantgarde — Wikipedia","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transavantgarde"},{"id":"wd-q224885","title":"Transavantgarde (Q224885) — Wikidata","url":"https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q224885"},{"id":"aat-300022218","title":"Transavanguardia — Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus 300022218","url":"https://vocab.getty.edu/aat/300022218"}],"manifestations":[],"studies":[]}

{"version":3,"name":"Transit map","description":"The diagram of a transport network drawn for a rider.
